objects: The transpose of the constraint matrix. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 22
structure: Duality is transposition. Strong duality holds whenever either problem is feasible, and Farkas’ lemma — the theorem of the alternative — is the statement that either 𝐴x = b has a non-negative solution or 𝐴⊤y ≥0, b⊤y < 0 does, but never both. Column space versus null space.
reduction: The dual problem is built from 𝐴⊤.

title: Quadratic Programme
objects: 𝑃⪰0; the solution is a KKT linear solve.
structure: With equality constraints only, the solution comes from one symmetric indefinite system ( 𝑃𝐴⊤ 𝐴0 )( x 𝜈) = ( −q b ). Solvable when 𝑃is positive definite on ker 𝐴— a reduced-Hessian condition.
reduction: The problem becomes one block linear system. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 23

title: Second-Order Cone Constraint
objects: The Lorentz cone, a convex but non-polyhedral set.
structure: Generalises linear constraints (norm zero) and convex quadratic ones. Self-dual under the standard in- ner product, which makes primal–dual interior point methods symmetric. Robust LP with ellipsoidal uncertainty becomes an SOCP.
reduction: The constraint is a norm bound on an aﬀine map.
status: Exact linear in the aﬀine map.

title: Semidefinite Programme
objects: Optimisation over the positive semidefinite cone.
structure: The variable is a matrix and the constraint is a spectral one. Subsumes LP (diagonal 𝑋) and SOCP. Relaxations of hard combinatorial problems — Goemans–Williamson MaxCut, Lovász theta — are SDPs, and the relaxation quality is a rank-one versus general-rank gap.
reduction: Nothing to reduce; the variable is a matrix.
status: Exact linear (in the matrix inner product).

title: Simplex Method Reduced Cost
objects: 𝐵the basis matrix; 𝑁the non-basic columns.
structure: Each pivot is a rank-one update to 𝐵−1, applied by Sherman–Morrison or by updating an LU fac- torisation — which is why a simplex iteration costs 𝑂(𝑚2) rather than 𝑂(𝑚3). Optimality is ̄c𝑁≥0, a sign condition on a computed vector.
reduction: Each iteration is a rank-one basis update.

title: Interior Point Barrier
objects: The log barrier, whose Hessian is a weighted Gram matrix.
structure: ∇2𝜙= ∑𝑖 ∇𝑓𝑖∇𝑓⊤ 𝑖 𝑓2 𝑖 + ⋯— a sum of rank-one terms, hence positive semidefinite. Each Newton step is a linear solve, and the number of steps is 𝑂(√𝑚ln(1/𝜖)), independent of the problem’s combinatorial size.
reduction: Each step is a linear solve with a structured Hessian.

title: Central Path Condition
objects: A perturbed complementarity condition.
structure: The path is parametrised by 𝜇, with 𝜇→0 recovering exact complementarity. Newton’s method applied to this system gives the primal–dual interior point iteration — the reason LP is solvable in polynomial time in practice.
reduction: The path is a family of linear systems indexed by 𝜇.

title: Gradient Descent
objects: For quadratics, the iteration matrix 𝐼−𝛼𝐴.
structure: On 𝑓= 1 2x⊤𝐴x the error evolves as (𝐼−𝛼𝐴)𝑘e0, so convergence requires 𝜌(𝐼−𝛼𝐴) < 1, that is 0 < 𝛼< 2/𝜆max. Optimal 𝛼= 2/(𝜆min + 𝜆max), giving rate (𝜅−1)/(𝜅+ 1).
reduction: The method becomes a stationary linear iteration.

title: Gradient Descent Convergence Rate
objects: The Hessian condition number.
structure: Every first-order rate in optimisation is a function of 𝜅. Ill-conditioning means a long narrow valley — the gradient points across it rather than along it, so progress is slow. Preconditioning is the standard remedy, and it is exactly a change of metric.
reduction: The rate is a condition number.

title: Nesterov Accelerated Gradient
objects: A two-term recurrence, hence a 2𝑛× 2𝑛block iteration matrix.
structure: Rate improves from 𝜅to √𝜅— provably optimal for first-order methods. The mechanism is that the block iteration matrix has complex eigenvalues of smaller modulus than the real ones of plain gradient descent, achieved by the momentum coupling.
reduction: The method becomes a block linear iteration.

title: Heavy Ball Momentum
objects: Polyak momentum; also a block iteration.
structure: Optimal parameters give rate (√𝜅−1)/(√𝜅+ 1) on quadratics — matching Nesterov. But it can fail to converge on general strongly convex functions, whereas Nesterov does not; the block matrix analysis is valid only in the quadratic case.
reduction: The method becomes a block linear iteration.

title: Newton’s Method for Optimisation
objects: One linear solve per iteration with the Hessian.
structure: Aﬀine invariant — the iterates are unchanged under any linear reparametrisation, so the condition number of 𝑓is irrelevant. That invariance is why Newton converges quadratically regardless of scaling, and why it costs 𝑂(𝑛3) per step.
reduction: Each step is a linear solve.

title: Newton Decrement
objects: A quadratic form in the inverse Hessian.
structure: Estimates the suboptimality: 𝑓−𝑓∗≈𝜆2/2. Aﬀine invariant like Newton itself, which makes it the correct stopping criterion — unlike ‖∇𝑓‖, which changes under rescaling.
reduction: The criterion is a quadratic form.

title: BFGS Update
objects: A rank-two symmetric update preserving positive definiteness.
structure: Maintains 𝐵≻0 provided y⊤s > 0 (the curvature condition, enforced by Wolfe line search). The inverse update is also rank two by Sherman–Morrison, giving 𝑂(𝑛2) per step. L-BFGS stores only the last 𝑚 pairs, reducing memory to 𝑂(𝑚𝑛).
reduction: The update is a rank-two modification.

title: Wolfe Conditions
objects: Two inequalities on directional derivatives.
structure: Both are conditions on the scalar function 𝜙(𝛼) = 𝑓(x + 𝛼p), whose derivative is ∇𝑓⊤p — a linear functional of the gradient. The curvature condition is what guarantees y⊤s > 0 and hence BFGS positive definiteness.
reduction: The conditions are on directional derivatives, hence linear functionals.

title: Trust Region Subproblem
objects: A quadratic minimised over a ball.
structure: Solvable exactly despite possible indefiniteness of 𝐵: the solution satisfies (𝐵+𝜆𝐼)p = −g with 𝜆≥0 chosen so the norm constraint is active. This is a shifted linear solve, and the “hard case” occurs when g is orthogonal to the eigenvector of 𝜆min(𝐵).
reduction: The subproblem becomes a shifted linear system.

title: Gauss–Newton Approximation
objects: The Jacobian Gram matrix replacing the full Hessian.
structure: Drops the second-derivative residual term, which is small near a good fit. 𝐽⊤𝐽⪰0 automatically, so the step is always a descent direction. Costs 𝑂(𝑚𝑛2) instead of requiring second derivatives, but 𝜅(𝐽⊤𝐽) = 𝜅(𝐽)2.
reduction: The Hessian becomes a Gram matrix.

title: Levenberg–Marquardt
objects: A damped Gauss–Newton system.
structure: Interpolates between Gauss–Newton (𝜆→0) and gradient descent (𝜆→∞). The shift guarantees invertibility even for rank-deficient 𝐽and improves conditioning — identical in form to ridge regression, and to the trust region solve.
reduction: The step is a regularised linear solve.

title: Conjugate Gradient Direction
objects: 𝐴-orthogonal search directions.
structure: Conjugacy means the directions are orthogonal in the 𝐴-inner product, so each step is exact along its direction and never needs revisiting — hence termination in 𝑛steps. The nonlinear versions (Fletcher–Reeves, Polak–Ribière) extend the formula heuristically.
reduction: Conjugacy is orthogonality in a weighted inner product.
also_in: Numerical Analysis. Stochastic and Large-Scale Optimisation

title: Stochastic Gradient Descent
objects: An unbiased gradient estimate with covariance Σ𝑔.
structure: 𝔼[∇𝑓𝑖] = ∇𝑓, so the drift is the true gradient; the noise has covariance Σ𝑔, and the asymptotic error is governed by tr(𝐻−1Σ𝑔) — a matrix trace. Cost per step is 𝑂(1) in the data size, which is the whole point.
reduction: The noise structure becomes a covariance matrix.
status: Exact linear in the second-order analysis.

title: Robbins–Monro Step Size Conditions
objects: Divergent sum for reach, convergent square for noise suppression. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 41
structure: The first condition ensures the iterates can travel arbitrarily far; the second ensures accumulated noise variance ∑𝛼2 𝑘tr Σ𝑔stays finite. 𝛼𝑘= 𝑐/𝑘satisfies both.
reduction: The conditions balance drift against accumulated variance.

title: SGD Convergence Rate
objects: Rate governed by 𝜇= 𝜆min(𝐻) and the gradient noise. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 42
structure: Sublinear 𝑂(1/𝑘) rather than the linear rate of full gradient descent — the price of noise. Variance- reduced methods (SVRG, SAGA) recover linear convergence by controlling Σ𝑔directly.
reduction: The rate involves the Hessian’s smallest eigenvalue.

title: Adam Update
objects: A diagonal preconditioner estimated from squared gradients. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 43
structure: diag( ̂v)−1/2 approximates 𝐻−1/2 restricted to the diagonal — a cheap diagonal preconditioner. It captures per-coordinate scale but not correlation, which is why it helps with badly scaled problems and not with rotated ones.
reduction: The method is diagonally preconditioned SGD.

title: AdaGrad Update
objects: Accumulated squared gradients as a diagonal metric. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 44
structure: The full-matrix version uses 𝐺−1/2 with 𝐺= ∑𝑗g𝑗g⊤ 𝑗— a genuine matrix preconditioner, but 𝑂(𝑛2) storage and 𝑂(𝑛3) inversion. The diagonal approximation is what makes it practical. Learning rates decay monotonically, which eventually stalls progress.
reduction: The method is preconditioned descent with an accumulated Gram matrix.

title: Mirror Descent
objects: Descent in a non-Euclidean geometry set by 𝜓.
structure: With 𝜓= 1 2‖ ⋅‖2 it reduces to gradient descent; with 𝜓the negative entropy on the simplex it gives exponentiated gradient. Choosing 𝜓is choosing a metric — the same act as preconditioning, generalised beyond quadratic metrics. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 45
reduction: The method generalises preconditioned descent.

title: Bregman Divergence
objects: The gap above the tangent plane.
structure: For 𝜓= 1 2x⊤𝐴x it is exactly the Mahalanobis distance 1 2‖x −y‖2 𝐴; for negative entropy it is the KL divergence. Generally asymmetric and not a metric, but non-negative by convexity.
reduction: The divergence is a quadratic form for quadratic 𝜓.

title: ADMM Iteration
objects: Alternating minimisation with a linear consistency constraint.
structure: For quadratic subproblems each step is a linear solve, and the same factorisation is reused across iterations — the reason ADMM scales. Convergence is guaranteed for convex problems, at a modest linear rate depending on 𝜌and the constraint matrices.
reduction: Each subproblem is a linear solve.

title: Frank–Wolfe Step
objects: A linear minimisation oracle over the feasible set.
structure: Each step solves a linear programme over 𝐶, avoiding projection entirely — cheap when 𝐶is a simplex or a nuclear-norm ball, where the LMO is a single vertex or a top singular vector. Rate is 𝑂(1/𝑘), and the iterates are sparse combinations of vertices.
reduction: Each step is a linear minimisation.

title: Projected Gradient Descent
objects: 𝑃𝐶the Euclidean projection.
structure: When 𝐶is an aﬀine subspace {𝐴x = b}, 𝑃𝐶is an aﬀine map with the projection matrix 𝐼−𝐴+𝐴— literally a matrix multiply. For a ball or box the projection is a cheap componentwise operation.
reduction: Projection is a matrix for subspace constraints.

title: Coordinate Descent Update
objects: For quadratics, 𝑥+ 𝑖= (𝑏𝑖−∑𝑗≠𝑖𝐴𝑖𝑗𝑥𝑗)/𝐴𝑖𝑖.
structure: This is exactly one Gauss–Seidel sweep. Convergence requires 𝐴positive definite; the rate depends on the diagonal dominance and the eigenvalue distribution. For separable regularisers such as ℓ1 the update remains closed-form, which is why coordinate descent dominates Lasso solvers.
reduction: The method is Gauss–Seidel iteration.

title: Dual Ascent
objects: Gradient ascent on the concave dual.
structure: The dual gradient is the constraint residual. For a quadratic primal the dual Hessian is −𝐴𝐻−1𝐴⊤, so the dual condition number involves both 𝐻and 𝐴— which is why poorly scaled constraints slow dual methods even when the primal is well conditioned.
reduction: The dual gradient is a linear residual.

title: Simulated Annealing Acceptance
objects: A Metropolis chain with temperature-dependent transition matrix.
structure: Each temperature defines a stochastic matrix 𝑃𝑇whose stationary distribution is the Boltzmann distribution. As 𝑇→0 the stationary mass concentrates on the global optimum, but the spectral gap of 𝑃𝑇 shrinks exponentially — which is why the required cooling schedule is logarithmic and impractical.
reduction: The algorithm is a family of stochastic matrices.

title: Branch and Bound Pruning
objects: Bounds from LP relaxations, which are linear solves.
structure: Each node solves an LP — pure linear algebra — but the tree search is combinatorial and worst-case exponential. The method is linear algebra inside an exponential envelope.
reduction: Each node is a linear programme.
status: Exact linear per node; the search is not.

title: Cutting Plane (Gomory Cut)
objects: A valid inequality derived from a tableau row.
structure: Generated by rounding a row of 𝐵−1𝐴— the cut is a linear inequality manufactured from the simplex tableau. Adding it tightens the polyhedron without excluding integer points. The floor operation is the only non-linear step.
reduction: Cuts are linear inequalities from a matrix row.
status: Exact linear apart from the rounding.

title: Integrality Gap
objects: The ratio between an integer optimum and its relaxation.
structure: The gap is 1 exactly when the constraint matrix is totally unimodular, since then the LP polytope has integral vertices — König’s and Hall’s theorems are instances. Total unimodularity is a determinant condition: every square submatrix has determinant in {0, ±1}.
reduction: Integrality becomes a determinant condition on submatrices.

title: Submodularity
objects: Diminishing returns on a set function.
structure: The discrete analogue of concavity. The Lovász extension is convex, so submodular minimisation is polynomial-time — a genuine bridge to convex optimisation. Log-determinant ln det(𝐼+ Σ𝑆) is submodular, which is why determinantal point processes and D-optimal design have greedy guarantees.
reduction: Submodularity becomes convexity of the Lovász extension.

title: Greedy Approximation Guarantee
objects: A guarantee for monotone submodular maximisation.
structure: The bound 1 −1/𝑒≈0.632 is optimal unless P = NP. For log-determinant objectives — sensor placement, experimental design — the greedy step is a rank-one update to a Cholesky factor, so each iteration is 𝑂(𝑛2).
reduction: Each greedy step is a rank-one update for determinantal objectives.

title: No Free Lunch Theorem
objects: An averaging argument over a uniform distribution on functions.
structure: A counting statement over function space with no linear content. Its practical force is limited: real objectives are not uniformly distributed, and structure (convexity, smoothness, low effective rank) is exactly what algorithms exploit.
reduction: Not available.

title: Minimax and Robust Optimisation
objects: An uncertainty set, often an ellipsoid {u ∶u⊤𝑃u ≤1}.
structure: With an ellipsoidal uncertainty set the inner maximisation has a closed form, max a⊤u = ‖𝑃−1/2a‖, converting the robust LP into an SOCP. Robustness costs one norm term, and the geometry of 𝒰determines the resulting problem class.
reduction: The inner problem becomes a norm of a transformed vector.

title: Expected Utility
objects: p the state probability vector; 𝑈the state-by-action payoff matrix.
structure: Expected utility is a bilinear form — linear in probabilities and linear in payoffs. The optimal action is arg max𝑎(𝑈⊤p)𝑎, a single matrix–vector product followed by a maximum. Everything else in normative decision theory is a corollary of this bilinearity.
reduction: The criterion is a matrix–vector product.

title: Von Neumann–Morgenstern Axioms
objects: Axioms forcing preferences to be represented by a linear functional.
structure: The independence axiom is the one doing the work — it requires preference to be preserved under mixing, which is exactly aﬀinity in the probability vector. The representation theorem says preferences satisfying the axioms are represented by p⊤u, unique up to positive aﬀine transformation of u.
reduction: The axioms characterise linear functionals on the simplex.
status: Exact linear. The axioms exist to guarantee linearity.

title: Savage Subjective Expected Utility
objects: Subjective probabilities derived from preference rather than given.
structure: The sure-thing principle plays the role of independence, forcing the representation to be linear in 𝜋. Both the probability vector and the utility vector are recovered from the preference ordering — the representation is a factorisation of preferences into a bilinear form.
reduction: Preferences factor into a bilinear form.

title: Arrow–Pratt Absolute Risk Aversion
objects: A curvature-to-slope ratio; the scalar case of −∇2𝑢(∇𝑢) −1.
structure: Invariant under positive aﬀine transformations of 𝑢, which is why it is the right measure. In the multivariate case the analogue is the matrix −(∇2𝑢)(∇𝑢) +, whose eigenvalues give direction-dependent risk aversion.
reduction: Risk aversion becomes a normalised Hessian.

title: Relative Risk Aversion
objects: Wealth-scaled curvature.
structure: Constant 𝑅characterises the CRRA family, which is exactly the family invariant under wealth scaling — a homogeneity condition. Scale invariance forces the power form, just as it forces power laws elsewhere in the compendium.
reduction: The measure is a scaled Hessian ratio.

title: CRRA Utility
objects: The unique utility with constant relative risk aversion.
structure: Its functional form is forced by the scale-invariance ODE −𝑤𝑢″/𝑢′ = 𝛾. Under lognormal returns the certainty equivalent has a closed form involving 𝜇−1 2𝛾𝜎2 — a mean minus a scaled variance, hence a linear-quadratic criterion.
reduction: Under lognormality the criterion becomes mean minus scaled variance.

title: CARA (Exponential) Utility
objects: Constant absolute risk aversion.
structure: With Gaussian outcomes the certainty equivalent is exactly 𝜇−𝛼 2 𝜎2 — a linear functional minus a quadratic form, with no approximation. This exact mean–variance reduction is why CARA plus Gaussian is the standard tractable pairing in finance and contract theory.
reduction: Under Gaussian outcomes the criterion is exactly mean–variance.

title: Certainty Equivalent
objects: Inversion of a scalar function applied to a linear functional.
structure: CE = 𝑢−1(p⊤u) — the expectation is linear, the inversion is not. All the nonlinearity of risk preference sits in 𝑢−1; the probabilistic part is a dot product.
reduction: Linear inside, nonlinear outside.

title: Risk Premium (Pratt Approximation)
objects: A second-order Taylor approximation.
structure: The multivariate version is 𝜋≈1 2 tr(𝐴Σ) for the risk-aversion matrix 𝐴— a trace of a matrix product, exactly the same form as the Itô correction. Second-order risk is a trace.
reduction: The premium becomes a trace of a matrix product.

title: Mean–Variance Preference
objects: A linear term minus a quadratic form.
structure: Maximised at w∗= 1 𝛾Σ−1𝜇— a single linear solve. This is the Markowitz portfolio, and the fact that the optimum is one matrix inverse applied to one vector is why mean–variance analysis dominates practice.
reduction: Optimisation becomes a linear solve.

title: Stochastic Dominance (First Order)
objects: A pointwise inequality between cumulative vectors.
structure: 𝑆p𝐴≤𝑆p𝐵componentwise, with 𝑆the cumulative-sum matrix. FSD implies preference for every increasing utility — a statement about a whole cone of linear functionals, hence a dual cone condition.
reduction: Dominance becomes a componentwise inequality after applying 𝑆.

title: Stochastic Dominance (Second Order)
objects: Double cumulative sums, 𝑆2p.
structure: SSD implies preference for every increasing concave utility. Applying 𝑆twice is the discrete double integral, so the hierarchy FSD ⊂SSD ⊂⋯corresponds to increasing powers of the cumulative-sum matrix — each level tests a smaller cone of utilities.
reduction: Higher-order dominance is higher powers of 𝑆.

title: Bayes Risk
objects: 𝐿the loss matrix; 𝛿the (possibly randomised) decision vector.
structure: Bilinear in prior and decision rule — the same structure as a zero-sum game payoff. Minimising over 𝛿for fixed 𝜋is a linear programme; the minimax version is the game value. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 14
reduction: Risk is a bilinear form.

title: Bayes Decision Rule
objects: arg min of 𝐿⊤ppost.
structure: One matrix–vector product per observation, followed by a minimum. The rule is deterministic and lies at a vertex of the decision simplex, since a linear function on a simplex attains its extremum at a vertex.
reduction: The rule is a matrix–vector product plus an argmin. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 15

title: Zero-One Loss and MAP
objects: The loss matrix is all-ones minus the identity.
structure: 𝐿⊤p = 1 −p, so minimising the expected loss is maximising the posterior. The all-ones matrix is rank one, which is exactly why the rule collapses to a simple argmax.
reduction: The special loss matrix reduces the rule to an argmax.

title: Minimax Decision Rule
objects: The value of a zero-sum game with payoff matrix 𝐿.
structure: By the minimax theorem this equals max𝜋min𝛿𝜋⊤𝐿𝛿, computable as a linear programme. The least favourable prior is the dual solution — nature’s optimal mixed strategy.
reduction: The rule is the solution of an LP.

title: Minimax Regret (Savage)
objects: A rank-one row-shift of the loss matrix.
structure: The regret matrix is 𝐿minus a rank-one correction 1m⊤where m holds column maxima. Minimax on 𝑅differs from minimax on 𝐿precisely because the shift is rank one and column-dependent, so it does not cancel.
reduction: Regret is a rank-one modification of the loss matrix.

title: Hurwicz Criterion
objects: A convex combination of row extremes.
structure: Interpolates between maximax (𝛼= 1) and maximin (𝛼= 0). Uses only two entries per row, discarding all intermediate information — a rank-2-like reduction of each row to its extremes, which is why it violates several consistency axioms.
reduction: The criterion is a convex combination of row extremes.

title: Laplace Criterion (Insuﬀicient Reason)
objects: The uniform prior applied to the loss matrix.
structure: Bayes risk with 𝜋= 1/𝑛— a row average, so the criterion is 𝐿1/𝑛. Not invariant under how the state space is partitioned, which is exactly the objection to the principle of insuﬀicient reason.
reduction: The criterion is a uniform-prior matrix product.

title: Admissibility
objects: Pareto optimality in the risk vector space.
structure: Admissible rules are the Pareto frontier of the achievable risk set, which is a convex polytope (the image of the decision simplex under 𝐿⊤). Admissibility is a face-of-a-polytope condition.
reduction: Admissibility becomes Pareto optimality on a polytope.

title: Complete Class Theorem
objects: Supporting hyperplanes of the risk set.
structure: Every point on the lower boundary of a convex set supports a hyperplane, whose normal is a prior. So every admissible rule is Bayes for some prior — the supporting hyperplane theorem applied to the risk polytope. This is the deepest structural result in the chapter and it is pure convex geometry.
reduction: The theorem is hyperplane separation on the risk set.

title: Expected Value of Sample Information
objects: A Jensen gap for the max functional over posterior distributions.
structure: Non-negative because max is convex and the posterior-averaging is linear. Information is valuable exactly to the extent that max and expectation fail to commute — the same mechanism as EVPI.
reduction: The value is a Jensen gap.

title: Value of Information Bound
objects: Monotonicity under coarsening of information.
structure: A garbling of a signal is multiplication of the likelihood matrix by a stochastic matrix (Blackwell’s theo- rem), and post-processing cannot increase value — the decision-theoretic data processing inequality. Information ordering is a matrix factorisation order.
reduction: Information degradation is multiplication by a stochastic matrix.
also_in: Information Theory. Sequential Decisions and Search

title: Dynamic Programming Value Recursion
objects: Stochastic matrices with a maximisation over actions.
structure: For a fixed policy the recursion is exactly V𝑡= r + 𝑃V𝑡+1, a backward linear iteration. The max over actions is the only nonlinearity, and it is what makes the operator piecewise linear rather than linear.
reduction: Policy evaluation is a linear recursion.

title: Optimal Stopping Condition
objects: Comparison of a vector against 𝑃V.
structure: The continuation region is {𝑠∶r < 𝑃V} — determined by a componentwise inequality between two vectors. On the continuation set, V solves a linear system restricted to those states.
reduction: The rule is a componentwise comparison; V solves a linear system.

title: Secretary Problem Threshold
objects: A combinatorial optimisation over cutoff rules.
structure: The success probability 𝑘 𝑛∑𝑗≥𝑘 1 𝑗−1 is maximised by calculus, not by any matrix computation. The problem’s structure is order-based, which no linear algebra captures.
reduction: Not available.

title: Gittins Index
objects: A ratio of two linear functionals, computed per arm.
structure: The index theorem decomposes an exponentially large multi-armed problem into independent per-arm computations — a decoupling exactly analogous to diagonalisation. Each index is a ratio of discounted-occupancy functionals, so each arm’s computation is a linear solve.
reduction: The index is a ratio of linear functionals; the theorem is a decoupling.

title: Upper Confidence Bound
objects: A mean plus a confidence radius.
structure: In the linear bandit setting the natural generalisation is x⊤̂𝜃+ 𝛽 √ x⊤𝑉−1x with 𝑉= ∑𝑡x𝑡x⊤ 𝑡— the confidence width is a quadratic form in the inverse design matrix, exactly as in experimental design.
reduction: The bonus becomes a quadratic form in the inverse Gram matrix.

title: Regret
objects: A cumulative difference of linear functionals.
structure: In the linear bandit case, regret is ∑𝑡x∗⊤𝜃−x⊤ 𝑡𝜃, and bounding it reduces to bounding ∑𝑡‖x𝑡‖𝑉−1 — an elliptical potential argument on the design matrix’s log-determinant.
reduction: Regret analysis becomes a log-determinant potential argument.

title: Lai–Robbins Lower Bound
objects: A KL divergence in the denominator. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 30
structure: The bound is information-theoretic, derived from a change-of-measure argument. For Gaussian arms KL = Δ2/2𝜎2, so the bound is a ratio of a linear gap to a quadratic distinguishability — a Mahalanobis-type quantity.
reduction: Gaussian case becomes a quadratic form.

title: Thompson Sampling Rule
objects: Posterior sampling; for Gaussian models a multivariate normal draw.
structure: With a Gaussian prior and linear rewards, the posterior is 𝑁(𝑉−1b, 𝜎2𝑉−1) and sampling is ̂𝜃+ 𝜎𝐿z with 𝐿the Cholesky factor. The entire algorithm is a sequence of rank-one updates and Cholesky draws.
reduction: Sampling becomes a Cholesky-factored Gaussian draw.
status: Exact linear for linear-Gaussian models. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 31

title: Exploration–Exploitation Trade-Off
objects: A scaling relation, not a matrix statement.
structure: For linear bandits the rate is 𝑂(𝑑 √ 𝑇) with 𝑑the parameter dimension — the trade-off scales with a dimension, which is a rank. Beyond that the statement is asymptotic rather than algebraic.
reduction: The dimension dependence is a rank.

title: Sequential Probability Ratio Test
objects: A random walk in ln Λ with drift given by a KL divergence.
structure: ln Λ𝑛is a sum of iid increments, so it is a random walk — a linear accumulation. Optimality (Wald– Wolfowitz) says it minimises expected sample size among all tests of given error rates.
reduction: The log-likelihood ratio accumulates linearly.

title: Wald’s Identity
objects: A stopping-time version of linearity of expectation.
structure: Valid for stopping times, so it extends linearity of expectation past a random horizon. It is the optional stopping theorem applied to the martingale ∑𝑋𝑖−𝑛𝜇, and gives the SPRT’s expected sample size directly.
reduction: The identity is linearity of expectation with a random index.

title: Arrow’s Impossibility Theorem
objects: None. Preference orderings are not vectors.
structure: Aggregating ordinal rankings has no linear structure — orderings do not form a vector space and there is no metric to average. Cardinal utilities can be averaged linearly, which is exactly the loophole: Arrow’s theorem is about the ordinal setting, and range voting escapes it by using cardinal information.
reduction: Not available for ordinal preferences.
status: No faithful linear form. The obstruction is precisely the absence of one.

title: Gibbard–Satterthwaite Theorem
objects: None linear.
structure: Strategy-proofness for ordinal rules over three or more alternatives forces dictatorship. As with Arrow, the impossibility stems from the ordinal setting; with money and quasi-linear utility, VCG mechanisms are strategy-proof — and quasi-linearity is exactly a linearity assumption.
reduction: Not available; the escape route is assuming linearity in money.

title: Condorcet Winner
objects: The pairwise majority matrix 𝑀with 𝑀𝑖𝑗the margin of 𝑖over 𝑗.
structure: 𝑀is skew-symmetric, so its spectrum is purely imaginary and it has even rank. A Condorcet winner is a row with all positive entries; cycles are the reason such a row may not exist, and the cycle space is exactly ker of the associated boundary operator — a Hodge decomposition of the ranking (HodgeRank).
reduction: Pairwise preferences become a skew-symmetric matrix.

title: Condorcet Jury Theorem
objects: A binomial tail; a linear functional of the vote-count distribution.
structure: 𝑃𝑛= w⊤pbin with w the majority indicator. Correlated voters break the result — the effective number of independent voters is 𝑛2/(1⊤𝑅1) for the correlation matrix 𝑅, so correlation is a quadratic form penalty.
reduction: The probability is a dot product; correlation enters as a quadratic form.

title: Borda Count
objects: A weighted sum of rank positions — a matrix–vector product.
structure: Cardinalises the ordinal input by assigning scores, which is precisely how it escapes Arrow’s framework, at the cost of violating IIA. Borda is the projection of the pairwise margin matrix onto the gradient (consistent) component in the HodgeRank decomposition.
reduction: The count is a linear score aggregation.

title: Shapley Value
objects: A linear functional of the characteristic function vector.
structure: Linear in 𝑣— the unique value satisfying eﬀiciency, symmetry, linearity, and the null player axiom. As a map from ℝ2𝑛to ℝ𝑛it is an explicit matrix, though of exponential size. Linearity is one of its defining axioms.
reduction: The value is a linear map on the game space.

title: Nash Bargaining Solution
objects: A product, hence a sum of logs.
structure: Maximising the Nash product is maximising ∑𝑖ln(𝑢𝑖−𝑑𝑖), a concave programme whose first-order condition is ∑𝑖 ∇𝑢𝑖 𝑢𝑖−𝑑𝑖= 0. The solution is where a hyperplane supports the bargaining set — the tangency condition equalises scaled marginal utilities.
reduction: The solution is a supporting hyperplane tangency.
status: Exact linear at the optimality condition.

title: Prospect Theory Value Function
objects: A kinked, reference-dependent value function.
structure: Nonlinear and non-differentiable at the reference point, with 𝜆≈2.25 giving loss aversion. The kink means no single Hessian exists at zero — the second-order machinery of expected utility does not apply.
reduction: Not available at the kink.

title: Probability Weighting Function
objects: A nonlinear map on the probability simplex.
structure: This is the decisive break with expected utility: weighting probabilities nonlinearly destroys the bilinear form p⊤u. Since 𝑤does not preserve convex combinations, the independence axiom fails — and with it, everything downstream.
reduction: Not available; nonlinearity in p is the point.
status: No faithful linear form. This entry is why the chapter’s later half resists.

title: Cumulative Prospect Theory Valuation
objects: Decision weights from differences of a weighted CDF.
structure: 𝜋= 𝑆−1𝑤(𝑆p) — cumulative sum, nonlinear map, then difference. The rank-dependent construction restores stochastic dominance, which the original prospect theory violated, but the composition remains nonlinear.
reduction: Linear sandwich around a nonlinear core.

title: Allais Paradox Inequality
objects: An empirical demonstration that preferences are not linear in p.
structure: The paradox is exactly a failure of the bilinear representation: two lotteries differing by a common consequence are ranked inconsistently, which cannot happen if preference is p⊤u. It is a proof that no utility vector fits the data.
reduction: The paradox demonstrates that no linear functional represents the preferences.
status: No faithful linear form, and that is the finding.

title: Ellsberg Paradox (Ambiguity Aversion)
objects: Non-existence of a probability vector. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 45
structure: The choices are inconsistent with any point in the simplex, so no single 𝜋exists. Resolutions replace the point with a convex set of priors, turning the criterion from a linear functional into a support function of a set.
reduction: A point becomes a convex set.
status: No faithful linear form with a single prior.

title: Maxmin Expected Utility (Gilboa–Schmeidler)
objects: A support function of a convex set of priors.
structure: Linear in u for each fixed prior, but the minimisation makes 𝑉concave rather than linear in u. It is the support function of 𝒞— piecewise linear when 𝒞is a polytope, and computable by an LP.
reduction: The criterion becomes a support function.
status: Exact linear per prior; concave overall. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 46

title: Choquet Expected Utility
objects: A capacity, which fails additivity.
structure: Non-additivity is exactly the failure of linearity: 𝜈(𝐴∪𝐵) ≠𝜈(𝐴) + 𝜈(𝐵) for disjoint sets. For convex capacities the Choquet integral equals the maxmin criterion over the core, recovering a support-function representation.
reduction: Available only for convex capacities, via the core.
status: No faithful linear form in general.

title: Hyperbolic Discounting
objects: A discount function that is not multiplicative in time.
structure: 𝐷(𝑠+ 𝑡) ≠𝐷(𝑠)𝐷(𝑡), so there is no semigroup structure — hence no generator matrix and no matrix exponential. Time inconsistency is the failure of the semigroup property, which is precisely what exponential discounting has.
reduction: Not available; the semigroup property fails.

title: Quasi-Hyperbolic (Beta-Delta) Discounting
objects: Exponential discounting with a one-off present-bias factor.
structure: For 𝑡≥1 it is a clean geometric sequence, so the future is time-consistent; the inconsistency is confined to the 𝛽jump at 𝑡= 0. That single rank-one-like modification is what produces procrastination.
reduction: Linear apart from a single multiplicative jump.

title: Exponential Discounting
objects: The unique time-consistent discount function.
structure: 𝐷(𝑠+ 𝑡) = 𝐷(𝑠)𝐷(𝑡) is the semigroup property, so the value operator is 𝛾𝑃and the value function is (𝐼−𝛾𝑃)−1r — a single linear solve. Time consistency and the existence of a matrix representation are the same fact.
reduction: Discounting becomes a scalar multiple of the transition matrix.

title: Drift Diffusion Model
objects: A first-passage problem for a linear SDE.
structure: The evidence accumulates linearly, so the process is Brownian motion with drift and the decision times follow an inverse Gaussian distribution. Accuracy is 1/(1 + 𝑒−2𝑣𝑎/𝜎2) — a logistic function of a signal-to-noise ratio.
reduction: Evidence accumulation is linear; the boundary is not.

title: Luce Choice Axiom
objects: Normalised value vector; independence from irrelevant alternatives.
structure: Ratios of choice probabilities depend only on the two options — a rank-one-like structure. The blue bus / red bus paradox is a violation, showing that IIA fails when options are correlated, which nested and mixed logit models fix by adding covariance structure.
reduction: Choice probabilities are a normalised value vector.

title: Softmax (Logit) Choice
objects: Exponentiate a linear score, then normalise.
structure: The score 𝑣𝑖= x⊤ 𝑖𝜃is exactly linear; the softmax is a fixed nonlinearity. Its Jacobian is diag(p) −pp⊤ — a rank-deficient positive semidefinite matrix, singular because probabilities sum to one.
reduction: Linear scores passed through a fixed nonlinearity.

title: Random Utility Model
objects: A linear systematic component plus a random term.
structure: Gumbel errors give logit; Gaussian errors give probit with correlation matrix Σ. The systematic part is exactly a linear predictor, and estimation is maximum likelihood with an IRLS inner loop.
reduction: Utility is linear in the covariates.
status: Exact linear in the systematic component.

title: Multi-Attribute Utility (Additive)
objects: A weighted sum of attribute utilities.
structure: Additivity requires mutual preferential independence — the condition under which the utility function decomposes as a sum. This is exactly the rank-one condition of field 13 applied to preferences: no interaction terms means no off-diagonal structure.
reduction: Aggregation is a dot product.

title: Entropy of a Decision Problem
objects: A concave functional of the probability vector.
structure: Concave, maximised by the uniform vector. Not linear, but its gradient −ln p −1 is what appears in every first-order condition of entropy-regularised decision problems, producing softmax solutions.
reduction: The gradient is what enters the linear optimality conditions.

title: Rational Inattention Objective
objects: A linear payoff term minus a mutual information cost.
structure: The solution is a softmax over actions with the prior as the default — entropy regularisation of a linear objective produces exponential weights, the same mechanism as in mirror descent and Gibbs measures. The information cost is a function of the joint distribution matrix.
reduction: Linear payoff plus an entropy penalty gives a softmax.

title: Satisficing Threshold
objects: A stopping rule with a fixed aspiration level.
structure: An optimal-stopping problem with a constant threshold; the value of the threshold solves a scalar fixed-point equation. The rule is a componentwise comparison, so it is linear in structure but the search order is combinatorial.
reduction: The rule is a componentwise threshold.

title: Regret Matching
objects: Normalised positive part of the cumulative regret vector.
structure: The regret vector accumulates linearly; the update is a normalised rectification. Guarantees conver- gence of the empirical play to the set of correlated equilibria — and that set is a polytope defined by linear inequalities.
reduction: Regret accumulates linearly; the equilibrium set is a polytope.

title: Normal Form Game
objects: For two players, a pair of payoff matrices 𝐴, 𝐵∈ℝ𝑚×𝑛.
structure: A finite two-player game is exactly two matrices. For 𝑛players the payoffs are order-𝑛tensors, so multiplayer games leave matrix algebra for tensor algebra — which is one reason they are harder.
reduction: The game is a payoff matrix (or tensor).

title: Best Response Correspondence
objects: Maximisation of a linear functional over the simplex.
structure: Since the objective is linear in x, the maximum is attained at a vertex — a pure strategy — unless there are ties, in which case the best-response set is the face spanned by the tied vertices. Mixed best responses exist only at indifference.
reduction: Best response is linear maximisation over a simplex.

title: Nash Equilibrium
objects: A pair of probability vectors satisfying simultaneous linear inequalities.
structure: The conditions are linear in each player’s strategy separately but coupled bilinearly — that coupling is what prevents equilibrium from being a linear programme in general. Zero-sum games (𝐵= −𝐴) are the case where the coupling collapses and LP suﬀices.
reduction: Equilibrium is a bilinear complementarity condition.
status: Exact linear for zero-sum; bilinear otherwise.

title: Nash Existence Theorem
objects: A fixed point of the best-response correspondence on a product of simplices.
structure: Proved by Kakutani’s fixed-point theorem, which is topological rather than algebraic. Existence is not a rank or spectral fact — this is the entry where the field departs from linear algebra, even though everything on either side of it is matrix-based.
reduction: Not available; the proof is topological.

title: Mixed Strategy Payoff
objects: The bilinear form defining the game.
structure: Linear in each argument separately, which is the entire reason mixed strategies work: the payoff to a mixture is the mixture of payoffs. Multilinearity is what makes the indifference conditions and the equilibrium characterisation possible.
reduction: The payoff is a bilinear form.

title: Indifference Condition
objects: A linear system on the support of the equilibrium strategy.
structure: Given the support, the equilibrium solves a square linear system: 𝐴y = 𝑣1 restricted to the support, plus 1⊤y = 1. So equilibrium computation reduces to guessing the support and solving — which is why the problem is combinatorial in the support rather than in the numbers.
reduction: Given a support, equilibrium is a linear solve.

title: Strict Dominance
objects: A row dominating another over the whole simplex. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 8
structure: Row 𝑖strictly dominates row 𝑗exactly when a𝑖> a𝑗componentwise. Domination by a mixed strategy is an LP feasibility question — whether ∃p ≥0 with 𝐴⊤p > a𝑗— so dominance testing is linear programming.
reduction: Dominance testing is LP feasibility.

title: Rationalisability
objects: Repeated LP feasibility tests shrinking the strategy sets.
structure: Each round removes rows and columns that are never best responses, detected by an LP. The order of elimination does not matter for strict dominance, which is a confluence property. The surviving set is the rationalisable set. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 9
reduction: Elimination is a sequence of LP tests.

title: Minimax Theorem
objects: Equality of two optimisation orders for a bilinear form.
structure: Exactly LP strong duality — the max problem and the min problem are dual linear programmes, and the theorem is that their optima coincide. Von Neumann’s theorem and LP duality were later recognised as the same result.
reduction: The theorem is LP duality.

title: Zero-Sum Game LP
objects: A linear programme whose optimum is the game value.
structure: Solvable in polynomial time, which puts zero-sum equilibrium in P — in sharp contrast to general-sum games. The dual LP gives the opponent’s optimal strategy, so both players’ strategies come from one primal–dual solve.
reduction: The game is a linear programme.

title: Correlated Equilibrium
objects: A joint distribution satisfying linear inequalities.
structure: The constraints are linear in the joint distribution, so the set of correlated equilibria is a polytope — computable by linear programming in polynomial time. Nash equilibria are the rank-one (product) points of that polytope, and it is exactly the rank-one restriction that makes Nash hard.
reduction: Correlated equilibrium is a polytope; Nash is its rank-one subset.
status: Exact linear. The cleanest illustration in the field of why Nash is hard.

title: Price of Anarchy
objects: A ratio of two optimisation values.
structure: For aﬀine congestion games PoA = 4/3, proved by a smoothness argument that is essentially a quadratic inequality on the cost vectors. The bound is a statement about a quadratic form dominating a bilinear one.
reduction: Smoothness arguments are quadratic inequalities.

title: Braess’s Paradox
objects: A flow problem where the equilibrium and optimum differ.
structure: Equilibrium flow minimises ∑𝑒∫ 𝑓𝑒 0 𝑐𝑒while the social optimum minimises ∑𝑒𝑓𝑒𝑐𝑒(𝑓𝑒) — two different convex objectives over the same flow polytope. The paradox is that enlarging the feasible set can worsen the first while the second improves.
reduction: Both are convex programmes on a flow polytope.
status: Exact linear in the constraint set.

title: Potential Game
objects: A single scalar function whose differences reproduce all payoff differences.
structure: Existence of Φ is an exactness condition: the payoff-difference field must be curl-free. In the Hodge decomposition of games, potential games are the gradient component and zero-sum games the harmonic one — every game decomposes uniquely into the two plus a nonstrategic part.
reduction: Potential existence is a curl-free condition.

title: Congestion Game Cost
objects: Costs depending only on the load vector n = 𝑀s.
structure: Every congestion game is a potential game with Φ = ∑𝑒∑𝑘≤𝑛𝑒𝑐𝑒(𝑘) (Rosenthal), so pure Nash equilibria always exist and better-response dynamics converge. The load is a linear function of the strategy profile.
reduction: Load is a linear map of the profile.

title: Extensive Form Game
objects: A tree; the sequence form linearises it.
structure: The naive conversion to normal form is exponential, but the sequence form represents behavioural strategies by realisation plans satisfying linear flow constraints — reducing the size to linear in the tree. Zero-sum extensive games then solve as LPs of polynomial size.
reduction: The sequence form makes the tree a linear constraint system.
status: Exact linear via the sequence form.

title: Backward Induction
objects: A dynamic programming recursion on the tree.
structure: Each step is a maximisation over a finite set, evaluated bottom-up in 𝑂(|𝑉|). For perfect-information games the result is unique generically. It is the same tropical recursion as shortest path, run on a game tree.
reduction: The recursion is a tropical (max-plus) evaluation.
status: Exact linear over the tropical semiring.

title: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
objects: A refinement eliminating non-credible threats.
structure: Imposes Nash conditions on every subtree, which in sequence form is a set of additional linear con- straints. Refinement is intersection with more half-spaces — the equilibrium set shrinks to a face.
reduction: The refinement adds linear constraints.
status: Exact linear in the sequence form.

title: Stackelberg Equilibrium
objects: A bilevel optimisation.
structure: Bilevel problems are non-convex in general, but for zero-sum games the Stackelberg and Nash values coincide by the minimax theorem. Computing an optimal mixed Stackelberg strategy in a general game is a set of LPs — one per follower best-response region.
reduction: Multiple LPs, one per follower response region.

title: Cournot Equilibrium
objects: With linear demand, a linear system in the quantity vector.
structure: Linear inverse demand 𝑃= 𝑎−𝑏𝑄gives first-order conditions 𝑎−𝑏(𝑄+ 𝑞𝑖) −𝑐= 0, that is (𝐼+ 11⊤)𝑏q = (𝑎−𝑐)1 — an identity-plus-rank-one system, invertible by Sherman–Morrison in closed form.
reduction: Equilibrium becomes a rank-one-updated linear solve.

title: Bertrand Paradox
objects: A discontinuous best-response correspondence.
structure: The demand function jumps at price ties, so the best response is discontinuous and no interior fixed point exists — equilibrium is at the boundary 𝑝= 𝑐. Discontinuity is what breaks the smooth first-order analysis available in Cournot.
reduction: Not available; the discontinuity is essential.

title: Hotelling Location Equilibrium
objects: A spatial competition model on an interval. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 22
structure: With fixed prices, minimal differentiation is the equilibrium — the median voter result. With en- dogenous prices no pure equilibrium exists in the linear-cost case (d’Aspremont), because the profit function is discontinuous. Linear structure holds only in the fixed-price version.
reduction: Linear only in the fixed-price case.

title: Rubinstein Alternating Offers
objects: Solution of a two-equation linear system in the two continuation values.
structure: Stationarity gives 𝑥= 1 −𝛿2𝑦and 𝑦= 1 −𝛿1𝑥, a 2 × 2 linear system whose unique solution is the equilibrium split. The unique subgame perfect equilibrium is one matrix inverse. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 23
reduction: Equilibrium is a 2 × 2 linear solve.

title: War of Attrition Equilibrium
objects: A mixed equilibrium in continuous time.
structure: The indifference condition — expected payoff constant across all stopping times — is a functional equation whose solution is exponential. The memorylessness of the exponential distribution is the continuous analogue of the indifference condition being a constant vector.
reduction: Indifference becomes a constant-payoff condition. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 24
status: Exact linear in the indifference condition.

title: Discounted Repeated Payoff
objects: A geometrically weighted linear functional of the payoff stream.
structure: The normalisation (1 −𝛿) makes 𝑉a convex combination, so repeated-game payoffs lie in the convex hull of stage payoffs. This convexity is exactly what the folk theorem exploits.
reduction: The payoff is a convex combination.
status: Exact linear. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 25

title: Folk Theorem
objects: The set of achievable payoffs is a polytope.
structure: Feasible payoffs form the convex hull of the stage-game payoff vectors — a polytope. Individual rationality cuts it with half-spaces 𝑣𝑖≥𝑣𝑖. The theorem says the resulting polytope is exactly the equilibrium payoff set in the limit, so the answer is a polyhedron.
reduction: The equilibrium payoff set is a polytope.

title: Minmax Payoff
objects: The value of a zero-sum game against the coalition of others.
structure: Computed as an LP, since it is a minimax over a bilinear form. It sets the individual rationality floor and hence the half-spaces bounding the folk theorem polytope.
reduction: The minmax value is an LP optimum.

title: Grim Trigger Sustainability
objects: A scalar inequality comparing deviation gain to punishment loss.
structure: Derived from comparing two geometric series, so it is a ratio of linear functionals of the payoff vector. The threshold discount factor is the point where the two linear expressions cross.
reduction: The condition compares two linear functionals.

title: One-Shot Deviation Principle
objects: Reduction of an infinite check to a per-period one.
structure: Relies on continuity at infinity (discounting), the same condition that makes the Bellman operator a contraction. Checking equilibrium becomes a finite set of linear comparisons rather than an infinite search.
reduction: The principle follows from contraction.

title: Prisoner’s Dilemma Payoff Ordering
objects: Inequalities on the four entries of a 2 × 2 payoff matrix.
structure: The dilemma is that the dominant-strategy equilibrium (𝑃, 𝑃) is Pareto-dominated by (𝑅, 𝑅). Both conditions are linear inequalities on matrix entries; the second ensures alternating defection is worse than mutual cooperation.
reduction: The game is defined by linear inequalities on matrix entries.

title: Bayesian Game
objects: A prior over type profiles; payoffs become type-conditional matrices.
structure: Harsanyi’s transformation converts incomplete information into a game with a chance move, so the Bayesian game becomes an ordinary game on an enlarged strategy space. Expected payoffs are p⊤applied to a stack of payoff matrices.
reduction: Types enlarge the matrix; expectations remain linear.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
objects: Best response in expectation over the conditional type distribution.
structure: The expectation is linear, so for each type the best response is again a linear maximisation over a simplex. The equilibrium is a fixed point across types — same bilinear coupling as the complete-information case.
reduction: Per-type best response is linear maximisation.

title: Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium
objects: Beliefs updated by Bayes’ rule — diagonal scaling plus normalisation.
structure: On the equilibrium path, belief updating is exactly the diagonal-rescaling operation of field 13. Off- path beliefs are unrestricted, which is why refinements (intuitive criterion, D1) are needed to pin them down.
reduction: Belief updating is diagonal scaling.
status: Exact linear on the equilibrium path.

title: Revelation Principle
objects: Composition of the mechanism with the equilibrium strategy map.
structure: The composite map is again a mechanism, so the search can be restricted to direct truthful ones. This is a change of variables that makes the design problem a linear programme in the allocation and payment rules.
reduction: The principle makes mechanism design an LP.

title: Incentive Compatibility
objects: A family of linear inequalities in the allocation and payment rules.
structure: Linear in the mechanism’s parameters, so the set of IC mechanisms is a polytope. Optimal mechanism design maximises a linear objective (expected revenue) over it — an LP, which is why Myerson’s characterisation is available in closed form.
reduction: IC constraints are linear inequalities.

title: Individual Rationality
objects: Additional linear inequalities.
structure: Cuts the IC polytope with further half-spaces. Together IC and IR define the feasible mechanism polytope, and the binding constraints at the optimum identify which types’ constraints matter — typically the lowest type for IR.
reduction: IR constraints are linear inequalities.

title: VCG Payment Rule
objects: An externality computed as a difference of two LP optima.
structure: Each agent pays the harm imposed on others, computed by re-solving the allocation problem without them. For linear allocation problems both terms are LP values, so VCG payments are differences of optimal objective values.
reduction: Payments are differences of LP optima.

title: Revenue Equivalence Theorem
objects: An envelope-theorem consequence. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 37
structure: IC forces the payment rule to be determined by the allocation rule up to a constant — the payment is the integral of the allocation, so revenue depends only on the allocation. This is a fundamental-theorem-of- calculus argument applied to a linear structure.
reduction: Payments are the integral of the allocation.

title: Second-Price Auction Truthfulness
objects: A payment independent of one’s own bid.
structure: Because the payment does not depend on 𝑏𝑖, the bidder’s objective is linear in the win indicator, so truth-telling maximises it pointwise. Decoupling payment from own report is exactly what makes the incentive constraints slack — the VCG mechanism specialised to one item.
reduction: The payoff is linear in the allocation indicator. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 38

title: First-Price Auction Equilibrium Bid
objects: Bid shading determined by an order statistic expectation.
structure: Derived from the IC differential equation, whose solution is the conditional expectation of the highest rival value. Bidding is nonlinear in 𝑣, but revenue equivalence guarantees the same expected revenue as the second-price auction.
reduction: Only through the linear IC characterisation.

title: Myerson Virtual Valuation
objects: The transformed valuation that revenue maximisation acts on.
structure: Optimal revenue is achieved by allocating to the highest virtual value, provided 𝜓is increasing — so revenue maximisation becomes welfare maximisation in transformed coordinates, which is an LP. The transformation converts a hard problem into a linear one.
reduction: Revenue maximisation becomes an LP after transformation.

title: Myerson–Satterthwaite Impossibility
objects: Infeasibility of a linear programme.
structure: The four requirements are linear constraints, and the theorem says the resulting polytope is empty. The proof is a duality argument exhibiting an infeasibility certificate — Farkas’ lemma applied to mechanism design.
reduction: The impossibility is LP infeasibility.

title: Signalling Single-Crossing Condition
objects: A monotonicity condition on the marginal rate of substitution.
structure: Ensures indifference curves of different types cross exactly once, which makes separating equilibria possible and monotone. It is the ordinal analogue of a positive-definiteness condition — a sign condition on a cross-derivative.
reduction: The condition is a sign condition on a mixed partial.

title: Spence Education Signalling
objects: A separating equilibrium sustained by the single-crossing condition.
structure: Education is costly and uninformative in itself; separation works because the cost gradient differs across types. The equilibrium is determined by an incentive constraint that binds — again a linear constraint at the optimum.
reduction: Separation is enforced by a binding linear constraint.

title: Characteristic Function
objects: A vector in ℝ2𝑛indexed by coalitions.
structure: The space of games is a vector space of dimension 2𝑛−1, with the unanimity games as a natural basis. Every solution concept that is linear (Shapley, Banzhaf) is a matrix acting on this space.
reduction: The game is a vector; linear solution concepts are matrices.

title: Superadditivity
objects: A family of linear inequalities on the game vector.
structure: Defines a convex cone in game space. Convex games (supermodular 𝑣) form a smaller cone on which the core is guaranteed nonempty and the Shapley value lies inside it.
reduction: The condition defines a cone of linear inequalities.

title: The Core
objects: A polytope defined by exponentially many linear inequalities.
structure: The core is exactly a polyhedron. It may be empty, and testing membership is an LP with 2𝑛 constraints — tractable when the constraints have structure (e.g. flow games, matching games).
reduction: The core is a polytope.

title: Bondareva–Shapley Theorem
objects: An LP duality condition.
structure: The core is nonempty exactly when the LP defining it is feasible, and by duality that is exactly balancedness — a condition on the existence of balanced weights. Farkas’ lemma again, in cooperative clothing.
reduction: Nonemptiness is LP feasibility.

title: Nucleolus
objects: A sequence of LPs, each fixing more constraints.
structure: Computed by solving a nested sequence of LPs, each minimising the maximum remaining excess and then fixing the binding constraints. Always exists, is unique, and lies in the core when the core is nonempty.
reduction: The nucleolus is a sequence of LPs.

title: Shapley–Shubik Power Index
objects: The Shapley value applied to a simple (0/1) game.
structure: Linear in 𝑣, hence an explicit matrix on the game space. For weighted voting games it measures pivotal frequency, and it is emphatically not proportional to the weights — a fact that surprises and that is visible from the matrix structure.
reduction: The index is a linear map on the game vector.

title: Banzhaf Power Index
objects: An unweighted average of marginal contributions.
structure: Also linear in 𝑣, differing from Shapley only in the weight vector — uniform over subsets rather than over orderings. Consequently it need not sum to one, so it is not eﬀicient in the Shapley sense.
reduction: The index is a different linear map on the same space.

title: Gale–Shapley Stability
objects: Ordinal preference lists; the stable matching lattice.
structure: The set of stable matchings forms a distributive lattice, not a polytope in the ordinal setting — but the fractional stable matching polytope has integral vertices, so stability can be expressed by linear inequalities after all. The algorithm itself is combinatorial and runs in 𝑂(𝑛2).
reduction: Available via the stable matching polytope.

title: Evolutionarily Stable Strategy
objects: A refinement of Nash stated as bilinear inequalities.
structure: An ESS is a Nash equilibrium with a local stability condition, equivalent to negative definiteness of 𝐴restricted to the tangent space of the simplex at x. Stability becomes a definiteness condition on a projected matrix.
reduction: Stability is definiteness on a subspace.

title: Replicator Dynamics
objects: Payoff computed by a matrix–vector product; the dynamics are quadratic.
structure: The fitness vector 𝐴x is linear, but the multiplication by 𝑥𝑖makes the dynamics quadratic. Nash equilibria are rest points; linearising at a rest point gives a Jacobian whose eigenvalues determine stability, with ESS implying asymptotic stability.
reduction: Fitness is linear; the dynamics are quadratic.
status: Linearised; the payoff structure is exactly linear.

title: Hawk–Dove Equilibrium
objects: The mixed equilibrium of a 2 × 2 game.
structure: Found from the indifference condition, which is a 2 × 2 linear solve. The equilibrium is an ESS when 𝑉< 𝐶, since the payoff matrix restricted to the simplex tangent is then negative definite.
reduction: The equilibrium is a 2 × 2 linear solve.

title: Hamilton’s Rule
objects: A single linear inequality in relatedness, benefit, and cost.
structure: Derivable from the Price equation as the condition for the covariance term to be positive. Its simplicity is deceptive — measuring 𝑟correctly is the diﬀiculty, and the rule is exact only under additive fitness effects.
reduction: The rule is a linear inequality.

title: Price Equation
objects: A covariance plus an expectation — both linear or bilinear. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 55
structure: An exact identity requiring no assumptions, decomposing evolutionary change into selection (covari- ance) and transmission (expectation) components. The covariance term is a bilinear form in fitness and trait vectors.
reduction: The decomposition is into a covariance and an expectation.

title: Fictitious Play Belief Update
objects: A running average of observed play.
structure: Belief updating is a linear recursion converging to the empirical frequency vector. Convergence to Nash holds for zero-sum, 2 × 𝑛, and potential games; it can cycle otherwise (Shapley’s counterexample), which is a failure of the associated dynamics to be gradient-like.
reduction: Belief updating is a linear average.

title: Multiplicative Weights Update
objects: Diagonal rescaling followed by normalisation.
structure: Regret is 𝑂( √ 𝑇ln 𝑛), and in zero-sum games the average play converges to the minimax equilibrium — giving an alternative proof of the minimax theorem. It is mirror descent with the entropic regulariser, hence The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 57 exponentiated gradient.
reduction: The update is diagonal scaling plus normalisation.

title: Nash Equilibrium Computation Complexity
objects: A complexity barrier, not a matrix statement.
structure: The honest limit of this chapter. Zero-sum equilibrium is an LP and solvable in polynomial time; correlated equilibrium is an LP and solvable in polynomial time; general Nash requires a rank-one (product) restriction on the correlated polytope, and that restriction is what makes it PPAD-complete. Linear algebra takes the field exactly as far as the product structure permits, and no further.
reduction: Not available; the obstruction is the rank-one constraint.
status: No faithful linear form — and the reason is precisely a rank condition. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 58

title: Newton’s First Law
objects: The null space of the force map; inertial frames.
structure: Defines the class of frames in which the dynamics is ̈x = 𝑀−1F with no extra terms. Transformations between inertial frames form the Galilean group, realised as 4 × 4 matrices acting on (x, 𝑡).
reduction: Inertial frames are the orbit of the Galilean matrix group.

title: Newton’s Second Law
objects: 𝑀the mass matrix, symmetric positive definite.
structure: Linear in ̈x always, so the acceleration is 𝑀−1F — one linear solve per timestep, which is exactly what every simulator computes. Nonlinearity, when present, lives entirely in F.
reduction: The law is a linear system for the accelerations.

title: Newton’s Third Law
objects: An antisymmetric interaction matrix.
structure: The force matrix 𝐹with entries F𝑖𝑗is antisymmetric, so ∑𝑖𝑗F𝑖𝑗= 0 — internal forces cancel in the total. Momentum conservation is exactly the statement that an antisymmetric matrix has zero total sum.
reduction: The law is antisymmetry of the interaction matrix.

title: Linear Momentum Conservation
objects: p = 𝑀v summed; conservation when Fext = 0.
structure: Total momentum is 1⊤𝑀v, a linear functional of the velocity vector. Its conservation follows from translation invariance via Noether — the generator of translations is the momentum, and invariance means it commutes with the Hamiltonian.
reduction: Momentum is a linear functional; conservation is a commutation.

title: Impulse–Momentum Theorem
objects: Integration of the force, a linear operation.
structure: For impulsive contact, the velocity jump is Δv = 𝑀−1𝐽⊤𝜆with 𝐽the contact Jacobian and 𝜆the impulse multipliers — a linear complementarity problem when unilateral constraints are present.
reduction: Impulses become a linear system in the multipliers.

title: Coeﬀicient of Restitution
objects: A linear relation between pre- and post-collision relative velocity.
structure: Combined with momentum conservation this gives a 2 × 2 linear system for the outgoing velocities, solvable in closed form. Energy is conserved exactly when 𝑒= 1, and the energy loss is a quadratic form in the relative velocity.
reduction: Collision resolution is a 2 × 2 linear solve.

title: Rocket Equation (Tsiolkovsky)
objects: Integration of a variable-mass momentum balance.
structure: Linear in ln 𝑚, which is why staging works multiplicatively: total Δ𝑣is the sum over stages. Delta-v budgets add linearly, and this additivity is the whole basis of mission design.
reduction: Linear in the logarithm of mass.

title: Centre of Mass
objects: A mass-weighted average — a normalised linear functional.
structure: Identical in form to the statistical mean with m as the weight vector. Centring the coordinates about R is the same operation that precedes principal component analysis, and it decouples translational from internal motion.
reduction: The centre of mass is a weighted average.

title: Variable Mass (Meshchersky) Equation
objects: Newton’s law with a mass-flux term.
structure: Still linear in ̇v, so the acceleration is a linear solve with a time-varying mass matrix. The thrust term is linear in the relative exhaust velocity.
reduction: The equation is linear in the acceleration.

title: Friction Laws
objects: A cone constraint on the contact force.
structure: The Coulomb friction cone is a second-order cone, so contact mechanics is naturally a conic programme. Polyhedral approximations of the cone turn it into a linear complementarity problem, which is what rigid-body simulators solve. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 11
reduction: Friction becomes a cone constraint.
status: Exact linear as a conic constraint.

title: Drag Force
objects: Quadratic in velocity.
structure: Genuinely nonlinear. Linear (Stokes) drag −𝑏v applies at low Reynolds number and gives an exactly solvable linear ODE; quadratic drag does not, and the crossover is at Re ≈1.
reduction: Linear only in the Stokes regime.
status: Linearised (Stokes drag) or no linear form (quadratic).

title: Terminal Velocity
objects: The fixed point of the drag-balance equation.
structure: A stable fixed point; linearising about it gives ̇𝛿𝑣= −𝜆𝛿𝑣with 𝜆= 2𝑔/𝑣𝑡, so approach to terminal velocity is exponential with a rate read off the Jacobian.
reduction: The approach linearises about the fixed point.

title: Work–Energy Theorem
objects: A line integral, hence a chain–cochain pairing.
structure: 𝑊= c⊤F for the signed displacement chain c. Path independence holds exactly when F ∈im 𝐵for the discrete gradient 𝐵— the conservative case.
reduction: Work is a chain–cochain pairing.

title: Kinetic Energy
objects: A quadratic form in the generalised velocities.
structure: 𝑀≻0 always, since kinetic energy is positive for any nonzero motion. In generalised coordinates 𝑀 depends on q, which is the source of the Christoffel-like terms in the equations of motion — the mass matrix is a metric.
reduction: Kinetic energy is a quadratic form.

title: Gravitational Potential Energy (Uniform Field)
objects: A linear functional of position.
structure: Exactly linear, so its gradient is the constant vector 𝑚g and its Hessian is zero. This is the only common potential with vanishing Hessian, which is why uniform-field problems have no restoring force.
reduction: The potential is a linear functional.

title: Conservative Force and Potential
objects: Membership in the image of the discrete gradient.
structure: F ∈im 𝐵exactly when 𝐶F = 0, and im 𝐵= ker 𝐶when the domain is simply connected. Conserva- tiveness is a subspace membership, and the obstruction is the first cohomology.
reduction: Conservativeness is a column-space condition.

title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy
objects: A quadratic plus a scalar function, constant along trajectories.
structure: ̇𝐸= ∇𝐸⊤𝐽∇𝐻= 0 by antisymmetry of 𝐽when 𝐸= 𝐻— energy conservation is the antisymmetry of the symplectic matrix, nothing more. Symplectic integrators preserve this structurally.
reduction: Conservation follows from skew-symmetry.

title: Power
objects: An inner product of force and velocity.
structure: Zero when force is perpendicular to velocity — which is why magnetic and constraint forces do no work. Bilinear in the two vectors.
reduction: Power is a dot product.

title: Effective Potential
objects: Reduction of a two-body problem to one radial dimension.
structure: Conservation of angular momentum eliminates the angular coordinate, reducing dimension by two. Stability of circular orbits is the sign of 𝑈″ eff — a 1 × 1 Hessian condition.
reduction: Symmetry reduction cuts the dimension; stability is a second derivative.
status: Exact linear in the stability analysis.

title: Virial Theorem
objects: Time-averaged trace-like identity.
structure: Derived from 𝑑 𝑑𝑡∑𝑖p𝑖⋅r𝑖averaging to zero for bounded motion. The quantity ∑𝑖p𝑖⋅r𝑖is tr of an outer-product matrix, so the theorem is a trace identity for bounded orbits.
reduction: The theorem is a time-averaged trace identity.

title: Angular Momentum
objects: The inertia tensor mapping angular velocity to angular momentum.
structure: L and 𝜔are parallel only when 𝜔is an eigenvector of 𝐼— that is, along a principal axis. Otherwise they differ in direction, which is the source of wobble in unbalanced rotors.
reduction: Angular momentum is a matrix–vector product.

title: Torque
objects: The skew-symmetric cross-product matrix.
structure: [r]× has rank 2 with null space span{r}, so radial forces produce no torque — which is exactly why central forces conserve angular momentum.
reduction: The cross product becomes a skew matrix.

title: Rotational Kinetic Energy
objects: A quadratic form in the inertia tensor.
structure: Positive definite for any body with nonzero extent. Its level sets are the inertia ellipsoid, whose semi- axes are 1/√𝐼𝑘along the principal directions — Poinsot’s construction visualises free rotation as this ellipsoid rolling on a plane.
reduction: Rotational energy is a quadratic form.

title: Parallel Axis Theorem
objects: A rank-structured additive shift of the inertia tensor.
structure: The correction is exactly the inertia tensor of a point mass at d — a rank-2 positive semidefinite matrix (rank 2 because d itself is in its null space). Identical in form to the covariance shift under translation.
reduction: The theorem is a rank-structured matrix addition.

title: Inertia Tensor
objects: A symmetric positive semidefinite 3 × 3 matrix.
structure: Symmetric, hence orthogonally diagonalisable: eigenvectors are the principal axes, eigenvalues the principal moments. It equals tr(Σ)𝐼3 −Σ for the mass covariance Σ, so the principal axes and the principal components are the same directions.
reduction: No reduction needed; the tensor is a matrix.

title: Euler’s Rigid Body Equations
objects: Linear in ̇𝜔, quadratic in 𝜔.
structure: The gyroscopic term is genuinely quadratic, so the equations are nonlinear. The intermediate axis theorem — rotation about the middle principal axis is unstable — follows from linearising and finding one positive eigenvalue when 𝐼1 < 𝐼2 < 𝐼3.
reduction: Linear in the angular acceleration; stability by linearisation.
status: Linearised for stability; exact linear in ̇𝜔.

title: Rolling Without Slipping
objects: A linear velocity constraint, 𝐴̇q = 0.
structure: A Pfaﬀian constraint. Holonomic in the planar case (integrable to a position constraint) but nonholo- nomic in three dimensions — the difference is whether the constraint one-form is exact, which is a curl condition on 𝐴.
reduction: The constraint is a linear condition on velocities.

title: Gyroscopic Precession Rate
objects: Rotation of the angular momentum vector by an applied torque.
structure: ̇L = Ω × L describes rotation at constant magnitude — the generator is skew, so L traces a cone. Precession is the action of a one-parameter rotation subgroup.
reduction: Precession is a skew-generated rotation.

title: Centripetal Acceleration
objects: The square of the skew angular-velocity matrix.
structure: [𝜔]2 × = 𝜔𝜔⊤−‖𝜔‖2𝐼, a symmetric negative semidefinite matrix — so the acceleration points inward. Explicitly a matrix acting on position.
reduction: The double cross product is a matrix square.

title: Coriolis Acceleration
objects: A skew-symmetric matrix acting on velocity.
structure: Skew-symmetry means the Coriolis force does no work: v⊤[𝜔]×v = 0 identically. It deflects without adding energy, which is why it shapes weather patterns without driving them.
reduction: The force is a skew matrix acting on velocity.

title: Centrifugal Acceleration
objects: The negative of the centripetal matrix. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 31
structure: Derivable from a potential −1 2‖𝜔× r‖2, a quadratic form — so unlike Coriolis it is conservative in the rotating frame. That difference is why one can define a geopotential but not a “Corioliopotential”.
reduction: The force is the gradient of a quadratic form.

title: Simple Harmonic Motion
objects: A 2 × 2 skew-like generator with imaginary eigenvalues.
structure: The state-space matrix ( 0 1 −𝜔2 0 ) has eigenvalues ±𝑖𝜔, so 𝑒𝐴𝑡is a rotation in scaled phase space — energy is conserved exactly. This is the archetype every normal mode reduces to.
reduction: The oscillator is a 2 × 2 linear system.

title: Simple Pendulum Period
objects: The linearisation sin 𝜃≈𝜃.
structure: Exactly linear only in the small-angle limit; the full equation is nonlinear with an amplitude-dependent period given by an elliptic integral. The linearisation error grows as 𝜃2/16 in relative period. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 33
reduction: Linearisation about the equilibrium.

title: Physical Pendulum Period
objects: The inertia about the pivot, from the parallel axis theorem.
structure: 𝐼= 𝐼cm + 𝑚𝑑2, so the period involves a rank-structured matrix shift. Minimised over 𝑑at the radius of gyration — an optimisation over the shift parameter.
reduction: The moment comes from a matrix shift.

title: Quality Factor
objects: Ratio of eigenvalue imaginary to real part.
structure: 𝑄= | Im 𝜆|/(2| Re 𝜆|) for the complex eigenvalue pair — a purely spectral quantity. High 𝑄means eigenvalues close to the imaginary axis, hence slow decay and sharp resonance.
reduction: 𝑄is an eigenvalue ratio.

title: Coupled Oscillator Normal Modes
objects: A symmetric-definite generalised eigenproblem.
structure: 𝐾, 𝑀symmetric with 𝑀≻0, so eigenvalues 𝜔2 are real and eigenvectors are 𝑀-orthogonal. Modes decouple the system completely: in modal coordinates the dynamics is 𝑛independent harmonic oscillators. This is the single most important computation in structural and molecular vibration.
reduction: Coupled motion becomes a generalised eigenproblem.

title: Newton’s Law of Gravitation
objects: Inverse-square, hence nonlinear in position.
structure: The 𝑁-body problem is nonlinear and non-integrable for 𝑁≥3. But the potential satisfies the linear Poisson equation ∇2Φ = 4𝜋𝐺𝜌, so the field computation is linear even though the motion is not — superposition holds for fields, not for trajectories.
reduction: The field equation is linear; the dynamics are not.
status: Exact linear for the field; no linear form for the motion. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 37

title: Gravitational Potential Energy (Two Bodies)
objects: A nonlinear function of separation.
structure: Its Hessian gives the tidal tensor 𝜕𝑖𝜕𝑗𝑈, which is symmetric traceless in vacuum (since ∇2𝑈= 0) — so it has eigenvalues summing to zero, one stretching and two compressing directions.
reduction: The second-order behaviour is a symmetric traceless matrix. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 38

title: Escape Velocity
objects: An energy threshold condition.
structure: The condition 𝑇+ 𝑈≥0 is a quadratic-in-velocity inequality — the boundary between bounded and unbounded orbits. Nonlinear in 𝑅, linear in 𝑣2.
reduction: The criterion is linear in 𝑣2.

title: Kepler’s Third Law
objects: A power-law relation; linear in log-log coordinates.
structure: ln 𝑇= 3 2 ln 𝑎+ 𝑐, so fitting is a two-parameter linear regression. The exponent 3/2 follows from the inverse-square law by dimensional analysis — a null-space computation on the dimensional matrix.
reduction: Linear in log coordinates.
also_in: Astronomy. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 40

title: Vis-Viva Equation
objects: Energy conservation rearranged.
structure: Linear in 𝑣2 and in 1/𝑟, so the orbit’s energy is an aﬀine function of the inverse radius. This linearity in 1/𝑟is why the substitution 𝑢= 1/𝑟turns the orbit equation into a linear harmonic oscillator equation.
reduction: Linear in 𝑣2 and 1/𝑟.
status: Exact linear in the transformed variables.

title: Reduced Mass
objects: Decoupling of the two-body problem by a linear change of coordinates.
structure: The transformation to centre-of-mass and relative coordinates is a linear map that block-diagonalises the mass matrix, converting a coupled two-body problem into two independent one-body problems. It is exactly a change of basis diagonalising 𝑀.
reduction: The transformation block-diagonalises the mass matrix.

title: Rutherford Scattering Cross Section
objects: The scattering amplitude in the Born approximation is a Fourier transform.
structure: In the Born approximation the amplitude is the Fourier transform of the potential — a linear map — and the cross section is its squared modulus. The divergence at small angles reflects the infinite range of the Coulomb potential.
reduction: The amplitude is a linear transform of the potential.
status: Exact linear in the Born approximation.

title: Tidal Force
objects: The tidal tensor 𝑇𝑖𝑗= −𝜕𝑖𝜕𝑗Φ.
structure: Symmetric and traceless in vacuum, with eigenvalues (+2, −1, −1) × 𝐺𝑀/𝑑3 — one stretching and two compressing directions. Tidal effects are the eigenstructure of the potential’s Hessian, and geodesic deviation in general relativity has the same form.
reduction: Tides are the Hessian of the potential.
