also_in: Gravitational Physics, Oceanography. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 44 Lagrangian and Hamiltonian Mechanics

title: Lagrangian
objects: A quadratic form minus a scalar potential.
structure: Quadratic in velocities always, which is what makes the momentum p = 𝑀̇q linear and the Legendre transform invertible whenever 𝑀≻0. The whole Hamiltonian formalism depends on that invertibility.
reduction: The kinetic term is a quadratic form.

title: Principle of Stationary Action
objects: Stationarity of a functional.
structure: For quadratic Lagrangians the action is a quadratic functional, so stationarity is a linear boundary value problem — 𝐾q = f after discretisation. The second variation is the Hessian, whose definiteness decides whether the path is a minimum.
reduction: Stationarity becomes a linear system for quadratic actions.

title: Euler–Lagrange Equations of Motion
structure: Linear in ̈q with mass matrix 𝑀; the Coriolis matrix 𝐶collects the velocity-quadratic terms and satisfies ̇ 𝑀−2𝐶skew — a structural identity used throughout robot control to prove passivity.
reduction: The equations are linear in the accelerations.

title: Generalised Momentum
objects: A linear map from velocities to momenta.
structure: Invertible exactly when 𝑀≻0, which is the condition for the Legendre transform to exist. Singular 𝑀means constraints and requires Dirac’s formalism — the degenerate case.
reduction: The momentum is a matrix–vector product.

title: Noether’s Theorem
objects: A conserved linear functional of the momentum.
structure: Each continuous symmetry generator X gives a conserved quantity p⊤X. For a linear symmetry group, X = 𝐴q and the conserved quantity is the bilinear form p⊤𝐴q — translations give momentum, rotations give angular momentum.
reduction: Conserved quantities are bilinear forms in the generators.

title: Lagrange Multipliers for Constraints
objects: A saddle-point (KKT) system.
structure: The combined system ( 𝑀𝐴⊤ 𝐴 0 )( ̈q −𝜆) = ( f b ) is symmetric indefinite and solvable when 𝐴has full row rank. This is exactly the KKT matrix of constrained optimisation.
reduction: Constrained dynamics is a block linear system.

title: D’Alembert’s Principle
objects: Orthogonality of the residual to the constraint-admissible subspace.
structure: Virtual displacements span ker 𝐴, so the principle says the residual lies in (ker 𝐴) ⟂= im 𝐴⊤— exactly the statement that constraint forces are multipliers. Constraint forces do no work because they are orthogonal to admissible motion.
reduction: The principle is an orthogonality condition between subspaces.

title: Hamiltonian
objects: A quadratic form in momentum plus a potential.
structure: The Legendre transform replaces 𝑀by 𝑀−1 — conjugation inverts the matrix, exactly as for the Fenchel conjugate of a quadratic. For quadratic 𝑈the whole Hamiltonian is a quadratic form and the dynamics is exactly linear.
reduction: The Hamiltonian is a quadratic form.

title: Hamilton’s Canonical Equations
objects: The canonical symplectic matrix.
structure: For quadratic 𝐻= 1 2z⊤𝑆z the dynamics is exactly ̇z = 𝐽𝑆z, a linear system whose generator is a Hamiltonian matrix. Its eigenvalues come in quadruples {𝜆, −𝜆, ̄𝜆, −̄𝜆}, which is why asymptotic stability is impossible in Hamiltonian systems.
reduction: The dynamics becomes a linear system with generator 𝐽𝑆.

title: Canonical Transformation Condition
objects: The symplectic group condition.
structure: Symplectic matrices have determinant one and preserve phase-space volume (Liouville). Their eigen- values come in reciprocal pairs, so stability is always marginal. Symplectic integrators satisfy this exactly at each step, which is why they conserve energy over exponentially long times.
reduction: Canonicity is a matrix identity.

title: Generating Function Relations
objects: A potential generating a symplectic map.
structure: For a quadratic generating function the resulting transformation is linear and symplectic, with the block structure determined by the Hessian of 𝐹. Quadratic generators give exactly the linear symplectic group.
reduction: Quadratic generators give linear symplectic maps.

title: Adiabatic Invariant
objects: A phase-space area, hence a determinant.
structure: The enclosed area is preserved because the evolution is symplectic and the parameter change is slow — an adiabatic theorem. Area preservation is det 𝑀= 1, so the invariant is a determinant statement.
reduction: The invariant is a preserved area, hence a determinant.

title: Small Oscillations About Equilibrium
objects: The generalised eigenproblem 𝐾a = 𝜔2𝑀a.
structure: Both matrices symmetric with 𝑀≻0; stability requires 𝐾⪰0. Simultaneous diagonalisation by a congruence transformation gives normal coordinates in which the system is 𝑛decoupled oscillators. Zero modes of 𝐾are rigid-body motions.
reduction: Small oscillations are a symmetric-definite eigenproblem.

title: Routhian Reduction
objects: A partial Legendre transform on the cyclic coordinates.
structure: Eliminates the ignorable coordinates, reducing the dimension by the number of symmetries. In matrix terms it is a Schur complement of the mass matrix with respect to the cyclic block — reduction by symmetry is block elimination.
reduction: Reduction is a Schur complement.

title: Larmor Formula
objects: Radiated power, quadratic in acceleration.
structure: Quadratic in a, hence a quadratic form a⊤𝑄a with 𝑄a multiple of the identity for a point charge. Radiation reaction makes the equation of motion third order, introducing the runaway solutions of the Abraham– Lorentz equation.
reduction: Radiated power is a quadratic form.

title: Chaos Onset Criterion (Lyapunov Time)
objects: The reciprocal of the largest Lyapunov exponent.
structure: The exponent is the asymptotic growth rate of the tangent-map matrix product, so predictability horizon is a spectral property of the linearised flow. For Hamiltonian systems the exponents pair as {±𝜆𝑖} by symplecticity, and their sum is zero.
reduction: The horizon is a tangent-map growth rate.
status: Exact linear on the tangent bundle.

title: Deformation Gradient
objects: The Jacobian of the deformation map.
structure: The single object from which all strain measures are built. 𝐹is not symmetric and includes rotation; det 𝐹> 0 enforces non-inversion of material. Every kinematic quantity in this chapter is a function of 𝐹.
reduction: No reduction needed — 𝐹is a matrix by definition.

title: Jacobian of Deformation
objects: The local volume ratio.
structure: 𝐽= 1 is incompressibility, 𝐽> 0 is required for physical admissibility. Its derivative is ̇𝐽= 𝐽tr(𝐿) = 𝐽∇⋅v by Jacobi’s formula — the continuity equation in disguise.
reduction: Volume change is a determinant.

title: Polar Decomposition
objects: Rotation times stretch.
structure: Separates rigid rotation from pure deformation uniquely. 𝑈= (𝐹⊤𝐹)1/2 is the right stretch tensor with principal stretches as eigenvalues; 𝑅is the nearest orthogonal matrix to 𝐹in every unitarily invariant norm. This is the same decomposition as the matrix polar decomposition of field 05.
reduction: Already matrix-native.

title: Right Cauchy–Green Tensor
objects: A symmetric positive definite Gram matrix.
structure: Rotation-invariant, since 𝑅cancels: 𝐶depends only on the stretch. Its eigenvalues are the squared principal stretches 𝜆2 𝑖, and det 𝐶= 𝐽2. It is the metric induced by the deformation.
reduction: The tensor is a Gram matrix of 𝐹.

title: Green–Lagrange Strain
objects: A symmetric strain measure, zero for rigid motion.
structure: Quadratic in 𝐹, hence nonlinear in the displacement — this is exactly where geometric nonlinearity enters. Expanding in the displacement gradient 𝐻gives 𝐸= 1 2(𝐻+ 𝐻⊤) + 1 2𝐻⊤𝐻; dropping the quadratic term gives small strain.
reduction: Quadratic in the deformation gradient.
status: Linearised to give the infinitesimal strain.

title: Infinitesimal Strain Tensor
objects: The symmetric part of the displacement gradient.
structure: 𝐻= sym(𝐻) + skew(𝐻) splits deformation from infinitesimal rotation exactly, and the skew part skew(𝐻) = 1 2[𝜔]× is the rotation vector. Valid when ‖𝐻‖ ≪1; the whole of linear elasticity rests on this truncation.
reduction: Strain is the symmetric part of a matrix.

title: Volumetric and Deviatoric Split
objects: Orthogonal decomposition into trace and traceless parts.
structure: An orthogonal projection in the Frobenius inner product: the spherical and deviatoric subspaces of symmetric matrices are orthogonal, of dimensions 1 and 5 in three dimensions. Volume change and shape change decouple, which is why bulk and shear moduli are independent.
reduction: The split is an orthogonal projection of matrix space.

title: Compatibility Condition
objects: Integrability of a strain field to a displacement field.
structure: 𝜀∈im(sym ∘∇) exactly when the curl-curl vanishes — a cohomological condition. Six strain com- ponents come from three displacements, so there are three independent compatibility equations; the count is a rank–nullity statement.
reduction: Compatibility is a column-space membership.

title: Velocity Gradient
objects: The spatial rate of deformation matrix.
structure: tr 𝐿= ∇⋅v is the volumetric rate; its symmetric and skew parts separate stretching from spin. The identity 𝐿= ̇𝐹𝐹−1 is the continuum analogue of the logarithmic derivative.
reduction: Already matrix-native.

title: Rate of Deformation and Spin
objects: The additive split of the velocity gradient.
structure: 𝐷drives dissipation (𝜎∶𝐷is the stress power) while 𝑊is the rigid spin and does no work against a symmetric stress. This is why objective stress rates subtract 𝑊— the Jaumann rate ̊𝜎= ̇𝜎−𝑊𝜎+ 𝜎𝑊.
reduction: The split is the symmetric–skew decomposition.
status: Exact linear. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 11

title: Material (Total) Derivative
objects: A linear operator on fields, discretised as 𝜕𝑡+ 𝑉𝐷.
structure: Linear in 𝜙for a given velocity field, and it is the velocity-dependence that makes Navier–Stokes nonlinear. The discrete advection operator 𝑉𝐷is skew-symmetric for divergence-free v on a periodic grid, hence energy-conserving.
reduction: The derivative is a linear operator for fixed v.
status: Exact linear in the transported field.

title: Reynolds Transport Theorem
objects: Differentiation of an integral over a moving domain.
structure: Derived from Jacobi’s formula ̇𝐽= 𝐽tr 𝐿— the domain motion contributes exactly the divergence term. Every conservation law in the field follows by applying this theorem to a different 𝜙.
reduction: The theorem follows from the determinant derivative.

title: Cauchy Stress Tensor
objects: A matrix mapping surface normals to traction vectors.
structure: Cauchy’s theorem asserts that traction depends linearly on the normal — the existence of the stress tensor is precisely a linearity claim, proved by a tetrahedron argument. It is the founding linear structure of the field.
reduction: Traction is a matrix–vector product.

title: Symmetry of Cauchy Stress
objects: Symmetry forced by angular momentum balance.
structure: Reduces nine components to six and guarantees real eigenvalues with orthogonal eigenvectors — the spectral theorem applies, giving principal stresses and directions. Symmetry fails only in micropolar media with body couples.
reduction: The balance law forces matrix symmetry.

title: First Piola–Kirchhoff Stress
objects: A two-point tensor, generally non-symmetric.
structure: Relates forces in the current configuration to areas in the reference one, which is what makes it the natural conjugate to ̇𝐹: the stress power is 𝑃∶ ̇𝐹. Non-symmetry reflects its mixed-configuration character.
reduction: A matrix congruence-like transformation of 𝜎.

title: Second Piola–Kirchhoff Stress
objects: A fully referential symmetric stress.
structure: Symmetric and work-conjugate to the Green–Lagrange strain: 𝑆∶ ̇𝐸is the stress power. Being a full congruence transformation 𝐹−1(⋅)𝐹−⊤, it preserves symmetry and inertia — the signature of the stress state is frame-independent.
reduction: The transformation is a matrix congruence.

title: Conservation of Mass (Continuity)
objects: A divergence-form conservation law; discretely ̇𝜌= −𝐷(𝜌⊙v).
structure: Linear in 𝜌for a given velocity field. The referential form 𝜌𝐽= 𝜌0 is a determinant statement — mass conservation is conservation of 𝜌det 𝐹.
reduction: Continuity is linear in the density.

title: Cauchy’s Equation of Motion
objects: Divergence of a matrix field.
structure: ∇⋅𝜎is a linear operator on the stress field, discretised as 𝐵⊤𝜎with 𝐵the discrete gradient. The left side is nonlinear only through the convective term v⊤∇v.
reduction: The divergence is a linear operator on the stress.

title: Static Equilibrium
objects: Discretised, 𝐾u = f.
structure: With linear elasticity the assembled system is symmetric positive definite once rigid-body modes are constrained — the null space of 𝐾is exactly the six rigid-body motions in three dimensions. Solving structures is solving this system.
reduction: Equilibrium becomes a sparse SPD linear system.

title: Energy Balance
objects: The stress power as a Frobenius inner product.
structure: 𝜎∶𝐷= tr(𝜎⊤𝐷) is bilinear in stress and rate of deformation. Only the symmetric part 𝐷contributes, since 𝜎is symmetric and the trace of a symmetric times a skew matrix vanishes.
reduction: Stress power is a matrix inner product.

title: Clausius–Duhem Inequality
objects: A sign constraint on a bilinear dissipation form.
structure: Restricts admissible constitutive laws: for viscous materials it forces the viscosity tensor to be positive semidefinite, since dissipation 𝐷∶ℂ∶𝐷≥0 must hold for all 𝐷. Thermodynamic admissibility is a definiteness condition.
reduction: The second law becomes positive semidefiniteness of a material tensor.
status: Exact linear as a definiteness condition.

title: Principal Stresses
objects: The eigenproblem of the stress tensor.
structure: Symmetry gives three real eigenvalues and orthogonal principal directions. On those planes the traction is purely normal — shear vanishes. Failure criteria are almost always stated in terms of these eigenvalues.
reduction: Principal stresses are eigenvalues.

title: Stress Invariants
objects: Coeﬀicients of the characteristic polynomial.
structure: Invariant under rotation because they are the elementary symmetric functions of the eigenvalues. Any isotropic scalar function of stress must depend on these three alone — the representation theorem for isotropic functions.
reduction: The invariants are characteristic polynomial coeﬀicients.

title: Von Mises Equivalent Stress
objects: The Frobenius norm of the deviatoric stress.
structure: Depends only on the deviator, hence pressure-independent — appropriate for metals, whose yielding is volume-preserving. The yield surface 𝜎𝑣= 𝜎𝑦is a cylinder in principal stress space with axis along 1.
reduction: The equivalent stress is a matrix norm.

title: Mohr’s Circle Relations
objects: A graphical representation of a 2 × 2 eigenvalue problem.
structure: The circle is the locus of (𝜎𝑛, 𝜏) as the plane rotates — a parametrisation of the orbit of the stress tensor under 𝑆𝑂(2) conjugation. Centre is 1 2 tr, radius is half the eigenvalue spread.
reduction: The circle is the rotation orbit of a symmetric matrix.

title: Maximum Shear Stress
objects: Half the eigenvalue spread.
structure: Half the difference between the largest and smallest eigenvalues, attained on planes at 45° to the corresponding principal directions. It is 1 2(𝜆max −𝜆min) — a spectral spread, and the basis of the Tresca criterion.
reduction: Maximum shear is a spectral spread.

title: Generalised Hooke’s Law
objects: A fourth-order stiffness tensor; a 6 × 6 matrix in Voigt notation.
structure: Symmetries reduce 81 components to 21 for the most general anisotropic material: minor symmetries from stress and strain symmetry, major symmetry from the existence of a strain energy. In Voigt form 𝐶is a 6 × 6 symmetric positive definite matrix.
reduction: The fourth-order tensor becomes a 6 × 6 matrix.

title: Isotropic Hooke’s Law
objects: Two constants suﬀice under full isotropy.
structure: The stiffness is 𝐶= 3𝐾ℙvol +2𝜇ℙdev — a spectral decomposition into the two orthogonal projections of the volumetric–deviatoric split, with eigenvalues 3𝐾(multiplicity 1) and 2𝜇(multiplicity 5). Isotropic elasticity has exactly two distinct eigenvalues.
reduction: The law is a spectral decomposition of the stiffness.

title: Elastic Modulus Relations
objects: Reparametrisations of the same two eigenvalues.
structure: All modulus pairs (𝐸, 𝜈), (𝐾, 𝜇), (𝜆, 𝜇) describe the same two eigenvalues of 𝐶. Positive definiteness requires 𝐾> 0 and 𝜇> 0, which translates to −1 < 𝜈< 1/2 — the physical range follows from a definiteness condition.
reduction: The relations reparametrise two eigenvalues.

title: Uniaxial Hooke’s Law
objects: The 1 × 1 case.
structure: The scalar law recovered by restricting the tensorial law to a uniaxial stress state and eliminating the lateral strains. 𝐸is not an eigenvalue of 𝐶— it is a compliance-derived quantity, which is why 𝐸and 𝜇are not directly comparable.
reduction: The scalar law is a restriction of the tensorial one.

title: Poisson’s Ratio
objects: An off-diagonal entry of the compliance matrix.
structure: Bounded by −1 < 𝜈< 1/2 from positive definiteness of 𝐶; 𝜈= 1/2 is exactly incompressibility (𝐾→∞), where the stiffness matrix becomes singular in the volumetric direction — the source of locking in finite elements.
reduction: The ratio is a compliance matrix entry.

title: Navier–Cauchy Equations
objects: A vector elliptic operator, discretised as a symmetric positive definite 𝐾.
structure: The operator is 𝜇Δ + (𝜆+ 𝜇)∇∇⋅, which the Helmholtz decomposition diagonalises into curl-free and divergence-free parts with distinct eigenvalues — giving the P and S wave speeds directly.
reduction: The PDE becomes a sparse SPD system.

title: P-Wave and S-Wave Speeds
objects: Eigenvalues of the acoustic (Christoffel) tensor.
structure: The Christoffel tensor Γ𝑖𝑘= 𝐶𝑖𝑗𝑘𝑙𝑛𝑗𝑛𝑙is symmetric positive definite, and its three eigenvalues divided by 𝜌give the squared wave speeds — one longitudinal, two transverse. Anisotropy splits the two shear speeds.
reduction: Wave speeds are eigenvalues of the Christoffel matrix.

title: Strain Energy Density
objects: A quadratic form in the strain.
structure: Positive definiteness of 𝐶is exactly the requirement that deformation costs energy — material stability. Its Hessian with respect to strain is 𝐶, which is why the stiffness is symmetric (equality of mixed partials).
reduction: Strain energy is a quadratic form.

title: Airy Stress Function
objects: A potential automatically satisfying equilibrium.
structure: Equilibrium is satisfied identically because the construction places 𝜎in ker(∇⋅) — a null-space parametrisation. Compatibility then requires ∇4𝜙= 0, the biharmonic equation.
reduction: The function parametrises the null space of the divergence.

title: Stress Concentration Factor
objects: An amplification factor, structurally a condition number.
structure: For an elliptical hole 𝐾𝑡= 1 + 2𝑎/𝑏, diverging as the ellipse sharpens into a crack. The amplification of a local field by geometry is exactly the role a condition number plays for a linear system.
reduction: The factor is a field amplification ratio.

title: Stress Intensity Factor
objects: The coeﬀicient of the 𝑟−1/2 singularity. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 37
structure: The near-tip field is a fixed eigenfunction of the elasticity operator in polar coordinates with exponent −1/2; 𝐾𝐼is the amplitude of that mode. Fracture mechanics is modal analysis of a singular field.
reduction: The factor is a modal amplitude.

title: Griﬀith Fracture Criterion
objects: An energy balance between released strain energy and created surface.
structure: Released energy is quadratic in stress (a quadratic form) while surface energy is linear in crack length — the competition of a quadratic against a linear term is what makes the criterion a threshold. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 38
reduction: The criterion balances a quadratic form against a linear term.
status: Exact linear in the energy terms.

title: Energy Release Rate
objects: The derivative of a quadratic potential with respect to crack length.
structure: Π = 1 2u⊤𝐾u −f⊤u, so 𝐺is a sensitivity of a quadratic form to a stiffness change — computable by the virtual crack extension method as −1 2u⊤(𝜕𝐾/𝜕𝑎)u.
reduction: The rate is a derivative of a quadratic form.

title: Paris Law
objects: A power law in the stress intensity range.
structure: Linear in log-log coordinates, so fitting is ordinary least squares on transformed data. Typically 𝑚≈3 for metals. Integration gives the fatigue life, and the exponent’s size is what makes life extremely sensitive to load amplitude.
reduction: Linear after logarithmic transformation.

title: Hyperelastic Constitutive Relation
objects: Stress as the gradient of a strain energy function.
structure: Guarantees path independence and thermodynamic consistency. The tangent stiffness 𝜕𝑆/𝜕𝐸is the Hessian of 𝑊, symmetric by construction — which is why hyperelastic finite element tangents are always symmetric.
reduction: Stress is a gradient; tangent stiffness is a Hessian.

title: Neo-Hookean Model
objects: Energy depending on the first invariant tr 𝐶.
structure: The simplest hyperelastic model, reducing to linear elasticity at small strain. Since 𝑊is linear in tr 𝐶, the stress is aﬀine in 𝐶— but 𝐶is quadratic in 𝐹, so the overall response is nonlinear.
reduction: Linear in the invariant, quadratic in 𝐹.

title: Mooney–Rivlin Model
objects: A two-invariant energy function.
structure: Adding the second invariant improves the fit at moderate strain. Fitting 𝐶10, 𝐶01 to test data is a linear least-squares problem, since 𝑊is linear in the parameters even though it is nonlinear in the deformation.
reduction: Linear in the material parameters.

title: Ogden Model
objects: Energy written directly in the principal stretches — the eigenvalues of 𝑈.
structure: Linear in 𝜇𝑝but nonlinear in 𝛼𝑝, so calibration is a separable nonlinear least-squares problem: solve linearly for 𝜇𝑝given 𝛼𝑝, and search over the 𝛼𝑝. That separability is exactly the variable projection method.
reduction: Linear in half the parameters.

title: Von Mises Yield Criterion
objects: A norm ball in deviatoric stress space.
structure: The yield surface is a cylinder of radius √2/3 𝜎𝑦about the hydrostatic axis — smooth and convex, which makes the flow rule single-valued everywhere. Convexity of the yield surface follows from Drucker’s postulate.
reduction: Yield is a norm constraint.

title: Tresca Yield Criterion
objects: A max over eigenvalue differences.
structure: The yield surface is a hexagonal prism — a polyhedron, hence piecewise linear. Corners make the normal non-unique, so the flow rule is set-valued there. Piecewise linearity means Tresca plasticity can be posed as a linear complementarity problem.
reduction: Yield is a polyhedral constraint on eigenvalues.

title: Mohr–Coulomb Criterion
objects: A pressure-dependent linear criterion.
structure: Linear in the normal stress, giving an irregular hexagonal pyramid in principal stress space. Appropri- ate for soils and rock, where hydrostatic pressure strengthens the material — the pressure dependence is exactly what von Mises omits.
reduction: The criterion is linear in the stress components.

title: Drucker–Prager Criterion
objects: A smooth cone in stress space.
structure: A smooth approximation to Mohr–Coulomb: a second-order cone constraint, hence convex and free of corners. Being an SOC constraint, plasticity with this criterion is a conic programme.
reduction: The criterion is a second-order cone constraint.

title: Associated Flow Rule
objects: Plastic strain rate normal to the yield surface.
structure: Normality plus convexity gives maximum plastic dissipation, and it makes the elastoplastic tangent stiffness symmetric — a major computational advantage. Non-associated rules (common in soils) break that symmetry and force unsymmetric solvers.
reduction: The rule is a normal-cone condition.
status: Exact linear as a normality condition.

title: Isotropic Hardening
objects: Uniform expansion of the yield surface.
structure: Scales the yield surface without moving its centre, so it is a scalar multiple of the original set. Cannot represent the Bauschinger effect, since the surface stays centred — that requires the next entry.
reduction: Hardening is a scalar scaling of the yield set.

title: Kinematic Hardening
objects: Translation of the yield surface by a back-stress tensor 𝛼.
structure: A rigid translation in stress space — an aﬀine shift of the yield set. Captures the Bauschinger effect and cyclic behaviour. Combined isotropic–kinematic models scale and translate simultaneously.
reduction: Hardening is an aﬀine shift of the yield set.

title: Ramberg–Osgood Relation
objects: A linear elastic term plus a power-law plastic term.
structure: Explicitly the sum of a linear and a nonlinear contribution — the decomposition of total strain into elastic and plastic parts made concrete. Only the first term admits a matrix form.
reduction: Linear in the elastic part only.

title: Maxwell Viscoelastic Model
objects: A first-order linear ODE — spring and dashpot in series.
structure: Relaxation modulus 𝐸(𝑡) = 𝐸𝑒−𝑡/𝜏with 𝜏= 𝜂/𝐸: the response is a matrix exponential. Fluid-like, since stress relaxes to zero under constant strain. Generalised Maxwell models sum several such exponentials — a Prony series.
reduction: The model is a linear ODE, hence a matrix exponential.

title: Kelvin–Voigt Model
objects: Spring and dashpot in parallel; also linear.
structure: Creep compliance 𝐽(𝑡) = 1 𝐸(1 −𝑒−𝑡/𝜏) — solid-like, since strain saturates. Maxwell and Kelvin–Voigt are the two elementary two-element models, and both are single-pole linear systems.
reduction: The model is a linear ODE.

title: Standard Linear Solid
objects: A three-parameter linear model with two time constants.
structure: Exhibits both instantaneous elasticity and equilibrium stiffness, so it captures creep and relaxation together. As a linear system it is a first-order transfer function with one pole and one zero.
reduction: The model is a first-order linear system.

title: Boltzmann Superposition Integral
objects: Convolution with the relaxation modulus.
structure: Linearity is the entire content — the response to a sum of histories is the sum of responses. Discretised, it is multiplication by a lower-triangular Toeplitz matrix, so viscoelasticity is a causal linear filter.
reduction: The response is a Toeplitz matrix product.

title: Complex Modulus
objects: The Fourier transform of the relaxation modulus.
structure: Storage and loss moduli are the real and imaginary parts, related by Kramers–Kronig — that is, by the Hilbert transform matrix. Causality forces one to determine the other, exactly as in the optics case.
reduction: The modulus is a Fourier-domain multiplier.

title: Time–Temperature Superposition (WLF)
objects: A horizontal shift of curves on a logarithmic time axis.
structure: Shifting is a translation in log 𝑡, hence a linear operation in that coordinate; master curve construction is fitting a single curve to shifted data, which is a linear least-squares problem given the shift factors.
reduction: Superposition is translation in log time.

title: Norton Creep Law
objects: A power law in stress with Arrhenius temperature dependence.
structure: Linear in ln ̇𝜀against ln 𝜎and 1/𝑇, so parameter fitting is a two-variable linear regression. Typically 𝑛= 3–8, and the exponent identifies the dominant creep mechanism.
reduction: Linear after logarithmic transformation.

title: Larson–Miller Parameter
objects: A time–temperature equivalence for rupture.
structure: Collapses rupture data at many temperatures onto a single master curve, which is a rank-one factori- sation of the two-variable rupture surface: log 𝑡𝑟becomes a function of 𝑃alone. Data collapse is a rank-one approximation.
reduction: The collapse is a rank-one factorisation.
status: Exact linear as a rank-one collapse. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 59

title: Thermal Strain
objects: A scalar multiple of the identity for isotropic materials.
structure: Purely volumetric with zero deviatoric part, so free thermal expansion produces no shear and no stress. Anisotropic materials have a symmetric expansion tensor 𝛼whose eigenvectors are the principal expansion directions.
reduction: Thermal strain is a scalar times the identity.

title: Duhamel–Neumann Constitutive Law
objects: Hooke’s law with a thermal eigenstrain subtracted.
structure: Linear in both 𝜀and Δ𝑇, so the stress is 𝐶𝜀−𝛽Δ𝑇with 𝛽= 𝐶∶𝛼𝐼the thermal stress coeﬀicient. In block form the mechanical–thermal coupling appears as the column −𝛽.
reduction: Coupling is a linear term in the temperature.

title: Thermal Stress in Full Constraint
objects: The stress when 𝜀= 0 is imposed.
structure: Setting the total strain to zero and solving gives the constraint reaction — a Lagrange multiplier for the kinematic constraint. The factor 1/(1 −𝜈) is the biaxial modulus, an entry of the constrained compliance.
reduction: The stress is a constraint multiplier.

title: Coupled Heat Equation with Deformation
objects: The block system ( 𝑀𝑢𝑢 0 𝐶𝑇𝑢𝐶𝑇𝑇) with a non-symmetric coupling.
structure: The mechanical-to-thermal coupling appears in the damping block while the thermal-to-mechanical coupling sits in the stiffness — the assembled system is unsymmetric unless scaled. Symmetrising it is possible by a diagonal rescaling, which is what monolithic thermoelastic solvers do.
reduction: Coupling becomes off-diagonal blocks.

title: Thermoelastic Damping (Zener)
objects: A Debye peak from a single-pole linear system.
structure: The coupled system has complex eigenvalues whose imaginary-to-real ratio gives 𝑄; the peak at 𝜔𝜏= 1 is where the two blocks exchange energy most eﬀiciently. Damping is an eigenvalue property of the coupled matrix.
reduction: Damping is a spectral property of the coupled system.

title: Biot Number
objects: A ratio of boundary to interior conductance.
structure: Bi ≪1 means the interior conduction matrix dominates the boundary term, so the temperature field is nearly uniform and the system collapses to one lumped degree of freedom — a rank-one reduction of the conduction matrix.
reduction: Small Biot number is a rank-one model reduction.

title: Thermal Shock Resistance Parameter
objects: The temperature drop causing failure under full constraint.
structure: Inverts the constrained-stress relation of entry 3 at the failure stress. It is a ratio of material constants, each an entry of the stiffness or expansion matrix.
reduction: The parameter inverts a linear stress relation.

title: Thermal Buckling Load
objects: A generalised eigenvalue problem (𝐾+ Δ𝑇𝐾𝑔)𝜙= 0.
structure: Buckling is the temperature at which the tangent stiffness first becomes singular — the smallest eigenvalue of the pencil (𝐾, −𝐾𝑔) with 𝐾𝑔the geometric stiffness from thermal compression. Instability is loss of positive definiteness.
reduction: Buckling is a generalised eigenproblem.
also_in: Structural Engineering. Poroelasticity and Porous Media

title: Terzaghi Effective Stress
objects: An additive decomposition of total stress.
structure: Pore pressure contributes only to the spherical part, so the deviatoric stress is unaffected — shear strength depends on 𝜎′ alone. This is an orthogonal split into volumetric and deviatoric components.
reduction: The split is a projection onto the spherical part.

title: Biot Effective Stress
objects: Terzaghi with a compressibility-corrected coeﬀicient.
structure: 𝛼𝐵→1 for incompressible grains, recovering Terzaghi. The coeﬀicient is a ratio of bulk moduli, hence a ratio of stiffness eigenvalues.
reduction: The coeﬀicient is a stiffness ratio.

title: Biot Poroelastic Constitutive Law
objects: A symmetric block matrix; m the Voigt identity vector.
structure: Symmetry of the off-diagonal blocks is the poroelastic reciprocity — the same coeﬀicient 𝛼𝐵appears in both couplings, which is an Onsager relation. Positive definiteness of the whole block matrix is thermodynamic admissibility.
reduction: The constitutive law is a symmetric block matrix.

title: Fluid Content Storage Equation
objects: A diffusion equation for pore pressure coupled to volumetric strain.
structure: Combining with the constitutive law gives ̇𝑝driven by both a Laplacian and ̇𝜀𝑣— the coupled system ( 𝐾−𝑄 𝑄⊤ 𝑆) is symmetric indefinite, exactly the KKT structure of a saddle-point problem.
reduction: The coupled system is a symmetric saddle-point matrix.

title: Darcy’s Law
objects: A permeability tensor mapping pressure gradient to flux.
structure: 𝑘is symmetric positive definite for a physically admissible medium — symmetry is an Onsager relation, positive definiteness is the second law. Anisotropic media have distinct eigenvalues, giving preferential flow directions.
reduction: Flux is a matrix times a gradient.

title: Terzaghi Consolidation Equation
objects: A diffusion equation for excess pore pressure.
structure: Identical in form to the heat equation, so the discretised operator is the symmetric negative semidefinite Laplacian and the solution is 𝑒−𝑐𝑣𝐿𝑡u0. Consolidation time scales as 𝐿2/𝑐𝑣from the smallest nonzero eigenvalue.
reduction: Consolidation is a matrix exponential.

title: Degree of Consolidation
objects: A modal expansion in the Laplacian eigenbasis.
structure: Each term is one eigenmode decaying at its own rate; the series is the spectral decomposition of 𝑒−𝐿𝑡 applied to the initial condition. Higher modes decay fastest, so the response is soon dominated by the first.
reduction: The series is a spectral expansion.

title: Skempton Coeﬀicient
objects: An off-diagonal ratio in the undrained compliance matrix.
structure: The pressure response to applied stress at constant fluid content — obtained by taking a Schur complement of the poroelastic block matrix with respect to the fluid degree of freedom. Undrained behaviour is a condensation.
reduction: The coeﬀicient is a Schur complement entry.

title: Poroelastic Wave Speeds (Biot)
objects: Eigenvalues of a 2 × 2 (or 3 × 3) coupled Christoffel matrix. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 18
structure: Coupling the solid and fluid momentum equations gives a generalised eigenproblem whose three roots are the two compressional speeds and one shear speed. The slow P wave is diffusive at low frequency — its eigenvalue has a large imaginary part.
reduction: Wave speeds are eigenvalues of a coupled matrix.

title: Kozeny–Carman Permeability
objects: A scalar constitutive correlation.
structure: An empirical relation between geometry and the permeability tensor’s magnitude. Nonlinear in porosity; only the resulting 𝑘enters linearly through Darcy’s law.
reduction: Not linear in the porosity.
status: Structural analogue. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 19

title: Richards Equation
objects: A diffusion equation with solution-dependent conductivity.
structure: Genuinely nonlinear, since 𝐾depends on 𝜃. Newton linearisation gives a sequence of symmetric positive definite systems, each with the current 𝐾(𝜃) frozen — the standard solution strategy.
reduction: Newton linearisation gives linear systems.
also_in: Hydrology. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 20 Fluid–Structure Interaction

title: Kinematic Interface Condition
objects: A linear constraint coupling two field variables.
structure: Enforced by Lagrange multipliers (mortar methods) giving a saddle-point block system, or by direct elimination. The constraint matrix is the interface trace operator, and its rank is the number of interface degrees of freedom.
reduction: The condition is a linear constraint.

title: Dynamic Interface Condition
objects: Traction continuity — the dual of the kinematic condition.
structure: The two interface conditions are adjoint: the kinematic constraint matrix and the traction transfer matrix are transposes. This transposition is what makes monolithic FSI systems symmetric when the physics permits.
reduction: The condition is the transpose of the kinematic constraint.

title: Added Mass Coeﬀicient
objects: An additive modification of the mass matrix.
structure: The fluid’s inertial reaction appears as an extra positive definite mass matrix, obtained by condensing out the fluid pressure — a Schur complement. For dense fluids 𝑀𝑎can exceed 𝑀𝑠, which destabilises partitioned solvers.
reduction: Added mass is a Schur complement of the fluid block.

title: Reduced Velocity
objects: A ratio comparing flow and structural timescales.
structure: 𝑓𝑛comes from the structural eigenproblem (𝐾−𝜔2𝑀)𝜙= 0, so the parameter compares a flow velocity to a spectral quantity. Lock-in occurs when the shedding frequency approaches an eigenvalue.
reduction: The frequency is an eigenvalue.

title: Strouhal Number
objects: The shedding frequency of the wake instability.
structure: Arises as the imaginary part of the least stable eigenvalue of the linearised Navier–Stokes operator about the steady wake — global stability analysis. The remarkable constancy near 0.2 is the near-invariance of that eigenvalue over a wide Reynolds range.
reduction: The frequency is an eigenvalue of the linearised operator.

title: Flutter Speed (Binary Model)
objects: A quadratic eigenvalue problem with a speed-dependent aerodynamic matrix.
structure: Flutter is the dynamic pressure 𝑞at which an eigenvalue crosses the imaginary axis — a Hopf bifurca- tion in the coupled system. The aerodynamic matrix 𝐴is non-symmetric, which is precisely what permits energy extraction from the flow.
reduction: Flutter is an eigenvalue crossing.

title: Divergence Speed
objects: A static instability — singularity of the coupled stiffness.
structure: Divergence is loss of invertibility of 𝐾+ 𝑞𝐴𝑠, the static analogue of buckling. It is a generalised eigenproblem for the critical dynamic pressure, with the null vector giving the divergence mode shape.
reduction: Divergence is a generalised eigenproblem.

title: Theodorsen Function
objects: A frequency-domain transfer function for unsteady lift.
structure: A complex multiplier on the quasi-steady lift, capturing the wake’s memory. Being causal, its real and imaginary parts satisfy Kramers–Kronig — related by the Hilbert transform matrix.
reduction: The function is a frequency-domain multiplier.

title: Womersley Number
objects: A ratio of unsteady inertia to viscous diffusion.
structure: Large Wo gives a plug-like profile with a thin Stokes layer; small Wo gives quasi-Poiseuille flow. The velocity profile is a Bessel-function eigenmode, so the parameter selects which eigenmode dominates.
reduction: The parameter selects a modal regime.

title: Moens–Korteweg Pulse Wave Velocity
objects: A wave speed from a coupled fluid–wall system.
structure: Emerges as the eigenvalue of a 2×2 hyperbolic system coupling flow rate and area, with wall compliance supplying the restoring term. Stiffer walls raise the speed, which is the basis of arterial stiffness measurement.
reduction: The speed is an eigenvalue of a coupled hyperbolic system.

title: Water Hammer (Joukowsky) Pressure Rise
objects: A Riemann invariant relation across a characteristic.
structure: 𝜌𝑐is the acoustic impedance — the off-diagonal entry linking pressure and velocity in the 2 × 2 characteristic system. Pressure and velocity jumps are coupled by exactly this impedance across each wave.
reduction: The relation is a characteristic (eigenvector) condition.

title: Piezoelectric Constitutive Equations
objects: A block matrix with the piezoelectric tensor 𝑒off-diagonal.
structure: The off-diagonal blocks are transposes of each other up to sign — a reciprocity relation guaranteeing that the coupled system derives from a single energy function. Direct and converse piezoelectric effects are the two off-diagonal blocks.
reduction: Coupling is an off-diagonal block pair.

title: Electromechanical Coupling Factor
objects: A normalised measure of off-diagonal dominance.
structure: Exactly the ratio of the off-diagonal product to the diagonal product in the 2 × 2 block matrix — the same quantity that controls the eigenvalue splitting. Positive definiteness requires 𝑘2 < 1, so the bound is a definiteness condition.
reduction: The factor measures block off-diagonal dominance.

title: Electrostrictive Strain
objects: Quadratic in the field, hence not linear.
structure: Present in all dielectrics, unlike piezoelectricity which requires broken centrosymmetry. Being quadratic, it produces no linear coupling block — linearising about a bias field 𝐸0 gives an effective piezoelectric coeﬀicient 2𝑄𝐸0.
reduction: Linearisation about a bias field gives a linear coupling.

title: Maxwell Stress Tensor
objects: A symmetric traceless-plus-isotropic matrix quadratic in the field.
structure: Quadratic in E, so the mechanical response is nonlinear in the field. The tensor is symmetric with eigenvalues ( 1 2𝜖𝐸2, −1 2𝜖𝐸2, −1 2𝜖𝐸2) — tension along the field lines and pressure across them.
reduction: Quadratic in the field; the tensor itself is a matrix.
status: Exact linear as a tensor, quadratic in the field.

title: Electrostatic Pull-In Voltage
objects: A saddle-node bifurcation in the coupled system.
structure: The effective stiffness 𝑘−𝜕𝐹𝑒/𝜕𝑔vanishes at pull-in — the tangent stiffness matrix becomes singular. Instability at one third of the gap is where the linearised system first loses positive definiteness.
reduction: Pull-in is loss of definiteness of the tangent stiffness.
status: Exact linear at the stability condition.

title: Magnetostrictive Strain
objects: Quadratic in magnetisation.
structure: Like electrostriction, quadratic and hence with no linear coupling block. Biasing about 𝑀0 gives an effective linear piezomagnetic coeﬀicient, which is how magnetostrictive actuators are operated.
reduction: Linearisation about a bias magnetisation.

title: Villari (Inverse Magnetostrictive) Effect
objects: The reciprocal off-diagonal block to magnetostriction.
structure: Reciprocity requires the two off-diagonal blocks to be transposes when both are linearised about the same bias — an Onsager relation. Used for stress sensing.
reduction: The effect is the transposed coupling block.

title: Magnetohydrodynamic Induction Equation
objects: Advection plus diffusion of a vector field.
structure: Linear in B for a prescribed v, so the kinematic dynamo problem is an eigenvalue problem for the induction operator — growth occurs when an eigenvalue has positive real part. The full MHD problem is nonlinear through the Lorentz force feedback.
reduction: The equation is linear in B for given v.
status: Exact linear in the kinematic problem.

title: Lorentz Force Density
objects: A skew matrix acting on the magnetic field.
structure: Skew-symmetry means the force is perpendicular to both current and field, so it does no work on the current carriers. Decomposes into magnetic pressure and tension via the Maxwell stress tensor.
reduction: The cross product is a skew matrix.

title: Magnetic Reynolds Number
objects: The ratio of advection to diffusion in the induction operator.
structure: The relative weight of the two terms in the induction equation. Large Rm means the advective (non- normal) part dominates, giving field line freezing and transient amplification; small Rm means the symmetric diffusive part dominates and the field decays.
reduction: The number weights two operator terms.

title: Hartmann Number
objects: The ratio of Lorentz to viscous forces.
structure: Large Ha produces the Hartmann boundary layer of thickness 𝐿/Ha, a boundary-layer eigenmode of the coupled operator. The flow profile flattens because the magnetic term dominates the viscous one in the interior.
reduction: The number weights two terms of a linear operator.

title: Chemical Potential with Stress
objects: A linear coupling of hydrostatic stress into the chemical potential.
structure: 𝜎ℎ= 1 3 tr 𝜎, so only the spherical part couples — the deviator does not affect diffusion at this order. The coupling coeﬀicient Ω is the partial molar volume.
reduction: The coupling is linear in a trace.

title: Stress-Assisted Diffusion Flux
objects: Two driving gradients with a matrix diffusivity.
structure: The flux is a linear map of the combined driving force ∇𝜇; writing it as J = −𝐿∇𝜇with 𝐿⪰0 makes the Onsager structure explicit. The two terms are the diagonal and off-diagonal contributions.
reduction: The flux is a matrix times a generalised gradient.

title: Diffusion-Induced Stress
objects: An eigenstrain from composition, structurally identical to thermal strain.
structure: Concentration plays exactly the role of temperature in the Duhamel–Neumann law, so the chemo- mechanical block matrix has the same form as the thermomechanical one. The analogy is exact at the level of the matrix structure.
reduction: Composition acts as a thermal-like eigenstrain.

title: Swelling Pressure (Flory–Rehner)
objects: A nonlinear function of the polymer fraction.
structure: Genuinely nonlinear in 𝜙. Linearising about the equilibrium swelling ratio gives an effective osmotic modulus, which is what enters the linearised poroelastic block matrix.
reduction: Linearisation about equilibrium gives a modulus.

title: Poroelastic Swelling Time
objects: The reciprocal of the smallest nonzero diffusion eigenvalue.
structure: Diffusive scaling means 𝜏is set by 𝜆1 of the discretised Laplacian on the domain, which scales as 𝐿−2. The relaxation spectrum is the full eigenvalue set.
reduction: The time constant is a reciprocal eigenvalue.

title: Nernst–Planck Equation
objects: Diffusion, migration, and advection combined linearly.
structure: Linear in the fluxes given the fields, but coupled to Poisson’s equation for 𝜙— the resulting Poisson– Nernst–Planck system is nonlinear through the 𝑐𝑖∇𝜙product. Linearising about equilibrium gives the Debye– Hückel theory.
reduction: Linear in the fluxes; nonlinear through the field coupling.

title: Poisson–Boltzmann Equation
objects: A nonlinear Poisson equation.
structure: The exponential makes it nonlinear; linearising for |𝑧𝑒𝜙| ≪𝑘𝑇gives the Debye–Hückel equation ∇2𝜙= 𝜅2𝜙— a Helmholtz operator whose eigenvalue 𝜅2 sets the screening length.
reduction: Debye–Hückel linearisation gives a Helmholtz operator.

title: Debye Length
objects: The reciprocal of the Helmholtz operator’s eigenvalue.
structure: 𝜆𝐷= 1/𝜅where 𝜅2 is the coeﬀicient in the linearised Poisson–Boltzmann operator. Screening is exponential decay at the rate set by that eigenvalue.
reduction: The length is a reciprocal operator eigenvalue.

title: Electroosmotic Velocity (Smoluchowski)
objects: A linear response of velocity to applied field.
structure: Plug-like flow, linear in 𝐸— one entry of the electrokinetic coupling matrix. The mobility −𝜖𝜁/𝜇is the off-diagonal Onsager coeﬀicient linking electrical and hydrodynamic transport.
reduction: The velocity is a linear response coeﬀicient.

title: Electrophoretic Mobility
objects: The particle-frame counterpart of electroosmosis.
structure: Same magnitude, opposite sign — the two effects are the same off-diagonal coeﬀicient viewed from two frames. Their equality is a reciprocity statement.
reduction: The mobility is the same coupling coeﬀicient.

title: Streaming Potential
objects: The reciprocal off-diagonal coeﬀicient to electroosmosis.
structure: Onsager reciprocity requires the pressure-driven current coeﬀicient to equal the field-driven flow coef- ficient — the electrokinetic matrix ( 𝐿11 𝐿12 𝐿21 𝐿22 ) is symmetric. Streaming potential and electroosmosis are 𝐿21 and 𝐿12.
reduction: The effect is the transposed coupling coeﬀicient.

title: Onsager Reciprocal Relations
objects: Symmetry of the transport coeﬀicient matrix.
structure: The central structural theorem of coupled transport: the phenomenological matrix is symmetric, a consequence of microscopic time-reversibility. Symmetry means the flux–force system is variational, guarantees real eigenvalues, and halves the number of independent coeﬀicients. In a magnetic field the relation becomes 𝐿𝑖𝑗(B) = 𝐿𝑗𝑖(−B).
reduction: Reciprocity is matrix symmetry.
status: Exact linear. The organising principle of this chapter.

title: Thermoelectric Coupled Transport
objects: A symmetric 2 × 2 block transport matrix.
structure: Seebeck and Peltier effects are the two off-diagonal entries, equal by Onsager after the factor 𝑇— the Kelvin relation Π = 𝑆𝑇. Positive semidefiniteness of the matrix is the second law.
reduction: Coupling is an off-diagonal transport block.

title: Thermoelectric Figure of Merit
objects: A normalised measure of off-diagonal dominance.
structure: Exactly the ratio of the squared off-diagonal to the product of diagonals in the transport matrix — the same structural quantity as the piezoelectric coupling factor. Eﬀiciency increases monotonically with 𝑍𝑇, and 𝑍𝑇→∞would reach Carnot.
reduction: The figure of merit measures block off-diagonal dominance.

title: Soret (Thermodiffusion) Flux
objects: An off-diagonal coeﬀicient coupling temperature gradient to mass flux.
structure: The 𝐿12 entry of the mass–heat transport matrix. Its sign varies with system, and it is the mechanism behind thermophoresis and isotope separation columns.
reduction: The effect is an off-diagonal transport coeﬀicient.

title: Dufour Effect
objects: The reciprocal of the Soret effect.
structure: 𝐿21 to Soret’s 𝐿12, equal by Onsager reciprocity. Usually negligible in liquids but significant in gases, where the two coeﬀicients are comparable.
reduction: The effect is the transposed coeﬀicient.

title: Coupled Field Problem Monolithic Form
objects: The general two-field block system. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 58
structure: The whole chapter in one equation. Symmetric off-diagonals (𝐴12 = 𝐴⊤ 21) give a variational structure and permit symmetric solvers; unsymmetric ones require GMRES. Block preconditioners built from the Schur complement 𝐴22 −𝐴21𝐴−1 11 𝐴12 are the standard approach.
reduction: All coupled problems have this form.
status: Exact linear. The organising form of the field.

title: Added Mass Instability Criterion (Partitioned FSI)
objects: Spectral radius of the partitioned iteration matrix. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 59
structure: Partitioned solvers are block Gauss–Seidel on the coupled system, converging only when 𝜌(𝐴−1 11 𝐴12𝐴−1 22 𝐴21) < 1. Heavy fluids make that product’s spectral radius exceed one, so no relaxation factor helps and monolithic solution is required.
reduction: Instability is a spectral radius condition on a block product.

title: Coupling Strength (Dimensionless)
objects: Normalised off-diagonal magnitude.
structure: The general form of 𝑘2 and 𝑍𝑇— a single number measuring how far the block matrix is from block- diagonal. Small Π𝑐justifies staggered solution and perturbative treatment; large Π𝑐forces monolithic coupling. The whole practical taxonomy of coupled problems reduces to this ratio. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 60
reduction: Coupling strength is a normalised off-diagonal norm.

title: Boltzmann Entropy
objects: The logarithm of a dimension — the number of accessible microstates.
structure: Ω is the dimension of the accessible subspace of Hilbert space, so entropy is 𝑘𝐵ln dim. Additivity for independent systems follows from dim(𝑉⊗𝑊) = dim 𝑉dim 𝑊, which becomes addition under the logarithm.
reduction: Entropy is the log of a subspace dimension.

title: Gibbs Entropy
objects: The von Neumann entropy of a density matrix.
structure: 𝜌is Hermitian positive semidefinite with unit trace — a quantum probability vector. Its entropy depends only on the eigenvalues, so it is invariant under unitary evolution: 𝑆is constant under 𝜌↦𝑈𝜌𝑈†.
reduction: Entropy is a spectral functional of a density matrix.

title: Microcanonical Ensemble
objects: The normalised projection onto the energy shell.
structure: Equal probability for all accessible states is exactly the normalised spectral projection 𝑃𝐸of the Hamiltonian onto a narrow energy window. tr 𝑃𝐸= Ω, so the rank of the projection is the multiplicity.
reduction: The ensemble is a normalised spectral projection.

title: Boltzmann Distribution
objects: The matrix exponential of the Hamiltonian, normalised.
structure: 𝜌is diagonal in the energy eigenbasis with entries 𝑒−𝛽𝐸𝑖, so it commutes with 𝐻and is therefore stationary. It is the maximum-entropy state at fixed mean energy — a constrained optimisation whose solution is exponential.
reduction: The distribution is a normalised matrix exponential.

title: Canonical Partition Function
objects: The trace of a matrix exponential.
structure: Basis-independent by cyclic invariance of the trace, which is why 𝑍depends only on the spectrum. For independent subsystems 𝐻= 𝐻1 ⊗𝐼+ 𝐼⊗𝐻2 gives 𝑍= 𝑍1𝑍2 — the trace of a Kronecker sum factorises.
reduction: The partition function is a matrix trace.
status: Exact linear. The organising object of the field.

title: Free Energy from the Partition Function
objects: The log-trace of a matrix exponential.
structure: ln tr 𝑒𝐴is convex in 𝐴, which is the thermodynamic stability condition. Its derivatives generate all cumulants: −𝜕𝛽𝐹/𝜕𝛽gives the energy, the second derivative gives the variance.
reduction: Free energy is a log-trace functional.

title: Average Energy
objects: A trace of a product — the quantum expectation.
structure: ⟨𝐴⟩= tr(𝜌𝐴) is linear in both 𝜌and 𝐴, a bilinear pairing. This is the Hilbert–Schmidt inner product, making observables and states dual to each other.
reduction: Expectation is a matrix inner product.

title: Energy Fluctuation and Heat Capacity
objects: The second derivative of ln 𝑍— a variance, hence a covariance matrix entry.
structure: ln 𝑍is the cumulant generating function, so its Hessian is the covariance matrix of the conserved quan- tities. Positivity of 𝐶𝑉is positive semidefiniteness of that Hessian — thermodynamic stability is a definiteness condition.
reduction: Fluctuations are the Hessian of ln 𝑍.

title: Grand Canonical Partition Function
objects: A trace with a two-parameter exponent. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 10
structure: ln 𝒵is jointly convex in (𝛽, 𝛽𝜇), and its Hessian is the covariance matrix of (𝐸, 𝑁). Particle number fluctuations ⟨Δ𝑁2⟩= 𝑘𝐵𝑇𝜕𝑁/𝜕𝜇are one entry of that matrix.
reduction: The generating function is a trace; fluctuations are its Hessian.

title: Classical Phase Space Partition Function
objects: The classical limit of the trace. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 11
structure: tr →∫𝑑Γ/ℎ3𝑁— the trace becomes a phase-space integral with ℎ3𝑁as the cell volume. The 𝑁! is the order of the permutation group being quotiented out, a group-theoretic correction.
reduction: The trace becomes a phase-space integral.

title: Equipartition Theorem
objects: Diagonality of a correlation matrix.
structure: For a quadratic Hamiltonian 𝐻= 1 2x⊤𝐴x the covariance is ⟨xx⊤⟩= 𝑘𝐵𝑇𝐴−1, so each quadratic mode carries 1 2𝑘𝐵𝑇regardless of its stiffness. Equipartition is the statement that the covariance is the inverse Hessian. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 12
reduction: The covariance is the inverse of the Hamiltonian’s Hessian.

title: Maxwell–Boltzmann Speed Distribution
objects: A Gaussian in velocity space with the radial Jacobian.
structure: The velocity distribution is 𝑁(0, 𝑘𝐵𝑇 𝑚𝐼) — isotropic Gaussian with covariance a multiple of the identity. Isotropy is invariance under 𝑂(3), which is exactly the statement that the covariance is a scalar matrix. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 13
reduction: The distribution is an isotropic Gaussian.

title: Characteristic Speeds
objects: Three moments of the same Gaussian.
structure: 𝑣2 rms = tr Σ for the velocity covariance — the trace, hence basis-independent. The ordering 𝑣𝑝< ̄𝑣< 𝑣rms follows from Jensen’s inequality applied to the convex square.
reduction: The speeds are moments of a Gaussian covariance.

title: Barometric Formula
objects: The Boltzmann factor for a linear potential.
structure: A linear potential gives an exponential density profile — the eigenfunction of the translation operator. The scale height 𝑘𝐵𝑇/𝑚𝑔is the decay rate, and the whole profile is 𝑒−𝛽𝑈with 𝑈linear.
reduction: The profile is a Boltzmann exponential of a linear potential.

title: Ideal Gas Partition Function
objects: A product over independent particles.
structure: Independence means the Hamiltonian is a Kronecker sum, so 𝑍factorises into 𝑁identical single- particle traces. The 𝑁! corrects for the indistinguishability quotient.
reduction: Independence gives a product of traces.

title: Sackur–Tetrode Equation
objects: Entropy from the log of a factorised trace.
structure: The 𝑁! correction is what makes 𝑆extensive — without it entropy fails to be homogeneous degree one, which is the Gibbs paradox. Extensivity is the Euler homogeneity condition of field 26.
reduction: Entropy is a log-trace made extensive by a quotient.

title: Density of States
objects: The spectral measure of the Hamiltonian.
structure: Literally the eigenvalue distribution of 𝐻— the same object as the spectral density of a random matrix. 𝑍= ∫𝑔(𝐸)𝑒−𝛽𝐸𝑑𝐸is its Laplace transform, so the partition function and the density of states are a transform pair.
reduction: The density of states is a spectral measure.

title: Factorisation of Molecular Partition Functions
objects: A Kronecker sum Hamiltonian giving a product of traces.
structure: Separability of the degrees of freedom means 𝐻= ⨁𝑘𝐻𝑘, so 𝑒−𝛽𝐻= ⨂𝑘𝑒−𝛽𝐻𝑘and the trace factorises. Coupling between modes breaks the factorisation, which is why anharmonicity is hard.
reduction: Separability is a Kronecker sum structure.

title: Vibrational Partition Function
objects: A geometric series — the trace of a harmonic oscillator’s Boltzmann matrix.
structure: The oscillator spectrum is arithmetic, 𝐸𝑛= ℏ𝜔(𝑛+ 1 2), so the trace is a geometric series. Convergence requires 𝛽ℏ𝜔> 0, and the sum is a resolvent-like expression (1 −𝑥)−1.
reduction: The trace is a geometric series over an arithmetic spectrum.

title: Einstein Solid Heat Capacity
objects: 3𝑁identical oscillators — a degenerate spectrum.
structure: All modes share one frequency, so the phonon spectral density is a single delta function. This gives the correct high-temperature limit but exponentially wrong low-temperature behaviour, because a single eigenvalue cannot reproduce the true density of states near zero.
reduction: The model replaces the spectrum by one eigenvalue.
status: Exact linear with a rank-one spectral approximation.

title: Debye Heat Capacity
objects: A continuous phonon spectral density 𝑔(𝜔) ∝𝜔2.
structure: Replacing the single Einstein eigenvalue by a quadratic density of states — the correct low-frequency form for a three-dimensional elastic medium — gives the 𝑇3 law. The improvement is entirely in the spectral density.
reduction: The model uses the correct low-frequency spectral density.

title: Fermi–Dirac Distribution
objects: Occupation numbers as eigenvalues of the one-particle density matrix.
structure: 0 ≤ ̄𝑛𝑖≤1 is forced by antisymmetry — the one-particle density matrix has eigenvalues bounded by one, which is the Pauli principle stated spectrally. The +1 in the denominator is exactly this bound.
reduction: Occupations are one-particle density matrix eigenvalues.

title: Bose–Einstein Distribution
objects: Unbounded occupations from symmetric states.
structure: The −1 permits ̄𝑛→∞as 𝐸→𝜇, which is condensation. Requires 𝜇< 𝐸0 for convergence — the chemical potential must stay below the ground state eigenvalue, and the transition occurs when it reaches it.
reduction: Occupations are density matrix eigenvalues without an upper bound.

title: Fermi Energy
objects: The 𝑁-th eigenvalue of the single-particle Hamiltonian.
structure: Filling the lowest 𝑁eigenstates gives the Fermi level as an order statistic of the spectrum. The Fermi surface is a level set of the dispersion relation, and its topology controls transport.
reduction: The Fermi energy is an order statistic of the spectrum.

title: Sommerfeld Expansion
objects: A low-temperature expansion about the step function.
structure: The Fermi function is a smoothed step whose derivative is sharply peaked at 𝜇— the expansion is a moment expansion of that kernel. It gives 𝐶𝑉∝𝑇for metals, linear in temperature because only states within 𝑘𝐵𝑇of 𝐸𝐹participate.
reduction: The expansion is a moment expansion of a peaked kernel.

title: Degeneracy Pressure
objects: Pressure from the filled spectrum alone, at zero temperature.
structure: Purely a consequence of the eigenvalue distribution and the exclusion bound on occupations — no interaction required. It supports white dwarfs and neutron stars, so a spectral bound holds up stars.
reduction: Pressure is a functional of the filled spectrum.

title: Bose–Einstein Condensation Temperature
objects: The temperature at which the ground-state eigenvalue’s occupation becomes macroscopic.
structure: Below 𝑇𝑐the density matrix acquires a macroscopic eigenvalue — condensation is the emergence of a rank-one component of order 𝑁. The condensate fraction is that eigenvalue divided by 𝑁, which is the Penrose–Onsager criterion for off-diagonal long-range order.
reduction: Condensation is a macroscopic density matrix eigenvalue.

title: Planck Distribution
objects: Bose statistics applied to the photon mode spectrum.
structure: The mode density ∝𝜈2 is the density of states of the electromagnetic field in a box — an eigenvalue count for the Laplacian. Planck’s law is a Bose occupation times a spectral density.
reduction: The law is an occupation times a density of states.

title: Rayleigh–Jeans and Wien Limits
objects: Two limits of the same occupation function.
structure: The classical limit replaces each mode’s occupation by 𝑘𝐵𝑇/ℎ𝜈— equipartition applied to every mode, which diverges when summed because the spectrum is unbounded. The ultraviolet catastrophe is a divergent trace.
reduction: The classical limit is equipartition over an unbounded spectrum.

title: Photon Gas Thermodynamics
objects: Integrals over the photon spectral density.
structure: The 𝑇4 law comes from integrating 𝜈3/(𝑒𝑥−1) over the quadratic mode density — a moment of the spectrum. The factor 1/3 in the pressure is the trace of the radiation stress tensor divided by three, reflecting masslessness.
reduction: The relations are spectral moments.

title: Ising Model Hamiltonian
objects: A quadratic form in the spin vector with the adjacency matrix.
structure: The energy is a quadratic form s⊤𝐴s with s ∈{±1}𝑛— the discreteness is what makes it hard. Relaxing to s ∈ℝ𝑛gives a solvable eigenvalue problem; the integer constraint makes ground state finding NP- hard.
reduction: The energy is a quadratic form on the hypercube.
status: Exact linear (quadratic form) with an integrality constraint.

title: Mean Field Self-Consistency
objects: A fixed-point equation replacing the matrix by its row sum.
structure: Mean field replaces 𝐴s by 𝑧̄𝑚1 — a rank-one approximation of the interaction matrix. The approxi- mation is exact when 𝐴= 𝐽/𝑛(fully connected), where the matrix genuinely has rank one.
reduction: Mean field is a rank-one approximation of the coupling matrix.

title: Curie–Weiss Law
objects: Divergence of a response function.
structure: Susceptibility is 𝜕𝑚/𝜕ℎ, an entry of the inverse Hessian of the free energy. It diverges when the Hessian becomes singular — the critical point is where an eigenvalue of the stability matrix reaches zero.
reduction: Divergence is an inverse-Hessian singularity.

title: Onsager Exact 2-D Ising Solution
objects: The transfer matrix’s largest eigenvalue.
structure: Onsager diagonalised the transfer matrix by mapping it to free fermions — the exact solution is a full eigendecomposition of a 2𝐿× 2𝐿matrix reduced by symmetry to a manageable form. The critical point is where the two largest eigenvalues become degenerate.
reduction: The solution is a transfer matrix diagonalisation.

title: Order Parameter
objects: A normalised linear functional of the state.
structure: Zero in the symmetric phase, nonzero below 𝑇𝑐— symmetry breaking is the ground state ceasing to be an eigenvector of the symmetry operator. The order parameter is the projection onto the broken direction.
reduction: The order parameter is a projection onto a symmetry direction.

title: Critical Exponents
objects: Eigenvalues of the linearised renormalisation group map.
structure: Each exponent is determined by an eigenvalue of 𝜕𝛽/𝜕g at the fixed point. Relevant directions have Re 𝜆> 0; the number of relevant eigenvalues is the codimension of the critical surface, hence how many parameters must be tuned.
reduction: Exponents are eigenvalues of a linearised flow.
status: Linearised, and the linearisation is exact for the exponents.

title: Scaling Relations
objects: Linear relations among the exponents.
structure: All exponents derive from just two independent eigenvalues of the RG matrix, so the four or five exponents satisfy linear constraints — a rank-two condition. The relations are exactly the statement that the exponent vector lies in a two-dimensional subspace.
reduction: The relations are a rank condition on the exponent vector.

title: Landau Free Energy Expansion
objects: A Taylor expansion truncated at quartic order.
structure: The quadratic coeﬀicient is the Hessian eigenvalue, changing sign at 𝑡= 0. The quartic term stabilises the expansion — a second-order transition is a Hessian eigenvalue crossing zero with a positive quartic, and a first-order transition occurs when 𝑏< 0.
reduction: The expansion is a Hessian with a quartic stabiliser.

title: Ginzburg–Landau Functional
objects: A quadratic form plus a quartic term.
structure: The quadratic part discretises to 𝑎𝐼+ ℏ2 2𝑚𝐿with 𝐿the Laplacian; instability begins when its smallest eigenvalue crosses zero. The correlation length is √ℏ2/2𝑚|𝑎| — the reciprocal square root of the eigenvalue gap.
reduction: The quadratic part is a shifted Laplacian.

title: Correlation Function
objects: Entries of the covariance matrix of the spin field.
structure: 𝐺is literally the covariance matrix, hence positive semidefinite. Exponential decay at rate 1/𝜉comes from the transfer matrix’s spectral gap: 𝜉−1 = ln(𝜆1/𝜆2). Criticality is 𝜆2 →𝜆1, so 𝜉→∞.
reduction: Correlations are a covariance matrix; the range is a spectral gap.

title: Fluctuation–Dissipation (Susceptibility Sum Rule)
objects: A quadratic form in the covariance matrix.
structure: Susceptibility is the total covariance contracted with the all-ones vector, so its divergence at criticality is the divergence of 1⊤Σ1 as correlations become long-ranged. Response and fluctuation are the same matrix viewed twice.
reduction: Susceptibility is a quadratic form in the covariance.

title: Renormalisation Group Recursion
objects: The linearised flow matrix 𝑀at the fixed point.
structure: Eigenvalues 𝜆𝑖= 𝑏𝑦𝑖with 𝑦𝑖> 0 relevant, 𝑦𝑖< 0 irrelevant. Critical exponents are ratios of these eigenvalues, and universality is the statement that 𝑀’s spectrum depends only on symmetry and dimension.
reduction: The RG is a nonlinear map linearised at its fixed point.

title: Universality Class
objects: Equality of the spectra of two linearised flow matrices.
structure: Different microscopic models flow to the same fixed point, so their 𝑀matrices have the same relevant eigenvalues. Irrelevant directions decay, which is why microscopic detail is forgotten — it lies in the contracting eigenspace.
reduction: Universality is spectral coincidence at a fixed point.

title: Upper Critical Dimension
objects: The dimension at which an eigenvalue changes sign.
structure: Above 𝑑𝑐the quartic coupling becomes irrelevant — its RG eigenvalue turns negative — so mean field theory becomes exact. The 𝜖= 4 −𝑑expansion perturbs about that eigenvalue crossing.
reduction: The critical dimension is an eigenvalue sign change.

title: Percolation Threshold
objects: A geometric phase transition with a spectral signature.
structure: On a Bethe lattice 𝑝𝑐= 1/(𝑧−1), which is the reciprocal of the branching matrix’s Perron eigenvalue. For general graphs the threshold relates to ⟨𝑘2⟩/⟨𝑘⟩, also a spectral quantity.
reduction: The threshold is a Perron eigenvalue condition.

title: Transfer Matrix Method
objects: The partition function as a trace of a matrix power.
structure: 𝑍= ∑𝑖𝜆𝑁 𝑖 →𝜆𝑁 1 as 𝑁→∞, so the free energy per site is −𝑘𝐵𝑇ln 𝜆1. Correlation length is 1/ ln(𝜆1/𝜆2), and a phase transition in one dimension requires 𝜆1 to become degenerate — which Perron– Frobenius forbids for a positive matrix. That is the one-line proof that there is no 1-D phase transition.
reduction: The partition function is a matrix power trace.
status: Exact linear. The most purely linear-algebraic entry in the field.

title: Mermin–Wagner Theorem
objects: Divergence of a mode sum.
structure: The fluctuation integral ∫𝑑𝑑𝑘/𝑘2 diverges at small 𝑘for 𝑑≤2 — a divergent sum over the Laplacian’s spectrum near zero. Long-wavelength modes destroy order, and the divergence is a spectral one.
reduction: The theorem is a divergence of a spectral sum.

title: Kosterlitz–Thouless Transition
objects: A topological transition with no local order parameter.
structure: Vortex unbinding — the transition is in the topology of the configuration, not in any linear functional of the field. Correlation functions decay as a power law on both sides, so no spectral gap opens. This is where the linear order-parameter framework genuinely fails. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 48
reduction: Not available; the order is topological.

title: Boltzmann Transport Equation
objects: Linear streaming with a nonlinear collision operator.
structure: The left side is exactly linear in 𝑓— a transport operator. The collision term is quadratic in 𝑓, which is the source of irreversibility. Linearising about equilibrium gives the linearised collision operator, which is symmetric negative semidefinite with a five-dimensional null space (the collision invariants).
reduction: Streaming is linear; collisions linearise about equilibrium.
status: Linearised. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 49

title: H-Theorem
objects: Monotonicity of a convex functional.
structure: The linearised collision operator is negative semidefinite, so ̇ 𝐻= −f⊤𝐶f ≤0 — the H-theorem is a definiteness statement. Its null space is the equilibrium manifold, spanned by the collision invariants.
reduction: The theorem is negative semidefiniteness of the collision operator.

title: Langevin Equation
objects: A linear SDE with a matrix friction and noise covariance.
structure: Exactly linear, so the stationary covariance solves the Lyapunov equation ΓΣ + ΣΓ⊤= 2𝐷. Equipar- tition Σ = 𝑘𝐵𝑇𝑀−1 then forces 𝐷= 𝛾𝑘𝐵𝑇— the fluctuation–dissipation relation is the solution of a Lyapunov equation.
reduction: The equation is a linear SDE; equilibrium is a Lyapunov solution.

title: Einstein Relation
objects: Off-diagonal consistency between mobility and diffusion matrices.
structure: 𝐷= 𝜇𝑘𝐵𝑇as matrices, not just scalars — anisotropic mobility gives anisotropic diffusion with the same eigenvectors. It is the fluctuation–dissipation theorem in its simplest form, and it follows from the Lyapunov equation above.
reduction: The relation equates two matrices up to a scalar.

title: Stokes–Einstein Relation
objects: Einstein’s relation with the Stokes mobility substituted.
structure: Combines the linear Stokes drag (mobility matrix) with the Einstein relation. For non-spherical particles the mobility matrix is anisotropic, giving a diffusion tensor with the same principal axes.
reduction: Substituting a linear mobility into a matrix identity.

title: Mean Squared Displacement
objects: The trace of the displacement covariance matrix.
structure: ⟨ΔrΔr⊤⟩= 2𝐷𝑡as a matrix; the MSD is its trace. Anomalous diffusion ∼𝑡𝛼signals that the underlying process is not a linear SDE with white noise.
reduction: The MSD is a covariance trace.

title: Green–Kubo Relations
objects: Transport coeﬀicients as time integrals of correlation matrices.
structure: Each transport coeﬀicient is the time integral of an autocorrelation matrix — so the Onsager matrix 𝐿is built entirely from equilibrium correlation functions. Symmetry of 𝐿follows from time-reversal symmetry of the correlations, which is the microscopic origin of Onsager reciprocity.
reduction: Transport coeﬀicients are integrals of correlation matrices.

title: Fluctuation–Dissipation Theorem
objects: A relation between the response and correlation spectra.
structure: Response and fluctuation are the imaginary part and the spectrum of the same matrix-valued function. Causality additionally links 𝜒′ and 𝜒″ by Kramers–Kronig — the Hilbert transform matrix. Two linear relations pin the whole response.
reduction: Response and fluctuation are two views of one matrix function.

title: Onsager Regression Hypothesis
objects: Spontaneous fluctuations decay by the same linear operator as macroscopic relaxation.
structure: Both are governed by the same generator matrix, so their decay is a sum of the same exponentials 𝑒−𝜆𝑖𝑡. The hypothesis is the assertion that one matrix controls both, which is what Green–Kubo makes precise.
reduction: One generator governs both processes.

title: Jarzynski Equality
objects: An exact identity for a nonlinear average.
structure: Exact for arbitrarily fast driving, but the average is of an exponential — a nonlinear functional dominated by rare trajectories. Jensen’s inequality applied to it recovers ⟨𝑊⟩≥Δ𝐹, the second law.
reduction: The second law follows by Jensen from a nonlinear average.

title: Crooks Fluctuation Theorem
objects: A ratio of forward and reverse path probabilities.
structure: A detailed-balance-like relation between two path measures, generalising the microscopic reversibility condition 𝜋𝑖𝑃𝑖𝑗= 𝜋𝑗𝑃𝑗𝑖to driven systems. Jarzynski follows by integration.
reduction: The theorem generalises detailed balance.

title: Landauer’s Principle
objects: The energy cost of a rank-reducing operation.
structure: Erasing a bit halves the dimension of the accessible state space, so entropy falls by 𝑘𝐵ln 2 — a rank reduction, which the second law says must be paid for. Reversible (unitary, rank-preserving) computation costs nothing in principle.
reduction: Erasure is a rank reduction.

title: State Vector and Born Rule
objects: A unit vector in a complex Hilbert space; 𝑃𝑖the eigenprojection.
structure: Probabilities are squared projection norms, so they automatically sum to one by the resolution of the identity ∑𝑖𝑃𝑖= 𝐼. The state is a vector; the probabilities are a quadratic form. Amplitudes superpose linearly and probabilities do not — interference is exactly that gap.
reduction: None needed.

title: Normalisation
objects: A unit vector on the complex sphere.
structure: Physical states are rays, not vectors — global phase is unobservable, so the state space is ℂℙ𝑛−1 rather than ℂ𝑛. Unitary evolution preserves the norm, so normalisation holds for all time automatically.
reduction: None needed.

title: Observables as Hermitian Operators
objects: A Hermitian matrix.
structure: Hermiticity gives real eigenvalues (measurable outcomes) and orthogonal eigenvectors (distinguishable states), so the spectral theorem does all the work. Every physical postulate about measurement is a corollary of 𝐴= 𝐴†.
reduction: None needed.

title: Expectation Value
objects: A quadratic form, or a trace pairing for mixed states.
structure: Linear in 𝜌and linear in 𝐴— a bilinear pairing that makes states and observables dual. Bounded by the extreme eigenvalues, so 𝜆min ≤⟨𝐴⟩≤𝜆max is the Rayleigh quotient bound.
reduction: None needed.

title: Completeness (Resolution of Identity)
objects: A sum of rank-one orthogonal projections.
structure: 𝑃𝑖𝑃𝑗= 𝛿𝑖𝑗𝑃𝑖and ∑𝑖𝑃𝑖= 𝐼— the spectral decomposition of the identity. Inserting it between operators is the standard manipulation, and it is just writing 𝐼in a chosen basis.
reduction: None needed.

title: Canonical Commutation Relation
objects: A commutator that cannot be satisfied by finite matrices.
structure: Taking traces gives tr[ ̂𝑥, ̂𝑝] = 0 but tr(𝑖ℏ𝐼) = 𝑖ℏ𝑛≠0 — so no finite-dimensional representation exists. The canonical commutation relation forces infinite dimensions, which is one of the sharpest facts in the subject and a purely trace-theoretic argument.
reduction: None needed.

title: Heisenberg Uncertainty Relation
objects: Cauchy–Schwarz applied to two operator-shifted vectors.
structure: The proof is Cauchy–Schwarz on (𝐴−⟨𝐴⟩) |𝜓⟩and (𝐵−⟨𝐵⟩) |𝜓⟩, with the commutator appearing as the imaginary part of the inner product. Uncertainty is an inner-product inequality, nothing more exotic.
reduction: The relation is Cauchy–Schwarz.

title: Energy–Time Uncertainty
objects: Not a commutator relation — time is a parameter, not an operator.
structure: Δ𝑡is the timescale over which an observable changes appreciably, Δ𝑡= 𝜎𝐴/|𝑑⟨𝐴⟩/𝑑𝑡|. The Mandelstam–Tamm derivation uses the Heisenberg equation, so it is still a commutator bound, but with a different reading.
reduction: The relation follows from the Heisenberg equation.
status: Exact linear, with a distinct interpretation.

title: Time-Dependent Schrödinger Equation
objects: A linear ODE with a Hermitian generator.
structure: Because 𝐻is Hermitian, 𝑖𝐻/ℏis anti-Hermitian, so the solution operator is unitary and the norm is preserved exactly. Quantum evolution is rotation in a complex vector space — this single equation is why the whole subject is linear algebra.
reduction: None needed.

title: Time-Independent Schrödinger Equation
objects: An eigenvalue problem.
structure: The entire content of atomic and molecular structure is finding eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix. Bound states are the discrete spectrum, scattering states the continuous. Degeneracy is eigenvalue multiplicity, and it always signals a symmetry.
reduction: None needed.
status: Exact linear. The eigenvalue problem of the physical sciences.

title: Time Evolution Operator
objects: The matrix exponential of a Hermitian generator.
structure: Unitary, so ‖𝑈‖ = 1 and 𝜅(𝑈) = 1 — evolution never amplifies error, which is why quantum dynamics is numerically benign. For time-dependent 𝐻it becomes a time-ordered exponential, and 𝑈(𝑡1)𝑈(𝑡2) ≠𝑈(𝑡1+𝑡2) unless the Hamiltonians commute.
reduction: None needed.

title: Heisenberg Equation of Motion
objects: Evolution by conjugation, 𝐴𝐻(𝑡) = 𝑈†𝐴𝑈.
structure: A similarity transformation, so the spectrum of 𝐴is constant in time — measurement outcomes are fixed, only their probabilities evolve. Conserved quantities are exactly those commuting with 𝐻, which is a statement about shared eigenvectors.
reduction: None needed.

title: Ehrenfest’s Theorem
objects: Expectation values obeying classical-looking equations.
structure: Exact for quadratic potentials, where ⟨∇𝑉⟩= ∇𝑉(⟨x⟩) because the gradient is linear. For anharmonic potentials the two differ — the classical limit is the statement that expectation and nonlinear function commute, which they generally do not.
reduction: None needed.
status: Exact linear; classical correspondence exact only for quadratic 𝑉.

title: Probability Current
objects: A bilinear (sesquilinear) form in the state.
structure: Together with |𝜓|2 it satisfies a continuity equation, which follows from Hermiticity of 𝐻— probability conservation is unitarity in local form. The current is quadratic in 𝜓, so it does not superpose.
reduction: None needed.

title: Density Matrix
objects: A Hermitian positive semidefinite unit-trace matrix.
