reduction: Stability follows from a quadratic Lyapunov function and skew-symmetry.

title: Impedance Control
objects: A prescribed second-order linear relation between motion and force.
structure: The controller imposes a desired mass–damper–spring matrix triple, so the robot behaves as a chosen linear mechanical system. Choosing 𝐾𝑑and 𝐵𝑑is choosing the closed-loop eigenvalues.
reduction: Impedance control assigns a second-order linear system.

title: Hybrid Force–Position Control
objects: A selection matrix splitting the task space.
structure: 𝑆is a projection: idempotent, splitting directions into force-controlled and position-controlled sub- spaces. The two subspaces must be orthogonal complements, which is exactly the constraint that a projection imposes.
reduction: The selection matrix is a projection onto complementary subspaces.

title: Admittance Control
objects: A causal inverse of impedance.
structure: Admittance maps force to motion where impedance maps motion to force, so the two are inverse transfer functions. Which one is stable depends on the environment’s stiffness — a coupled stability condition on the product of the two operators.
reduction: Admittance is the inverse operator of impedance.

title: Grasp Matrix and Force Closure
objects: A matrix mapping contact forces to an object wrench.
structure: Force closure requires 𝐺to be surjective onto the wrench space and the required contact forces to lie in the friction cone — a rank condition plus a positivity condition. It is exactly the same structure as feasibility in a conic program.
reduction: Force closure is a rank condition plus cone membership.

title: Grasp Quality (Ferrari–Canny)
objects: The radius of the largest ball inscribed in the grasp wrench space.
structure: The grasp wrench space is the convex hull of the contact wrench primitives, and 𝑄is the distance from the origin to its nearest facet. Computing it is a convex hull plus a distance computation.
reduction: Grasp quality is a distance from the origin to a convex hull’s boundary.

title: Visual Servoing Control Law
objects: A pseudoinverse of the image Jacobian applied to a feature error.
structure: The interaction matrix 𝐿𝑠maps camera velocity to feature velocity, and the control is a damped pseudoinverse solve — structurally identical to inverse kinematics. Image-based servoing can drive the camera through configurations that are geometrically absurd, because the pseudoinverse minimises image error, not Cartesian error.
reduction: Visual servoing is a pseudoinverse solve on the image Jacobian.

title: Model Predictive Control for Robots
objects: A quadratic program over a finite horizon.
structure: With linear dynamics and quadratic cost the problem is exactly a QP whose Hessian is block-banded — solvable in time linear in the horizon by Riccati recursion. Constraints add inequalities, keeping it a QP. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 58
reduction: MPC is a banded quadratic program.

title: Control Barrier Function Safety Constraint
objects: A linear inequality in the control input.
structure: Because ̇ℎ= 𝐿𝑓ℎ+ 𝐿𝑔ℎu is aﬀine in u, the safety condition is a linear constraint — so safe control is a quadratic program that minimally modifies a nominal input. Safety filtering reduces to projecting onto a half-space, which is why it runs at kilohertz rates. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 59
reduction: Safety is a linear constraint; filtering is a projection.

title: Adjacency Matrix
objects: The matrix that is the network.
structure: Symmetric for undirected graphs, so its eigenvalues are real and its eigenvectors orthogonal. (𝐴𝑘)𝑖𝑗 counts walks of length 𝑘from 𝑖to 𝑗— the single most useful fact in the field, and it makes every path-based quantity a matrix power.
reduction: Already native — the network is a matrix; walks are its powers.

title: Degree and Degree Sequence
objects: The vector of row sums, k = 𝐴1.
structure: Exactly the adjacency matrix applied to the all-ones vector, and the degree matrix 𝐷= diag(k) appears throughout. The sequence sorted descending is the degree distribution’s empirical form.
reduction: Degree is 𝐴1.

title: Handshaking Lemma
objects: A trace-like identity.
structure: Exactly 1⊤𝐴1 = 2𝑚— summing all entries counts each edge twice. It is the simplest conservation statement about the matrix.
reduction: The lemma sums all matrix entries.

title: Density
objects: The normalised total of the adjacency matrix.
structure: The mean off-diagonal entry, so density is the matrix’s average. Real networks are sparse, meaning 𝑚= 𝑂(𝑛) rather than 𝑂(𝑛2) — which is why sparse matrix algorithms dominate the computational side.
reduction: Density is the mean matrix entry.

title: Average Degree and Sparsity
objects: The mean of the degree vector.
structure: Constant average degree as 𝑛grows means the matrix has 𝑂(𝑛) nonzeros, so storage and matrix–vector products cost 𝑂(𝑛). That sparsity is what makes large-network computation feasible at all.
reduction: Sparsity bounds the matrix’s nonzero count.

title: Degree Distribution
objects: The empirical distribution of the row sums.
structure: A first-order summary of the matrix that discards all correlation structure — two networks with identical degree distributions can be entirely different. The configuration model of entry 29 is the maximum entropy network with a given degree sequence.
reduction: The distribution summarises the row sums, discarding correlations.

title: Power-Law Degree Distribution
objects: A heavy-tailed degree distribution.
structure: Linear in log–log, and 𝛾< 3 makes the second moment diverge — which is what drives the vanishing epidemic threshold of entry 49 and the spectral radius’ unbounded growth. The exponent is estimated by maximum likelihood, not by naive regression on a histogram.
reduction: The distribution is log-linear; 𝛾< 3 makes ⟨𝑘2⟩diverge.

title: Excess Degree Distribution
objects: The degree distribution seen from the end of an edge.
structure: Size-biased by degree, which is the friendship paradox — your friends have more friends than you, on average, exactly because edges sample nodes proportionally to degree. Its mean is ⟨𝑘2⟩/ ⟨𝑘⟩−1, the branching ratio.
reduction: Edge sampling is degree-biased; the mean excess degree is the branching ratio.

title: Clustering Coeﬀicient (Local)
objects: A normalised count of triangles at a node.
structure: 𝑒𝑖is computable from 𝐴2 restricted to 𝑖’s neighbourhood, so the local clustering is a ratio of matrix- power quantities. Averaging over nodes gives a different quantity from entry 10.
reduction: Local clustering counts triangles from the adjacency square.

title: Transitivity (Global Clustering)
objects: A ratio of two matrix-power functionals.
structure: Literally a trace over an off-diagonal sum — one of the cleanest matrix expressions in the field. It differs from the average local clustering because it weights high-degree nodes more.
reduction: Transitivity is tr(𝐴3) over an 𝐴2 sum.

title: Shortest Path Length and Diameter
objects: Entries of the min-plus matrix closure.
structure: The distance matrix is 𝐴∗in the min-plus semiring, computable by Floyd–Warshall in 𝑂(𝑛3) or by BFS from each node in 𝑂(𝑛𝑚). Diameter is that matrix’s maximum entry.
reduction: Distances are a min-plus matrix closure.

title: Degree Assortativity
objects: A normalised quadratic form in the modularity matrix.
structure: The numerator contracts the modularity matrix 𝐵= 𝐴−kk⊤/2𝑚with the degree vector, so assorta- tivity is exactly a Pearson correlation of degrees across edges. Social networks are assortative, technological ones disassortative.
reduction: Assortativity is a quadratic form in the modularity matrix.

title: Reciprocity
objects: A ratio measuring the matrix’s symmetry.
structure: The numerator is tr(𝐴2) for a directed graph, so reciprocity measures how close 𝐴is to symmetric. It is the fraction of the matrix’s mass in its symmetric part.
reduction: Reciprocity measures the matrix’s symmetric component.

title: Motif Significance
objects: A standardised subgraph count. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 15
structure: Small subgraph counts are traces of adjacency polynomials — triangles are tr(𝐴3)/6, and larger motifs need inclusion–exclusion over walk counts. The null preserves the degree sequence, which is a margin-preserving randomisation.
reduction: Motif counts are adjacency polynomial traces.

title: Degree Centrality
objects: A normalised row sum. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 16
structure: The zeroth-order centrality — it counts immediate neighbours and nothing beyond. All the following measures extend it to longer walks.
reduction: Degree centrality is a normalised row sum.

title: Closeness Centrality
objects: A reciprocal row sum of the distance matrix.
structure: Undefined for disconnected graphs because some distances are infinite, which is why entry 17 exists. It is a min-plus computation feeding a reciprocal.
reduction: Closeness is a reciprocal row sum of the min-plus distance matrix. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 17

title: Harmonic Centrality
objects: A sum of reciprocal distances.
structure: Swapping the reciprocal inside the sum makes infinite distances contribute zero, so it handles discon- nected graphs gracefully. It is the same row of the distance matrix, transformed elementwise before summing.
reduction: Harmonic centrality transforms before summing rather than after.

title: Betweenness Centrality
objects: A count over shortest path enumerations.
structure: Brandes’ algorithm computes it in 𝑂(𝑛𝑚) by accumulating dependencies along BFS trees — a back- ward accumulation on the shortest path DAG, structurally like backpropagation. It is a path-counting quantity, not a spectral one.
reduction: Betweenness is a backward accumulation on shortest path DAGs.

title: Eigenvector Centrality
objects: The Perron eigenvector.
structure: Computable by power iteration x ←𝐴x/ ‖𝐴x‖, which converges at rate |𝜆2/𝜆1|. Perron–Frobenius guarantees a unique positive eigenvector for a connected network.
reduction: Eigenvector centrality is the Perron eigenvector via power iteration.

title: Katz Centrality
objects: A Neumann series over all walk lengths, geometrically discounted.
structure: Exactly ∑𝑘𝛼𝑘𝐴𝑘1, converging when 𝛼< 1/𝜆1 — so Katz centrality is a resolvent evaluation. It fixes eigenvector centrality’s failure on directed acyclic graphs by adding the constant term.
reduction: Katz centrality is a resolvent — a discounted sum of walk counts.

title: PageRank
objects: The stationary distribution of a damped random walk.
structure: The damping makes the matrix irreducible and aperiodic, guaranteeing a unique stationary vector by Perron–Frobenius — that is the whole reason for 𝛼= 0.85. Convergence rate is exactly 𝛼, so about fifty iterations suﬀice regardless of network size.
reduction: PageRank is a stationary distribution; damping guarantees uniqueness and sets the rate.

title: HITS Hubs and Authorities
objects: The leading singular vectors of the adjacency matrix.
structure: Substituting gives h = 𝐴𝐴⊤h and a = 𝐴⊤𝐴a, so hubs and authorities are the left and right singular vectors — HITS is the SVD’s leading pair. That identification is exact.
reduction: HITS computes the adjacency matrix’s leading singular vectors.

title: k-Core Decomposition
objects: A nested sequence of subgraphs.
structure: A peeling algorithm running in 𝑂(𝑚), producing a monotone nested family — the cores are ordered by inclusion. It is combinatorial rather than spectral, and it identifies the densely connected nucleus.
reduction: Core decomposition is a monotone peeling; it is combinatorial.

title: Subgraph Centrality
objects: A diagonal entry of the adjacency matrix exponential.
structure: Literally ∑𝑘(𝐴𝑘)𝑖𝑖/𝑘! — closed walks of every length, factorially discounted. The matrix exponential’s spectral decomposition makes it computable from 𝐴’s eigenpairs, and the estimation is a Lanczos quadrature.
reduction: Subgraph centrality is a diagonal of 𝑒𝐴.

title: Percolation and Bridging Centrality
objects: A measure of a node’s role in the component structure.
structure: Removing a node changes the number of connected components, which is the multiplicity of the Laplacian’s zero eigenvalue — so bridging importance is a spectral multiplicity change. Articulation points are the extreme case.
reduction: Connectivity role is a Laplacian null space dimension change.

title: Erdős–Rényi Random Graph
objects: A random symmetric matrix with independent Bernoulli entries.
structure: Its spectrum follows the semicircle law in the dense regime, with the Perron eigenvalue ≈𝑛𝑝separated from the bulk. The degree distribution is binomial, approaching Poisson — much lighter-tailed than real networks.
reduction: ER graphs are random matrices with semicircle bulk spectra.

title: Giant Component Threshold
objects: A branching process criticality condition.
structure: The expected number of new nodes reached per step is ⟨𝑘⟩, so a giant component appears exactly when that branching ratio crosses one. It is the same unit-spectral-radius condition as every threshold in this chapter.
reduction: The threshold is a unit branching ratio.

title: Molloy–Reed Criterion
objects: A threshold in terms of the first two degree moments.
structure: The mean excess degree must exceed one, which requires the second moment — so heavy-tailed networks with divergent ⟨𝑘2⟩always have a giant component. That divergence is the source of scale-free networks’ robustness.
reduction: The criterion is a second-moment branching condition.

title: Configuration Model
objects: The maximum entropy ensemble with a given degree sequence.
structure: The expected adjacency is 𝑘𝑖𝑘𝑗/2𝑚— exactly a rank-one matrix, which is why the modularity matrix subtracts it. That rank-one null expectation appears throughout the chapter.
reduction: The null expected adjacency is a rank-one outer product.

title: Watts–Strogatz Small World
objects: An interpolation between a circulant and a random matrix.
structure: The lattice’s adjacency is circulant (diagonalised by the Fourier basis) and rewiring adds random off-diagonal entries — so the model interpolates between two spectral extremes. A few rewirings collapse the path length while clustering survives, which is the small-world effect.
reduction: The model interpolates between a circulant and a random matrix.

title: Barabási–Albert Preferential Attachment
objects: A growth rule producing 𝛾= 3.
structure: The degree distribution’s master equation is linear and solvable exactly, giving the cubic power law. Growth plus preferential attachment are both necessary — either alone gives an exponential distribution.
reduction: The degree distribution solves a linear master equation.

title: Price Model and Fitness
objects: Attachment weighted by an intrinsic fitness.
structure: Fitness lets latecomers overtake, and the resulting distribution is a mixture of power laws — a Bose– Einstein condensation occurs when one fitness dominates. That condensation is a rank-one collapse of the growth process.
reduction: Fitness gives a mixture of power laws; condensation is a rank-one collapse.

title: Exponential Random Graph Model
objects: A maximum entropy family over graphs.
structure: Log-linear in the suﬀicient statistics, so it is the exponential family matched to those statistics. De- generacy arises when the statistics are non-convex functions on the graph space, concentrating the mass at extremes.
reduction: ERGM is a log-linear exponential family.

title: Stochastic Block Model
objects: A low-rank expected adjacency 𝑍𝐵𝑍⊤.
structure: Exactly a rank-𝑘factorisation with a membership indicator matrix, so recovery is a low-rank matrix estimation problem. Spectral methods work because 𝐴’s leading eigenvectors concentrate around its expecta- tion’s.
reduction: The SBM is a low-rank factorisation; recovery is spectral.

title: Spatial and Geometric Random Graphs
objects: An adjacency defined by a distance threshold.
structure: High clustering arises automatically because the connection relation is nearly transitive in a metric space, but path lengths grow polynomially rather than logarithmically. Geometry buys clustering and costs small-worldness.
reduction: The adjacency is a thresholded distance matrix.

title: Hyperbolic Network Model
objects: A geometric graph in negatively curved space.
structure: Exponential volume growth in hyperbolic space produces power-law degrees and high clustering si- multaneously — a geometric explanation for both. Greedy routing succeeds with high probability because the geometry encodes the shortest paths.
reduction: Hyperbolic geometry generates scale-free structure from a distance threshold.

title: Modularity
objects: A quadratic form in the modularity matrix 𝐵= 𝐴−kk⊤/2𝑚.
structure: Exactly 1 2𝑚tr(𝑆⊤𝐵𝑆) for an assignment matrix 𝑆, so maximising modularity is a discrete quadratic optimisation. Relaxing 𝑆to be real gives 𝐵’s leading eigenvector — Newman’s spectral bisection, which is exact for the relaxation.
reduction: Modularity is a quadratic form in 𝐵; its relaxation is an eigenvector.

title: Resolution-Limited Modularity
objects: A scale bound intrinsic to the null model.
structure: The null term 𝑘𝑖𝑘𝑗/2𝑚shrinks with network size, so small dense groups become invisible against it — a normalisation artefact rather than a data limitation. The resolution parameter 𝛾rescales that term to tune the detected scale.
reduction: The limit is a normalisation of the null term.

title: Louvain and Leiden Algorithms
objects: A multilevel greedy optimisation of the modularity form.
structure: Each aggregation step contracts the adjacency matrix into a smaller one — a coarsening, exactly as in algebraic multigrid. Leiden adds a refinement guaranteeing connected communities, which Louvain can violate.
reduction: The algorithms are multilevel matrix coarsenings.

title: Map Equation (Infomap)
objects: An expected code length for describing a random walk. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 40
structure: Minimises the description length of a random walk’s trajectory, so communities are regions where the walk lingers — a compression rather than a density criterion. It uses the walk’s stationary distribution, which is a Perron eigenvector.
reduction: Infomap minimises a code length over a random walk’s stationary distribution.

title: Normalised Mutual Information
objects: A normalised comparison of two partitions.
structure: Mutual information measures the confusion matrix’s departure from its rank-one margin product, normalised to [0, 1]. It is permutation-invariant because permutations act on both margins.
reduction: NMI is a normalised rank-one departure of the confusion matrix.
status: Exact linear. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 41

title: Detectability Threshold
objects: A phase transition below which no algorithm can find the communities.
structure: Exactly the point at which the signal eigenvalue emerges from the random matrix bulk — a BBP tran- sition from random matrix theory. Below it the community structure is present but spectrally indistinguishable from noise, and the impossibility is information-theoretic, not algorithmic.
reduction: Detectability is a BBP eigenvalue transition.
status: Exact linear. One of the field’s sharpest spectral results. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 42

title: Overlapping Community (Clique Percolation)
objects: A percolation on the clique adjacency structure.
structure: Builds a clique–clique overlap matrix and finds its components, so it is connectivity analysis on a derived matrix. Clique finding is NP-hard in general, which limits it to small 𝑘.
reduction: The method finds components of a clique overlap matrix.

title: Core–Periphery Structure
objects: A rank-one pattern in the adjacency matrix.
structure: The idealised core–periphery adjacency is cc⊤for a coreness vector — exactly rank one, so detection is a rank-one fit. It is the complement of assortative community structure, which is block diagonal.
reduction: Core–periphery is a rank-one adjacency pattern.

title: Graph Laplacian
objects: A symmetric positive semidefinite matrix.
structure: x⊤𝐿x = ∑(𝑖,𝑗)∈𝐸(𝑥𝑖−𝑥𝑗)2 ≥0, so 𝐿is positive semidefinite with 1 in its null space. The multiplicity of eigenvalue zero equals the number of connected components — an exact rank statement.
reduction: The Laplacian is positive semidefinite; its null space counts components.

title: Algebraic Connectivity
objects: The Fiedler value — the second smallest Laplacian eigenvalue.
structure: Zero exactly when the graph is disconnected, and larger values mean better connectivity. It bounds the mixing rate, the synchronisability, and the cut quality — a single number governing many dynamical properties.
reduction: Algebraic connectivity is the second Laplacian eigenvalue.

title: Cheeger Inequality
objects: A two-sided bound linking a spectral and a combinatorial quantity.
structure: The conductance ℎ(𝐺) is a combinatorial minimum over cuts — NP-hard to compute — while 𝜆2 is a polynomial-time eigenvalue. The inequality says the spectral relaxation is a provably good approximation, which is the theoretical justification for spectral clustering.
reduction: Cheeger bounds a combinatorial cut by a spectral quantity.

title: Spectral Clustering
objects: An eigenvector-based partition.
structure: The Fiedler vector minimises x⊤𝐿x subject to orthogonality with 1 — a Rayleigh quotient minimisa- tion, which is the continuous relaxation of the minimum cut. Using 𝑘eigenvectors and 𝑘-means generalises it to 𝑘clusters.
reduction: Spectral clustering minimises a Rayleigh quotient — the relaxed cut.

title: Spectral Radius and Epidemic Threshold
objects: The reciprocal of the adjacency matrix’s largest eigenvalue.
structure: Exactly the condition for the linearised epidemic dynamics to have a positive growth eigenvalue, so the epidemic threshold is a spectral radius statement. For scale-free networks with 𝛾< 3, 𝜆1 grows without bound and the threshold vanishes — which is why such networks cannot be protected by uniform vaccination.
reduction: The threshold is a reciprocal spectral radius.

title: Random Walk Stationary Distribution
objects: The Perron eigenvector of the transition matrix 𝑃= 𝐷−1𝐴.
structure: Degree-proportional for an undirected connected graph, which is why edge sampling is degree-biased. It is exactly the left eigenvector of 𝑃with eigenvalue one.
reduction: The stationary distribution is a Perron eigenvector.

title: Mixing Time and Spectral Gap
objects: A reciprocal spectral gap.
structure: The second eigenvalue of the transition matrix governs how fast the walk forgets its start, so mixing time is a reciprocal eigenvalue — the same structure as every relaxation time in this compendium. Expander graphs have large gaps and mix in 𝑂(log 𝑛) steps.
reduction: Mixing time is a reciprocal spectral gap.

title: SIS Epidemic on Networks
objects: A linear coupling term with a saturating nonlinearity.
structure: Linearising about the disease-free state gives the Jacobian −𝐼+ 𝜆𝐴, whose leading eigenvalue crosses zero at 𝜆= 1/𝜆1 — entry 49’s threshold, derived directly. The nonlinearity only bounds the growth.
reduction: The threshold is a Jacobian eigenvalue crossing; the coupling is 𝐴.

title: Percolation Threshold
objects: A branching ratio condition in the first two moments.
structure: Random node removal fails to destroy scale-free networks because ⟨𝑘2⟩diverges, sending 𝑝𝑐→0. It is the same moment condition as Molloy–Reed, applied to a thinned network.
reduction: Percolation is a moment-based branching condition.

title: Targeted Attack Vulnerability
objects: The complementary case to entry 53.
structure: Removing the highest-degree nodes cuts the second moment fastest, so the branching ratio drops immediately — robustness to random failure and fragility to targeted attack are two consequences of one heavy tail. That duality is the field’s most cited result.
reduction: Targeted removal attacks the second moment directly.

title: Cascading Failure Load Model
objects: An iterative redistribution on the network.
structure: Each redistribution is a linear map determined by the current topology, but the topology changes as nodes fail — so the process is a sequence of linear maps on a shrinking graph. The threshold behaviour comes from that coupling, not from any single map.
reduction: Cascades are a sequence of linear redistributions on a changing graph.

title: Kuramoto Synchronisation on a Network
objects: Phase coupling through the adjacency matrix.
structure: Linearising about the synchronised state gives ̇𝜃= −𝐾𝐿𝜃— exactly Laplacian diffusion, so synchro- nisation speed is governed by 𝜆2. The all-to-all case reduces to a rank-one mean-field.
reduction: Near synchrony the dynamics are Laplacian diffusion.

title: Master Stability Function
objects: A ratio of the extreme Laplacian eigenvalues.
structure: Stability of the synchronous state requires every nonzero Laplacian eigenvalue scaled by the coupling to lie in a stability interval, so a small eigenvalue ratio makes that possible for a wider coupling range. It separates the dynamics (the stability interval) from the topology (the spectrum) exactly.
reduction: Synchronisability is a Laplacian eigenratio; dynamics and topology separate.

title: Structural Controllability
objects: A combinatorial matching quantity, not a spectral one.
structure: Liu, Slotine, and Barabási’s result is that the number of required driver nodes follows from a maxi- mum bipartite matching on the network — the unmatched nodes must be driven. It is a rank statement in a combinatorial rather than spectral sense, computable in polynomial time by Hopcroft–Karp.
reduction: Controllability is a maximum matching, not an eigenvalue computation.

title: Network Eﬀiciency
objects: A mean reciprocal distance.
structure: Exactly the average of the harmonic centralities, so it handles disconnected graphs gracefully. Local eﬀiciency computed on neighbourhoods measures fault tolerance.
reduction: Eﬀiciency is a mean reciprocal of the distance matrix.

title: Temporal and Multilayer Networks
objects: A fourth-order tensor rather than a matrix.
structure: Layers and time steps add indices, so the natural object is a tensor and the supra-adjacency repre- sentation flattens it into a large block matrix. Tensor decompositions generalise the SVD, but non-commuting time-ordered products mean paths must respect temporal ordering — reachability is no longer a simple matrix power.
reduction: Multilayer networks are tensors; supra-adjacency flattens them to matrices.

title: Shannon Entropy
objects: An inner product of a probability vector with a surprisal vector.
structure: Exactly p⊤s with 𝑠𝑖= −log 𝑝𝑖— linear in p given s, and concave in p overall. Its maximum on the simplex is at the uniform distribution, which is a symmetry argument.
reduction: Entropy is an inner product with the surprisal vector.

title: Joint Entropy
objects: The same functional applied to the joint probability matrix.
structure: Treats the joint distribution as a flattened vector, so all the entropy identities carry over. Subadditivity 𝐻(𝑋, 𝑌) ≤𝐻(𝑋) + 𝐻(𝑌) is exactly the non-negativity of mutual information.
reduction: Joint entropy flattens the matrix and applies the same functional.

title: Conditional Entropy
objects: A weighted average of row entropies.
structure: Exactly ∑𝑖𝑝𝑖𝐻(𝑌∣𝑋= 𝑖) — an inner product of the marginal with the vector of row entropies. Conditioning never increases entropy, which is Jensen’s inequality applied to the concave entropy function.
reduction: Conditional entropy is a marginal-weighted average of row entropies.

title: Chain Rule for Entropy
objects: An exact additive decomposition.
structure: Follows immediately from the logarithm turning the product 𝑝𝑖𝑗= 𝑝𝑖𝑝𝑗∣𝑖into a sum — the whole chain rule is that one algebraic fact. It extends to any number of variables by iteration.
reduction: The chain rule is log-additivity of a probability factorisation.

title: Mutual Information
objects: A divergence between the joint matrix and its rank-one margin product.
structure: Zero exactly when 𝑃= pq⊤— that is, when the joint matrix has rank one. Mutual information is therefore a measure of departure from rank one, which is the same object as in every independence test in this compendium.
reduction: Mutual information measures departure from a rank-one joint.

title: Mutual Information Identities
objects: Linear relations among four entropy quantities.
structure: The Venn diagram of information is exact for two variables because the identities are linear — three quantities determine the fourth. For three or more variables the “interaction information” can be negative, so the diagram picture breaks.
reduction: The identities are linear relations on an entropy vector.

title: Conditional Mutual Information
objects: A linear contrast of two conditional entropies.
structure: Non-negative always, but it can exceed the unconditional 𝐼(𝑋; 𝑌) — conditioning can create depen- dence, which is exactly the collider effect from causal inference. That non-monotonicity is why information diagrams mislead.
reduction: The quantity is a linear entropy contrast; conditioning can increase it.

title: Kullback–Leibler Divergence
objects: An inner product of p with a log-ratio vector.
structure: Linear in 𝑃given the log-ratio, but neither symmetric nor a metric. Its non-negativity is Jensen’s inequality, and it is the exponential family’s natural geometry.
reduction: KL is a linear functional of 𝑃against a log-ratio vector.

title: Jensen–Shannon Divergence
objects: A symmetrised divergence about a linear midpoint.
structure: The midpoint 𝑀= (𝑃+ 𝑄)/2 is a convex combination, and the symmetrisation makes √ JSD a genuine metric. It equals the mutual information between the sample and its source label.
reduction: Symmetrisation about a linear midpoint yields a metric.

title: Cross Entropy
objects: An inner product of the true distribution with the model’s surprisal.
structure: Exactly linear in 𝑃against −log q, and it decomposes into an irreducible entropy plus a divergence. Minimising cross entropy is minimising KL, since 𝐻(𝑃) is fixed — which is why it is the standard classification loss.
reduction: Cross entropy is a linear functional splitting into entropy plus divergence.

title: Differential Entropy
objects: The continuous analogue, not coordinate invariant.
structure: Under a linear change of variables y = 𝐴x it shifts by log |det 𝐴| — so differential entropy transforms by a log determinant, which is exactly why it can be negative and why only differences of it are meaningful. Mutual information is invariant, because the determinants cancel.
reduction: Differential entropy shifts by log |det 𝐴|; mutual information is invariant.

title: Maximum Entropy Distributions
objects: A concave maximisation with linear moment constraints.
structure: The constraints are exactly linear functionals of the distribution, so the solution is an exponential family 𝑝∝exp(∑𝜆𝑘𝑓𝑘) with the Lagrange multipliers as natural parameters. Every named distribution in statistics arises this way from some set of linear constraints.
reduction: MaxEnt is concave maximisation over linear constraints; the solution is exponential.

title: Gaussian Entropy
objects: A log determinant of the covariance matrix.
structure: Exactly 1 2 log det Σ up to a constant, so Gaussian entropy is a spectral quantity — the sum of log eigenvalues. Maximum entropy for a fixed covariance means the Gaussian is the least assumptive choice.
reduction: Gaussian entropy is a log determinant — a sum of log eigenvalues.

title: Rényi Entropy
objects: A one-parameter family of ℓ𝛼-norm-based entropies.
structure: Exactly 𝛼 1−𝛼log ‖p‖𝛼, so the family is indexed by which norm is used. 𝛼→1 gives Shannon, 𝛼= 2 gives collision entropy, 𝛼→∞gives min-entropy. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 15
reduction: Rényi entropies are log norms of the probability vector.

title: Min-Entropy
objects: The ℓ∞limit of the family.
structure: Determined by the single largest probability, so it is the most conservative entropy measure — which is why cryptography uses it for randomness extraction. It lower-bounds every other Rényi entropy.
reduction: Min-entropy is the log of the sup norm.

title: Tsallis Entropy
objects: A non-additive entropy family.
structure: Non-additive for independent systems — 𝑆𝑞(𝐴, 𝐵) = 𝑆𝑞(𝐴) + 𝑆𝑞(𝐵) + (1 −𝑞)𝑆𝑞(𝐴)𝑆𝑞(𝐵) — so it deliberately breaks the additivity that makes Shannon entropy natural. That is its point and its controversy.
reduction: Tsallis entropy breaks additivity by construction.

title: Fisher Information
objects: The expected outer product of the score — a matrix.
structure: Exactly 𝐸[ss⊤] with s the score vector, so it is a positive semidefinite matrix whose inverse bounds estimator covariance (Cramér–Rao). It is the local curvature of the KL divergence — the Fisher–Rao metric.
reduction: Fisher information is a score covariance matrix and a local KL metric.

title: Data Processing Inequality
objects: A monotonicity under composition of stochastic matrices.
structure: Post-processing is multiplication by a stochastic matrix, and mutual information cannot increase under it — a contraction property. It is why no clever processing can create information that was not in the data.
reduction: Processing is stochastic matrix multiplication; information contracts.

title: Fano’s Inequality
objects: A lower bound on the error probability from conditional entropy.
structure: Linear in 𝑃𝑒up to the binary entropy term, so it converts an information quantity into an error bound. It is the workhorse of every converse proof in the field, including the channel coding converse.
reduction: Fano bounds error linearly in terms of residual entropy.

title: Source Coding Theorem
objects: A lower bound on expected code length.
structure: Expected length is an inner product of the probability vector with the length vector, so the theorem says that inner product cannot fall below the entropy. It is the converse half of compression.
reduction: Expected length is an inner product bounded below by entropy.

title: Kraft–McMillan Inequality
objects: A feasibility constraint on the length vector.
structure: Exactly the condition for a prefix code to exist, and it defines a convex feasible region in length space. Minimising the inner product p⊤ℓover that region gives ℓ𝑖= −log 𝑝𝑖— a constrained optimisation whose solution is the entropy.
reduction: Kraft defines a convex region; optimal coding minimises a linear objective on it.

title: Shannon–Fano–Elias Code Length
objects: A rounded-up optimal length.
structure: The ceiling costs at most one bit per symbol, so the code is within two bits of the entropy. Integer constraints are the only reason optimal coding does not achieve the bound exactly.
reduction: Rounding the optimal real length costs a bounded excess.

title: Huffman Coding
objects: A greedy tree construction that is provably optimal.
structure: Optimality follows from an exchange argument — the two least probable symbols must be siblings at maximum depth. The resulting expected length is within one bit of entropy, and the greedy step is justified by a matroid-like exchange property.
reduction: Huffman is a greedy construction justified by an exchange argument.

title: Arithmetic Coding
objects: A nested sequence of interval subdivisions.
structure: Each symbol maps the current interval to a subinterval by an aﬀine map with scale 𝑝𝑖— so the final interval’s length is exactly the sequence probability, and its log is the code length. Arithmetic coding is a composition of aﬀine contractions.
reduction: Coding composes aﬀine interval contractions; length is the log of the product.

title: Asymptotic Equipartition Property
objects: A law of large numbers on the log probability.
structure: Exactly the sample mean of the surprisal converging to its expectation, so the AEP is the LLN applied to a linear functional. It is the reason typical sets exist.
reduction: The AEP is the law of large numbers on surprisal.

title: Typical Set Size
objects: An exponentially small subset carrying almost all probability.
structure: Out of |𝒳| 𝑛sequences only 2𝑛𝐻matter, so compression works by indexing that subset — the log of the count is 𝑛times a linear functional. Everything in source coding follows from this counting.
reduction: The log of the typical set size is 𝑛times a linear functional.

title: Lempel–Ziv Universal Coding
objects: A dictionary construction achieving the entropy rate without knowing it.
structure: Universality means the same algorithm is asymptotically optimal for every stationary ergodic source — a remarkable property, and it works because the parsing count grows as 𝑛/ log 𝑛for a source of entropy rate 𝐻. The construction itself is combinatorial.
reduction: The parsing is combinatorial; the limit is the entropy rate.

title: Entropy Rate
objects: A per-symbol limit of the joint entropy.
structure: Equivalently lim 𝐻(𝑋𝑛∣𝑋1, … , 𝑋𝑛−1) — the two definitions agree for stationary processes, which is a Cesàro convergence statement. It is the compression limit for a source with memory.
reduction: The entropy rate is a Cesàro limit of a linear functional.

title: Markov Source Entropy Rate
objects: A stationary-distribution-weighted average of row entropies.
structure: Exactly 𝜋⊤h where 𝜋is the Perron eigenvector of 𝑃and h the vector of row entropies — an inner product of an eigenvector with an entropy vector. The whole calculation is spectral plus a contraction.
reduction: The rate contracts a Perron eigenvector with row entropies.

title: Minimum Description Length
objects: A two-part code length minimisation.
structure: Exactly a sum of two code lengths, so model selection is a linear trade-off in bits — and the model complexity term is asymptotically 𝑘 2 log 𝑛, matching BIC. It is Occam’s razor as a linear objective. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 30
reduction: MDL minimises a sum of two lengths.

title: Channel Capacity
objects: A concave maximisation over the input simplex.
structure: Mutual information is concave in the input distribution for a fixed channel matrix, so the maximum is unique and computable — the Blahut–Arimoto algorithm alternates two closed-form updates. The channel itself is a stochastic matrix.
reduction: Capacity is concave maximisation over a simplex; the channel is a matrix. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 31

title: Binary Symmetric Channel
objects: A channel matrix ( 1−𝑝 𝑝 𝑝 1−𝑝).
structure: Symmetric, so the capacity-achieving input is uniform by a symmetry argument and the capacity is one minus the noise entropy. At 𝑝= 1/2 the matrix has rank one and the capacity is zero — a rank statement.
reduction: Symmetry gives a uniform optimal input; 𝑝= 1/2 makes the matrix rank one.

title: Binary Entropy Function
objects: A concave function on [0, 1].
structure: Maximised at 𝑝= 1/2 and symmetric about it, and its concavity is what makes every capacity formula involving it well behaved. It appears throughout coding theory as the exponent in volume bounds.
reduction: The function is the two-point entropy; concavity drives the optimisations.

title: Binary Erasure Channel
objects: A channel with a third output symbol.
structure: Capacity is exactly the fraction of unerased symbols, because erasures are known — the receiver’s uncertainty is entirely about which positions were lost, not about their values. That makes the capacity linear in 𝜀, unlike the BSC.
reduction: Erasure capacity is exactly linear in the erasure rate.

title: Shannon–Hartley Capacity
objects: The capacity of a bandlimited Gaussian channel.
structure: Linear in bandwidth and logarithmic in signal-to-noise ratio, so bandwidth is the cheaper resource. It follows from entry 36 with 𝐵independent uses per second.
reduction: Capacity is linear in bandwidth, log in SNR.

title: Gaussian Channel Capacity
objects: The per-use capacity of an additive Gaussian channel.
structure: The Gaussian input is optimal because it maximises entropy for a given power — a maximum entropy argument. The capacity is a log determinant in the vector case, which is entry 38.
reduction: Gaussian capacity follows from a maximum entropy argument.

title: Water-Filling Power Allocation
objects: A rectified constant-level allocation.
structure: Maximising ∑1 2 log(1 + 𝑃𝑖/𝑁𝑖) subject to ∑𝑃𝑖= 𝑃gives a Lagrange condition where the marginal returns are equal — hence a constant water level above the noise floor. It is the canonical concave resource allocation solution, and the same structure appears in portfolio theory and in Neyman allocation.
reduction: Water-filling is a Lagrange condition equalising marginal returns.

title: MIMO Capacity
objects: A log determinant, equal to a sum over singular values.
structure: The channel matrix’s SVD decouples the MIMO channel into parallel scalar channels with gains 𝜎2 𝑖, so capacity scales with min(𝑛𝑡, 𝑛𝑟) — the matrix’s rank. This is the single most consequential linear-algebraic result in modern communications: capacity is a rank, and antennas buy rank.
reduction: The SVD decouples the channel; capacity is a sum over singular values.
status: Exact linear. Capacity scaling is a rank statement.

title: Channel Coding Theorem
objects: An achievability result proved by random coding.
structure: Random codebooks work because typical sequences are nearly orthogonal in the sense that joint typicality is unlikely by chance — a counting argument on typical sets. The converse uses Fano’s inequality.
reduction: Achievability is a counting argument on typical sets.

title: Rate–Distortion Function
objects: A convex minimisation with a linear distortion constraint.
structure: The distortion constraint is exactly a linear functional of the conditional distribution, so the problem is convex minimisation over a polytope-constrained set. It is the exact dual of the capacity problem, and Blahut– Arimoto solves both.
reduction: Rate–distortion is convex minimisation with a linear constraint.

title: Gaussian Rate–Distortion
objects: A closed form for the Gaussian source.
structure: Log-linear in the distortion, so each bit halves the distortion — 6 dB per bit, matching the quantisation SNR formula. For vector sources it becomes reverse water-filling over the covariance’s eigenvalues.
reduction: Gaussian rate–distortion is log-linear; the vector case is reverse water-filling on eigenvalues.

title: Information Bottleneck
objects: A trade-off between two mutual informations.
structure: Exactly a linear combination of two information quantities with 𝛽as the trade-off parameter, solved by alternating self-consistent equations. It generalises rate–distortion by learning the distortion measure from the relevance variable.
reduction: The bottleneck is a linear combination of two informations.

title: Slepian–Wolf Distributed Coding
objects: A rate region defined by linear inequalities.
structure: Exactly a polytope in rate space — three half-planes whose intersection is the achievable region. The surprising result is that separate encoding loses nothing, so the corner points are achievable without communi- cation between encoders.
reduction: The rate region is a polytope defined by linear inequalities.

title: Multiple Access Channel Capacity
objects: A pentagon-shaped rate region.
structure: Again a polytope, and its corner points are achieved by successive interference cancellation — decoding one user while treating the other as noise, then subtracting. The corners correspond to different decoding orders, and time-sharing fills the edges.
reduction: The capacity region is a polytope; corners correspond to decoding orders.

title: Broadcast Channel and Superposition Coding
objects: A layered code exploiting a channel ordering.
structure: For degraded broadcast channels the receivers are ordered by quality, so superposition with successive decoding is optimal — the ordering is what makes the region tractable. Dirty paper coding handles the non- degraded Gaussian vector case, achieving capacity by pre-subtracting known interference.
reduction: Superposition exploits a channel ordering; dirty paper pre-subtracts interference.

title: Hamming Distance and Error Correction
objects: A packing condition on spheres in Hamming space.
structure: Decoding spheres of radius 𝑡around codewords must be disjoint, so the condition is exactly a geometric packing statement in 𝔽𝑛 2 with the Hamming metric. All the bounds below are packing or covering arguments.
reduction: Error correction is sphere packing in a metric space over 𝔽2.

title: Hamming Bound
objects: A sphere packing bound.
structure: Counts that the decoding spheres cannot overflow the space — exactly a volume argument. Codes meeting it with equality are perfect, and there are very few of them.
reduction: The bound is a volume count in Hamming space.

title: Singleton and Gilbert–Varshamov Bounds
objects: An upper bound from rank and a lower bound from counting.
structure: The Singleton bound follows because 𝑑−1 coordinates can be punctured while keeping the code’s dimension — a rank argument on the generator matrix. MDS codes meet it, and Reed–Solomon codes are MDS.
reduction: Singleton is a rank argument; GV is a covering count.

title: Structure: The code is literally a subspace: 𝐺’s rows are a basis, 𝐻spans the dual (null) space, and 𝐺𝐻⊤= 0.
structure: The code is literally a subspace: 𝐺’s rows are a basis, 𝐻spans the dual (null) space, and 𝐺𝐻⊤= 0. Decoding computes the syndrome 𝐻r⊤, which depends only on the error and not the codeword — the cleanest use of a null space in engineering.
reduction: A linear code is a subspace; syndrome decoding is a null space computation.

title: Hamming Code Parameters
objects: A perfect single-error-correcting code.
structure: The parity check matrix’s columns are all nonzero vectors of 𝔽𝑟 2, so every single-bit error gives a distinct nonzero syndrome — the syndrome is the error position in binary. That construction is exact and elegant.
reduction: The parity check columns enumerate 𝔽𝑟 2 � {0}; syndromes locate errors.

title: Reed–Solomon Code
objects: Evaluations of polynomials of degree below 𝑘.
structure: The generator matrix is a Vandermonde matrix, and any 𝑘evaluations determine the polynomial uniquely — which is exactly why the code is MDS. Decoding solves a key equation, a structured linear system.
reduction: Reed–Solomon is polynomial evaluation; the generator is Vandermonde.

title: Convolutional Code and Viterbi Decoding
objects: A linear filter over 𝔽2 decoded by dynamic programming.
structure: Encoding is convolution — a Toeplitz matrix over 𝔽2 — and Viterbi decoding is max-plus matrix multiplication along the trellis. Both halves are linear, in two different semirings.
reduction: Encoding is a Toeplitz product; decoding is max-plus.
status: Exact linear. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 51

title: Turbo Code Iterative Decoding
objects: An iterative message passing between two component decoders.
structure: Each decoder computes soft outputs and passes extrinsic log-likelihood ratios — additive in log-odds — to the other. Convergence is analysed by EXIT charts, which track the mutual information exchange as a one-dimensional map.
reduction: Turbo decoding exchanges additive log-likelihood ratios.

title: LDPC Belief Propagation
objects: Message passing on a bipartite graph defined by a sparse parity check matrix.
structure: The variable node update is a sum of log-likelihood ratios — exactly linear — while the check node update is a nonlinear tanh combination. Sparsity of 𝐻makes the graph locally tree-like, which is why belief propagation nearly achieves capacity.
reduction: Variable updates are additive in log-odds; sparsity of 𝐻makes the graph tree-like.

title: Polar Code Channel Polarisation
objects: A recursive Kronecker product transformation.
structure: The generator is 𝐺⊗𝑛for 𝐺= ( 1 0 1 1 ) — a Kronecker power, which is why the construction is recursive and has an 𝑂(𝑛log 𝑛) transform. Polarisation is a martingale convergence result on the channel capacities, and it gives the first explicit capacity-achieving construction with low complexity.
reduction: Polar codes are a Kronecker power transform; polarisation is a martingale limit.

title: Perfect secrecy is a
reduction: Perfect secrecy is a uniform group action; the key bound follows from entropy.

title: Unicity Distance
objects: A ratio of key entropy to plaintext redundancy.
structure: The number of ciphertext characters after which the key becomes uniquely determined — a linear accumulation of redundancy consuming key entropy. Compression before encryption raises it by reducing 𝐷.
reduction: Unicity is entropy divided by a per-symbol redundancy rate.

title: Wiretap Channel Secrecy Capacity
objects: A difference of two mutual informations, rectified.
structure: Exactly a linear contrast of two informations, positive only when the legitimate channel is better than the eavesdropper’s. It gives information-theoretic security without any computational assumption, which is its appeal.
reduction: Secrecy capacity is a rectified information difference.

title: Landauer’s Principle
objects: A thermodynamic cost of logical irreversibility.
structure: Erasure maps two states to one — a rank-reducing, non-invertible operation — and that loss of phase space volume is what costs energy. Reversible computation is exactly the use of invertible (permutation) operations, which have no such cost.
reduction: Erasure is a non-invertible map; reversible computing uses permutations.

title: Von Neumann Entropy and Holevo Bound
objects: A matrix function of the density operator, and a mixing entropy difference.
structure: Von Neumann entropy is exactly the Shannon entropy of 𝜌’s eigenvalues — the classical formula applied to a spectrum. The Holevo bound limits accessible classical information to 𝜒, and it is a concavity statement about the entropy function on the space of density matrices. Quantum information theory is classical information theory applied to eigenvalues, with non-commutativity supplying everything genuinely new.
reduction: Quantum entropy is classical entropy of a spectrum; Holevo is a concavity bound.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Speedup
objects: A ratio of two execution times.
structure: Linear speedup 𝑆𝑝= 𝑝is the ideal, and superlinear speedup indicates a cache effect — the aggregate cache grew with the processor count, so the comparison baseline changed. It is a ratio, so it does not compose additively.
reduction: Speedup is a time ratio; superlinearity signals a changed baseline.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Eﬀiciency
objects: A normalised speedup.
structure: Exactly speedup divided by resources, so it measures the fraction of ideal scaling achieved. Its product with 𝑝is the speedup, which makes iso-eﬀiciency curves hyperbolas in the (𝑝, 𝑆) plane.
reduction: Eﬀiciency normalises speedup by resource count.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Amdahl’s Law
objects: A speedup bound from a fixed serial fraction.
structure: Total work decomposes exactly into a serial and a parallel part — a two-component linear split of the work vector — and only the second divides. The bound 𝑆∞= 1/𝑓is the limit as the parallel term vanishes.
reduction: The law is a two-component linear work decomposition.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Gustafson–Barsis Law
objects: Speedup under a fixed execution time rather than fixed problem size.
structure: Exactly aﬀine in 𝑝, because the problem grows with the machine so the parallel work scales. Amdahl and Gustafson are the same decomposition with different quantities held constant — a change of the constraint, not of the model.
reduction: Scaled speedup is aﬀine in processor count.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Karp–Flatt Metric
objects: An experimentally determined serial fraction.
structure: Inverting Amdahl’s law for 𝑓gives this expression, so an increasing 𝑓𝑒with 𝑝reveals overhead beyond the serial fraction. It is a diagnostic obtained by inverting a linear model.
reduction: The metric inverts the Amdahl decomposition.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Strong and Weak Scaling
objects: Two different limits of the same model.
structure: Strong scaling holds the problem fixed and is bounded by Amdahl; weak scaling grows it and follows Gustafson. Which regime applies is a choice of how the work vector scales with 𝑝.
reduction: The two regimes differ in how the work vector scales.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Isoeﬀiciency Function
objects: An implicit relation defining how work must grow to hold eﬀiciency.
structure: Solving for 𝑊as a function of 𝑝gives the scalability signature — a linear isoeﬀiciency means perfect scalability, higher powers mean poorer. It is an implicit function derived from the overhead’s linear structure.
reduction: Isoeﬀiciency solves an implicit relation on the overhead.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Cost and Cost Optimality
objects: A processor–time product.
structure: Cost optimal means 𝑝𝑇𝑝= Θ(𝑇1) — no asymptotic work is wasted, so eﬀiciency stays bounded away from zero. It is a product of two quantities, hence additive in logs.
reduction: Cost is a product; optimality bounds it against the serial work.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Overhead Function
objects: An exact linear difference measuring wasted work.
structure: Includes communication, idling, and excess computation, all of which add — so the overhead is a sum of independent contributions. Modelling each term separately is what makes performance prediction tractable.
reduction: Overhead is a linear difference decomposing into additive sources.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Roofline Model
objects: A minimum of two linear bounds. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 11
structure: Piecewise linear in the arithmetic intensity, with a single kink at the machine balance point 𝑃peak/𝐵. Whether a kernel is compute- or memory-bound is decided by which side of that kink it falls on.
reduction: The roofline is a minimum of two linear functions.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Arithmetic Intensity
objects: A ratio determining the roofline position.
structure: Matrix multiplication has 𝐼= 𝑂(𝑛) and can be tiled to approach peak, while a vector operation has 𝐼= 𝑂(1) and is bandwidth-bound. That difference is the reason dense linear algebra dominates benchmark results. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 12
reduction: Intensity is a work-to-traﬀic ratio positioning the kernel on the roofline.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Little’s Law for Concurrency
objects: A stock–flow identity.
structure: Exactly linear and distribution-free, requiring only stability — so hiding latency requires proportionally more concurrency. It is the same identity as in queueing and in epidemiology’s prevalence relation.
reduction: The law is a linear stock–flow identity.
status: Exact linear. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 13

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Communication Time Model
objects: An aﬀine cost in message size.
structure: Latency 𝛼and inverse bandwidth 𝛽are the intercept and slope, so message aggregation trades many intercepts for one. The crossover size 𝛼/𝛽tells you when to combine messages.
reduction: Communication cost is aﬀine in message size. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 14

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: LogP Model
objects: A four-parameter refinement of entry 13.
structure: Separates latency, overhead, gap, and processor count, so the total cost is a linear combination of these with problem-dependent coeﬀicients. It captures pipelining limits that the two-parameter model misses.
reduction: LogP is a four-term linear cost model.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: BSP Superstep Cost
objects: A sum of computation, communication, and synchronisation.
structure: Exactly additive across the three phases, and the total program cost is the sum over supersteps — a linear accumulation. The bulk-synchronous structure is what makes cost composition additive at all.
reduction: BSP cost is an additive three-term model, summed over supersteps.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Bisection Bandwidth
objects: A minimum cut of the network graph.
structure: Exactly a graph min-cut, and by max-flow min-cut duality it bounds the achievable all-to-all through- put. It is the single most important network metric for communication-heavy workloads.
reduction: Bisection bandwidth is a min-cut; duality bounds throughput.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Network Diameter and Degree
objects: Two properties of the topology graph.
structure: The Moore bound relates them — a degree-𝑘diameter-𝑑graph has at most 𝑂(𝑘𝑑) nodes, a counting argument. Topologies trade degree against diameter, and the diameter is the distance matrix’s maximum entry.
reduction: Diameter is a distance matrix maximum; the Moore bound is a count.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Fat Tree Bandwidth
objects: A topology designed to keep the min-cut constant.
structure: Increasing link capacity toward the root keeps the bisection bandwidth proportional to the node count — so the cut value is designed rather than emergent. Tapered fat trees trade cost for reduced bisection.
reduction: The topology engineers the min-cut value.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Dragonfly Topology
objects: A hierarchical graph with small diameter.
structure: Two levels of all-to-all give diameter three at modest degree, and adaptive routing spreads load across paths — a flow assignment problem on the graph. It exploits high-radix switches to approach the Moore bound.
reduction: The topology is a hierarchical graph; routing is a flow assignment.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Collective Communication Cost
objects: A cost model for a structured communication pattern.
structure: The ring algorithm’s cost is exactly linear in 𝑝for latency and independent of 𝑝for bandwidth, so it is bandwidth-optimal. Recursive doubling gives log 𝑝latency instead, and the choice depends on where the message size sits relative to 𝛼/𝛽.
reduction: Collective cost is a linear model; algorithm choice optimises the trade.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Broadcast and Scatter Costs
objects: A tree-structured communication cost.
structure: Binomial tree broadcast costs log 𝑝steps, while scatter–allgather costs 2 log 𝑝latency but only 𝑚𝛽 bandwidth — the same two-regime structure as entry 20. Message size selects the algorithm.
reduction: Broadcast cost is a tree depth times a linear message cost.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Bandwidth–Latency Product
objects: A stock–flow product — Little’s law again.
structure: Exactly the number of bytes that must be outstanding to saturate the link, so deep pipelining is required on high-bandwidth long-latency networks. It sets the minimum buffer size.
reduction: The product is a stock–flow identity.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Communication–Computation Overlap
objects: A maximum rather than a sum.
structure: Perfect overlap replaces addition with maximum — a change from ℓ1 to ℓ∞composition, which is exactly the difference between serial and parallel resource use. Real overlap is partial, giving something between.
reduction: Overlap replaces a sum by a maximum.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Communication Lower Bound
objects: A geometric bound on data movement for matrix multiplication.
structure: The Loomis–Whitney inequality bounds the volume of a three-dimensional iteration space by the product of its three projections’ areas, so a working set of size 𝑀can cover only 𝑀3/2 operations. That geometric inequality gives the tile size √𝑀/3 and hence the bound — one of the most elegant results in the field, and it is pure geometry.
reduction: The bound is Loomis–Whitney on the iteration space’s projections.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Average Memory Access Time
objects: An aﬀine combination nested across levels.
structure: Each level’s penalty is the next level’s AMAT, so the total is a nested chain of aﬀine maps — a continued composition. Miss rates multiply down the hierarchy.
reduction: AMAT is a nested aﬀine composition.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Cache Miss Classification
objects: An additive attribution of misses.
structure: Measured by differencing against idealised caches, so the categories are defined by subtraction — approximately additive but not orthogonal. Coherence misses are the parallel-specific addition.
reduction: The categories are difference-based attributions.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: False Sharing Cost
objects: Coherence traﬀic from unrelated data sharing a line.
structure: The unit of coherence is the line, not the word, so the sharing pattern is determined by the address- to-line map — a coarsening. Padding to line boundaries is a change of the data layout that decouples the mapping.
reduction: False sharing arises from a coarsening of the address map.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Cache Coherence Protocol States
objects: A finite state machine per cache line.
structure: Exactly a labelled transition system, and its correctness is a reachability property — the invariant is that at most one cache holds a line in Modified state. Verification is model checking on the state graph.
reduction: Coherence is a finite state machine with a reachability invariant.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Directory Protocol Scalability
objects: A sharer set representation.
structure: A full bit vector costs 𝑝bits per line, so storage is quadratic in the machine size — limited sharer lists trade exactness for space. It is a sparse representation trade-off on a sharing matrix.
reduction: The directory is a sharing matrix; limited lists are a sparse approximation.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: NUMA Access Ratio
objects: A ratio of two access latencies. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 30
structure: The full latency structure is a matrix over node pairs, and placement optimisation minimises the traﬀic-weighted sum of its entries — a quadratic assignment problem. First-touch policy is a greedy heuristic for it.
reduction: NUMA placement minimises a traﬀic-weighted latency matrix contraction.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Memory Bandwidth per Core
objects: A per-core share of a shared resource.
structure: Bandwidth grows more slowly than core count, so the per-core share falls — this is the memory wall, and it moves kernels leftward on the roofline. It is a simple division with severe consequences. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 31
reduction: Per-core bandwidth is a shared resource division.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Cache-Oblivious Complexity
objects: An optimal transfer count achieved without tuning.
structure: Recursive divide-and-conquer is self-similar at every scale, so it automatically matches whatever cache sizes exist — the recursion’s scale invariance is what makes it oblivious. It is the same fractal argument as in cache-oblivious matrix multiplication.
reduction: Optimality follows from the recursion’s scale invariance.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: PRAM Work–Depth
objects: Brent’s theorem — a linear bound in two quantities.
structure: Exactly aﬀine in the work and the depth, so the two quantities fully characterise a computation’s parallel potential. It is the fundamental theorem of parallel algorithm analysis.
reduction: Brent’s bound is aﬀine in work and depth.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Parallelism and Span
objects: A ratio bounding useful processor count.
structure: Adding processors beyond 𝑊/𝐷gives no further speedup, since the critical path dominates — so the ratio is the maximum exploitable parallelism. The span is the longest path in the computation DAG.
reduction: Parallelism is a work-to-critical-path ratio.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Parallel Prefix (Scan)
objects: A cumulative application of an associative operator.
structure: Associativity permits a tree reduction and a downward sweep, giving 𝑂(log 𝑛) depth with 𝑂(𝑛) work — Blelloch’s algorithm. Scan is exactly a triangular linear operator when ⊕is addition, and the parallel algorithm is a factorisation of that triangular matrix into log 𝑛sparse factors.
reduction: Scan is a triangular operator factorised into log 𝑛sparse steps.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Parallel Reduction
objects: A tree contraction of an associative operator.
structure: Exactly a binary tree of pairwise combinations, so depth is logarithmic and work is linear. Floating- point addition is not truly associative, which is why reduction results depend on the tree shape — a genuine reproducibility issue caused by an algebraic assumption failing.
reduction: Reduction is a tree contraction; non-associativity of floating point breaks determinism.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Parallel Sorting Lower Bound
objects: A bound combining work and depth terms.
structure: The first term is the work bound divided by processors and the second is the unavoidable depth — exactly Brent’s structure. It is the sum of two independent constraints.
reduction: The bound is a sum of a work and a depth term.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Bitonic Sort Complexity
objects: A sorting network with a fixed comparison pattern.
structure: The comparison pattern is data-independent, so it is a fixed sequence of permutation-and-compare stages — a product of structured operators. That obliviousness makes it ideal for GPUs and for hardware, despite the extra log 𝑛factor.
reduction: The network is a fixed product of compare-exchange operators.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Matrix Multiplication (Cannon’s Algorithm)
objects: A systolic algorithm on a √𝑝× √𝑝processor grid.
structure: Initial skewing is a permutation of the block matrices, then each step is a local multiply and a cyclic shift — so the whole algorithm is a sequence of permutations and block products. It achieves the communication lower bound of entry 24, using 𝑂(𝑛2/√𝑝) words per processor.
reduction: Cannon’s algorithm is permutations plus block products; it attains the lower bound.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Parallel FFT
objects: A distributed butterfly network computation.
structure: The FFT is a factorisation of the DFT matrix into log 𝑛sparse factors, and the parallel version dis- tributes those factors — but the transpose steps require an all-to-all, which dominates the cost. Communication, not arithmetic, is the bottleneck.
reduction: The FFT factorises the DFT matrix; distribution makes the transpose dominant.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Domain Decomposition Surface-to-Volume
objects: A geometric scaling of the halo exchange.
structure: Computation scales with the subdomain volume and communication with its surface, so the ratio falls as subdomains grow — which is why weak scaling works better than strong. It is a pure geometry argument.
reduction: The ratio is a surface-to-volume geometric scaling.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Parallel Monte Carlo Eﬀiciency
objects: An embarrassingly parallel computation with a variance bound.
structure: Independent samples mean variances add, so the error falls as 1/ √ 𝑁regardless of how the samples are distributed — the estimator is a linear functional and the parallelism is free. Stream independence is the only correctness requirement.
reduction: Independent sampling makes the estimator a trivially decomposable sum.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Speculative Execution Gain
objects: An expected value — a linear combination of two outcomes.
structure: Exactly linear in the success probability, so speculation pays when 𝑝> 𝑐/(𝑔+ 𝑐). Branch predictors raise 𝑝, which is why their accuracy matters quadratically for deep pipelines.
reduction: Speculative gain is a linear expectation.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: CAP Theorem
objects: An impossibility result about three properties.
structure: A proof by contradiction using a partitioned execution — combinatorial rather than algebraic. It is stated as a trilemma but is really a statement about behaviour during partitions, since partitions cannot be forgone.
reduction: The theorem is a combinatorial impossibility; no linear structure applies.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: PACELC Extension
objects: A refinement adding the non-partitioned case.
structure: Makes explicit that the latency–consistency trade-off exists even without partitions — a second binary choice conditioned on the first. It is a decision tree, not a continuous trade-off.
reduction: The extension is a conditional binary classification.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: FLP Impossibility
objects: A bivalence argument on the space of executions.
structure: The proof constructs an infinite execution that never decides, by showing a bivalent configuration always has a bivalent successor — a topological connectivity argument on the configuration space. It is one of The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 45 the deepest results in the field and has no matrix formulation.
reduction: The proof is a connectivity argument on configuration space.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Byzantine Fault Tolerance Bound
objects: A counting condition on honest majorities.
structure: Two disjoint quorums of size 𝑛−𝑓must overlap in more than 𝑓nodes, which gives the bound by a counting argument. It is exactly a pigeonhole condition, and it appears again in entry 48.
reduction: The bound is a counting (pigeonhole) argument. The LKVexa Compendium — Calculus Edition 46

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Quorum Intersection
objects: An overlap condition on subsets.
structure: Exactly the inclusion–exclusion condition guaranteeing two quorums share a node, which is what makes consistency possible. Weighted quorums generalise it to a linear inequality on weights.
reduction: Intersection is an inclusion–exclusion inequality.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Paxos and Raft Round Complexity
objects: A message round count.
structure: The prepare and accept phases each cost one round trip, and stable leadership eliminates the first — an amortisation. The counting is combinatorial, and the correctness rests on quorum intersection.
reduction: Round counting is combinatorial; correctness rests on entry 48.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Lamport Logical Clock
objects: A monotone map from events to integers.
structure: Consistent with the happens-before partial order but not complete — it embeds a partial order into a total one, which necessarily loses information. Concurrent events get ordered arbitrarily.
reduction: The clock embeds a partial order into a total one, losing concurrency.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Vector Clock
objects: A vector of per-process counters, ordered componentwise.
structure: Exactly captures the partial order because the componentwise order on ℕ𝑛is the right structure — incomparable vectors correspond to concurrent events. The cost is 𝑂(𝑛) space per timestamp, which is the price of representing a partial order faithfully.
reduction: Vector clocks embed the causal partial order into the componentwise order on ℕ𝑛.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Consistent Hashing
objects: A mapping of keys onto a circular space.
structure: Placing nodes and keys on a ring means adding a node only steals from its successor — a locality property of the circular order. Virtual nodes smooth the load by sampling the ring more finely, reducing the variance of the partition sizes.
reduction: Consistent hashing exploits locality of a circular ordering.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: CRDT Convergence
objects: A join-semilattice.
structure: Convergence follows because the merge operation is a least upper bound in a lattice, so applying updates in any order reaches the same supremum. It is an algebraic guarantee — replicas converge without coordination because the algebra forces it.
reduction: CRDTs converge because merges are lattice joins.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Two-Phase Commit Blocking
objects: A protocol with a state in which progress is impossible.
structure: Participants that have voted but not learned the outcome cannot safely proceed — an uncertainty state in the protocol’s state machine. Three-phase commit adds a state to break it, at the cost of extra rounds and weaker fault assumptions.
reduction: Blocking is an uncertainty state in the protocol automaton.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Load Imbalance Factor
objects: A ratio of maximum to mean — an ℓ∞over ℓ1 comparison.
structure: Parallel time is governed by the maximum, not the mean, so imbalance directly multiplies the runtime. It is exactly the ratio of two norms of the work vector, and reducing it is a load balancing (partitioning) problem.
reduction: Imbalance is an ℓ∞/ℓ1 norm ratio of the work vector.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Work Stealing Bound
objects: Brent’s bound achieved by a randomised scheduler.
structure: Randomised stealing achieves the work–depth bound in expectation, with the steal count bounded by 𝑂(𝑝𝐷) — a probabilistic argument on the number of failed steals. The bound is tight up to constants.
reduction: Work stealing achieves the aﬀine work–depth bound in expectation.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: List Scheduling Bound
objects: A worst-case approximation ratio.
structure: Graham’s bound follows from two lower bounds — total work over 𝑝and the critical path — and the schedule cannot exceed their sum. It is exactly a sum of two linear lower bounds, and the factor two comes from combining them.
reduction: The bound sums two linear lower bounds.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Checkpoint Interval (Young–Daly)
objects: A minimiser of a sum of two opposing costs.
structure: Checkpoint overhead falls as the interval grows while expected lost work rises, so minimising 𝐶/𝑇+ 𝑇/(2 MTBF) gives the square root — the same structure as the economic order quantity. It is a one-variable convex minimisation.
reduction: The interval minimises a sum of a reciprocal and a linear term.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: System Mean Time Between Failures
objects: Failure rates adding across components.
structure: Rates add for series systems, so the reciprocal times combine harmonically — exactly the same rule as parallel resistances and effective population size. At exascale this makes failures a routine event rather than an exception.
reduction: Failure rates add; MTBFs combine harmonically.

chapter: Parallel and Distributed Computing — Calculus Edition
title: Energy–Delay Product and Power Scaling
objects: A multiplicative power model and a product metric.
structure: Since 𝑓∝𝑉roughly, power scales as the cube of frequency and energy per operation as the square of voltage — so slowing down saves energy superlinearly. The energy–delay product is a product of two competing quantities, and minimising it is a log-space optimisation where the two log-linear trends cross.
reduction: Power is multiplicative; the EDP optimum is where two log-linear trends balance.
